## XII.

Constat itaque Paracelsistarum, Weigelianorum, Mysticorum, Quakerorum & cæterorum, qui communi illuminatorum nomine vocari solent, opiniones fanaticas in eo conspirare, quod præter corpus & animam rationalem sit in homine substantialis quædam pars divinitus ipsi, &, ut plerique non dissimulant, ex ipsa divina essentia concessa. Eandem doctrinam de tribus partibus hominis satis prolixe explicat Felgenhawer im *Vorhoff/ im heiligen und Allerheiligsten am Tempel GOttes*: cujus fanatici libelli lectiones singulæ singularum partium rationes & Fanaticorum de iis somnia satis declarant. Conferri etiam meretur Bartholomaei Sclei *anständige allgemeine GOttes Lehre*/ nec non das *Buch des Zeugnisses des verborgenen Ackerschatzes*/ cujus Autor se ipsum vocat HIEL, das *einwesige Leben GOttes*/ ut & des von GOtt hocherleuchteten Matthes Weyer *gründlicher Unterricht*/ & similia a furiis illis conscripta librorum portenta, indigna sane quibus legendis quis bonas ac irrevocabiles horas perdat.

## XIII.

Cæterum hæc de triplici hominis parte doctrina principem in ipsorum Matæologia locum obtinet. Hanc enim non modo Christianismi totius, sed omnis in universum sapientiæ, quæ in cælo & terra est, fundamentum continere ineptissime jactitat Autor des *Vorhoffs* Cap. XII. At vero si quem forte lateat se quinque habere sensus, vel quæ sit visus vel auditus aut reliquorum natura, anne propterea statuendum, quod isti munere suo fungi nequeant? Non equidem puto. Interim Andreas Christophorus Rafelius hoc dogma tantis extollit encomiis ut non vereatur in *Der Neujahrs Posaune* hunc in modum de eo loqui: *Das ist eigentlich der rechte Grund-Fels/ und das gewisse Fundament/ darauff das Hauß unsers Christenthums soll gesetzet/ geleget und fundiret werden/ soll es bestehen: und daraus alles predigen/ lesen/ schreiben/ GOttes Wort hören/ singen/ beten/ gute Wers*

understood by this Spirit or spiritual substance, it is best to hear their own testimony. The <term>Shoemaker-Theologian Jacob Boehme</term> understands by "spirit" the internal spiritual man, a spiritual substance that constitutes the third essential part of man, existing in all people—both the faithful and the unfaithful—which was weakened by the fall of the first man but not completely extinguished. See *The Great Mystery*, chapter 20. <term>Barclay</term> explains the opinion of the Quakers concerning this third part in his *Apology for the True Christian Religion*, theses 5 and 6. They certainly agree with the others in this: that all people everywhere, as many as come into the world, have within themselves, besides a body and a soul, a spiritual substance implanted by God himself to govern them in spiritual matters, just as reason directs them in natural matters. Barclay says this spiritual substance is the <term>vehicle of God</term> <gloss>Latin: vehiculum Dei</gloss>, in which the eternal Word (which was with God and was God) exists and immediately dwells—a real and spiritual substance. He also claims this is the internal <term>substantial seed</term> in our hearts, which subsists even in the hearts of the wicked, even when they sin mortally. All of them, therefore, conspire in the idea that besides the organic body (equipped with a vegetative and sensitive soul) and the rational soul itself, there is a certain third substance really distinct from the rational soul. In relation to spiritual things, this substance is almost the same kind of principle for understanding and desiring as the rational soul is in relation to those things we know naturally.

### XI.

The origin of this spiritual substance is not clearly explained by Barclay or his associates, who craftily disguise it. We saw in section 4 that the Weigelians and Boehmists do not hide its divine origin. Indeed, <term>Abraham von Franckenberg</term> professes this in so many words in *Know Thyself*, page 110: <note>original: "Der ewige Mensch ist aus dem ewig-sprechendem Wort Gottes / aus der Licht-Welt / aus Gottes eigenem Wesen"</note> "The eternal man is from the eternally-speaking Word of God, from the world of light, from God's own essence." And on page 52: "If I were of another matter than from God himself, how then would I be his child?"

<summary>This page defines the "Spirit" as a third substance or "substantial seed" dwelling in all humans, which Quakers call the "vehicle of God" and Boehmists link to God's own essence.</summary>

# Book Six

<margin>The sea and the hidden rivers</margin>
the sea receives an entrance, as it holds just as much space there; or perhaps even more, since the upper regions had to be shared with so many living creatures. Desolate places, even without an inhabitant, float more freely on the waves. Who would prevent the waters from fluctuating there and being driven by the winds, which every interval of the earth and every space of air creates? Therefore, a storm, having arisen greater than usual, can shake a part of the earth, having been driven more vehemently. For among us, too, many places that had been far from the sea were suddenly struck by its approach, and the waves invaded villas placed within view, which were heard from afar. There, too, the sea can retreat and uncover the lower depths, which does not happen without a movement of the substance. I do not believe you will hesitate for long to believe that there are subterranean rivers and a hidden sea. For whence do these things spring? Whence do they come to us, if not because the origin of moisture is contained within? Come, when you see the <term>Tigris</term> <gloss>a great river in Western Asia</gloss> interrupted, drying up in the middle of its course—and it is not turned away entirely, but diminishes little by little as the waters become invisible, and then is consumed—where do you think it goes, if not into the dark places of the earth? Especially since you see it emerge again, no smaller than the one that had flowed before. What of when you see the <term>Alpheus</term> <gloss>a river in Greece</gloss>, celebrated by the poets in Achaia, submerged, and then pouring forth in Sicily, after having crossed the sea, the most pleasant fountain of <term>Arethusa</term> <gloss>a nymph transformed into a fountain</gloss>? Moreover, you are not unaware that among the opinions held by those who narrate the flooding of the <term>Nilus</term> <gloss>the Nile river</gloss>, one is that it breaks forth and increases from the earth, not from waters above, but from those returned from the depths. Indeed, I myself <note>referring to the historian's own experience or report</note> have seen two centurions whom Nero Caesar, a man who loves truth as much as he loves other virtues, had sent to investigate the source of the Nile.

<summary>Seneca discusses subterranean waters, the connectivity of hidden seas, and the mysterious sources of rivers like the Tigris and the Nile.</summary>

De lactuca. Ca. XXII.
Lactuca vt dicit Isidorus ex lactei humoris exuberantia est vocata. vel quia nutricientes mulieres lacte implet. hec in viris veneris motum arcet cuius duplex est species. scilicet domestica et agrestis qua feralia vocamus. quod dorsum eius aculeos habet duros ad modum ferre. vt dicit Isidorus libro. xvii. capitulo ultimo. de qua dicit Plinius in dietis. lactuca agrestis domestice in forma est similis. sed longiores habet frondes. subtiliores. asperiores. et minus virides. propter sue humiditatis paruitatem. et ideo multum est amaritudinis et ponticitatis respectu illius que domestica est. quia maioris est caloris et siccitatis. et ideo multi dicunt quod menstrua puocat et humores crudos expellit. vt dicit Dyascorides. lactuca pro domestica frigida est et humida secundum gradum et in neutra qualitate excedit modum. et ideo eius usus grauisui medicine. subtilibus subam et marie qui erit recens. et ideo cito digeritur et stomachi arsuram et morsuram et colera rubea sedat. sanguinis ebullitionem refrigerat. infomnietate placat. capitis dolorem et fumo colerico sanat. lac in mulieribus multiplicat et semen in viris generat augumentar. et accidit propter bonitatem sanguinis que gignit in pfecta quantitate. et in pfecta etate sed quando antiquatur et indurat minuitur eius humiditas et amaricat. et vsu eius sanguis pessimus generatur. virtus visina inde deficit et debilitatur. cuius causa est sensus animalis mortificatio. quod cum sua ponticitate ipsum suffocat naturale. et ideo talis lactuca generare voletib. maxime est nociua. nam materia gelat. coagulat seminale. et precipue semen eius si in cibo aut in potu sepe assumatur. De lappa. Ca. XXIII.
Lappa est herba habens folia lata et spissa circa terram habens in sumitatibus bastularum quedam capitella spinosa et aculeata sed recurua que vestibus transeuntium solent adherere. Vnde dicit Isidorus libro. xvii. lappa est dicta eo quod habeat caulez in gente terram dispositam et grecis philatropos vocatur. quod vestibus hominum adhereat ob asperitatem sui. et nascit iuxta muros. et ob philatropos. i. amans hominem. quia quadam affectione videat homis adherere vestibus. # Book XVII

<note>A decorative initial L begins the section.</note> The collector gathers the barks of the lentisk or mastic tree at the end of spring, cuts them, and cleanses the area and places clean cloths underneath so that nothing falls onto the ground. Therefore, that which is clear and clean and white is to be selected; that which admits foreign matter and is dark is to be thrown away. It cleanses and purifies the brain and makes one expectorate mucus. It assists the digestive power and attenuates viscosity. Liquefied on a warm tile, it marvelously solidifies all broken gems, etc. Pliny also says, as does Dioscorides, that the lentisk is a thorny tree with a deep root, divided into many parts, having fruit like the myrtle, but smaller and red. When it is mature, its rough wool inside the skin and its juice heal the flux of women.

<note>A decorative initial D begins the section.</note> On the Lily, Ch. XXI
The lily is a herb of milky flower, whose whiteness shines among the foliage, though a gold color glows within. Regarding the lily, Dioscorides and Platearius say: The lily is hot and moist. And one is wild, another domestic, and one bears a purple flower, and another a white one, which is efficacious, and another a saffron or purple one. Moreover, the lily is a maturative; therefore, it avails against abscesses if it is crushed with lard. Also, it possesses a softening quality; therefore, it avails against the hardness of the spleen if its juice is mixed with old oil and well-incorporated, and the region of the spleen is anointed with it. Also, it possesses a cleansing force; therefore, it avails for beautifying the face if its powder is mixed with rose water and the face is washed with it. Also, it is mitigative; therefore, its leaves, boiled and applied, avail for places that have been burned. The root does the same if crushed with oil and applied. Also, it is extractive and resolutive, and it induces the menstrual purge. Also, it possesses a repressive quality against tumors; therefore, it avails against abscesses and inflammatory redness if the root is crushed with oil and applied. <note>Thus</note> Dioscorides. Regarding the lily, Pliny says: "The roots of the lily are ennobled in many ways by their flower. For, carried with wine, it heals the bite of a serpent and avails against foulness and poison. Boiled in wine and mixed with oil, it dissolves corns and nodes of the feet. It restores hair to burned places. Boiled in wine with honey added, it aids the veins or nerves of fish <note>likely an error for "nerves/tendons of the body"</note>. Boiled leaves in wine heal wounds. The seed applied with sulfur is good for the sacred fire. The flower and leaves assist the needs of ulcers." <note>Thus</note> Pliny, Book XX, Ch. XII. Also in the same book, Ch. V: "The lily rose is the first in nobility, and from the kinship of the flower, a noble ointment or oil is made, which is called oil of lilies. Thus also from roses, rose oil is accustomed to be made." From the root proceeds a stalk sometimes three cubits long; then from its summit the flower hangs down, repairing and dilating itself from a narrow point into breadth in the manner of a little bell, inverted in the circuit of the lips, having within as if a thin thread containing in itself the seed, yellow in the middle. Wherefore the lily lacks nothing of glory, as it is abundant in the effectiveness of the fragrance of color and odor. Its color is threefold: white, red, and purple. <note>Thus</note> Pliny, Book XX, Ch. V. But the lily has a root with many bulbs assisting it, like garlic, as Aristotle says in the book *On Vegetables*. And in each bulb is the seed-germ, and therefore in every place it grows where it is planted. Regarding this, look there and in the same place regarding garlic in the letter A. Aristotle says furthermore to the aforementioned: "The stalk of the lily is knotty and curves into the ground, and it is multiplied and propagated by seed and root, and if you do not find the bulb immediately within a few days, you will find it, and from every node of its stalk it emits a little bulb as if that were of its tunics or of the bulbs, namely bulbs of the root, and this is very marvelous." Also in the same place it follows: "The flowers of the lily are first green, then they become white. And if the stalk is cut off entirely from the root, because all the humor of the stalk is included, the natural heat in the marrow turns itself to the upper part of the stalk and digests the matter of the flower itself, and then the little flower expands and becomes white, the humor having first been digested." And therefore, as poets have compared the lily to the human intellect, it solicits at the end for the eternal. Also in the same place, it is said that the lily has no seed-reason in the seed and root, and it differs and goes further, like garlic, and has a seed-reason in many places. Regarding this, look there and regarding garlic and onions in the letter A and L. The lily, moreover, with the stalk newly cut with the flower, if inserted into clay soil, keeps its flower in freshness for a long time. The lily flower, when it is whole and intact, remains long and smells sweetly. Broken by the hands and rubbed, it stinks much. The flower itself, with the seed, holds it in place of fruit. The whole power which the lily has in the stalk and root, it shows in the head, namely in the flower and in the seed. And the more the flower rises high on the stalk, the more humbly the head inclines. Its flower is, moreover, exterior and flat, sweet to the touch, and round in form, delightful and joyful to the sight. Internally, it is sprinkled with golden grains in its cavity, which tincture like saffron. And seven little stalks sustain these tincture grains. Wherefore, it is composed of very white leaves simultaneously touching each other, and from seven grains, it places its seed in the place of fruit with marvelous beauty, and by the benefit of the flower, it is protected by the tenderness of the seed from the harm of cold air.

# Red metals, however, are different in their color and mixture from those already mentioned: as we have sufficiently shown when we dealt with the colors of metals.

Iron has a specific nature of its own beyond the other elements. Let us therefore speak of the composition of **copper** <note>original: "eris"; here referring to copper or its alloys</note>, assuming what has long been proven: that every metal is composed of **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>. Let us suppose that the quicksilver is good and not dreggy or muddy, yet not entirely purged of external moisture. Let the substance of the sulfur be dreggy, burning, and partially ignited, just as it is mixed with the quicksilver in substance and quality. For now, without doubt, it turns the quicksilver red; because both are not fully refined, they cannot mix well. Then it creates copper, which is not of an entirely good mixture. Because of this, much of it is consumed and much evaporates in the fire, since the sulfur is partially burnt. Therefore, some parts of the quicksilver are purified more than others, and the superfluous moisture in them is consumed; in those parts, it will seem to have **veins of gold**. In other parts, however, where it is less "digested" <term>digestio; the natural "cooking" or ripening of minerals in the earth</term>, it will be scaly, base, and earthy due to the burning. We have clearly found this diversity in the copper found in the German regions, in the place called <margin>Goslar</margin> **Goslar**. Therefore, this copper is esteemed better than all others, as if having veins of gold mixed in. It is not improbable that the sulfur of that copper is mixed with red **arsenic** in some quantity, and therefore the sulfur of that metal is more "burning" than that of others.

<margin>Copper is turned into brass</margin>
Now we know the material of copper: it is a metal made from quicksilver, having a bit more than is proper through the mixture of burning sulfur, which leads it to a red form. The nature by which sulfur is "burning" has been sufficiently determined in what preceded. **Arsenic**, when calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to remove volatile substances</note>, turns black from red; but afterward, when **sublimated** <note>turned into vapor and then solidified</note> in an **alutel** <note>original: "alutel"; a pear-shaped vessel used in alchemy for sublimation</note>, which is a covered vessel with a high neck as we have often said, it returns white like snow. If such calcination and sublimation are repeated often, it becomes very white and very sharp. Because of this sharpness, when joined to copper by melting, it penetrates it and turns it white. However, if it stays in the fire a long time, the copper will "breathe out" the arsenic, and then the original color of the copper returns, as is easily proven in alchemical works. Those who work much with copper in our regions—namely in Paris, Cologne, and other places where I have been and seen experiments—turn copper into **brass** <note>original: "auricalcum"; orichalcum</note> by using the powder of a stone called **calamine** <note>zinc ore</note>. When the stone evaporates, a dim splendor still remains, inclining somewhat toward the appearance of gold. To make it whiter and thus more similar to the yellow of gold, they mix in a little **tin**. Because of this, the brass loses much of the ductility <note>the ability to be hammered thin or drawn into wire</note> of the copper. Those who wish to deceive and induce a splendor similar to gold "bind" the stone so that it remains longer in the copper in the fire and does not evaporate quickly.

It is "bound" by **glass oil**: fragments of glass are toasted and turned into powder, which is sprinkled into the crucible over the copper after the calamine has been put in. Then the melted glass floats over the copper and does not allow the stone or its virtue to evaporate; instead, it reflects the vapor of the stone back into the copper. Thus, for a while, it strongly purges the copper and burns away the dreggy materials in it. Eventually, however, even the glass oil evaporates, and then the virtue of the stone evaporates; but the brass is made much more splendid than it would be without it. He who intends to make it resemble gold even more repeats these purgings with the glass oil often, and in place of tin, he takes **silver** and mixes it with the brass. This makes it so ruddy and yellow in color that many believe it to be gold, though in truth it remains in the species of copper.

<margin>Hermes</margin>
**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says that if powdered **tutty** <note>original: "tuchia"; zinc oxide collected from smelting furnaces</note>, whether white or red, is added to melted copper, it converts it to the color of gold. What tutty is will be discussed in the following book where we deal with intermediate substances. But let it suffice here that by the "burning" of the tutty, the earthiness is removed and it purges the copper of its superfluous moisture; therefore, it will then be more beautiful. However, the virtue of the tutty also evaporates through fire if it stands in the fire for a long time. Unless another "medicine" <note>an additive or reagent</note> is used, the tutty will evaporate, and then the original color of the copper returns. Hermes also says, and experience agrees, that if such copper is sprinkled with vinegar or the urine of a virgin male child, the virtue of the urine or vinegar will penetrate the substance of the copper and turn it green. If, however, the copper is placed by itself over pressed grape skins, it will be converted into an excellent, shining green color by the vapor of the wine alone. But if **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic ore</note> or arsenic is brought near this color, especially if it is burnt, it destroys the green and induces a dark, earthy color inclining toward opacity. The cause of this is easily shown from what has been said. For salt is opening, and therefore it opens the substance of the copper, especially if it has been hammered into thin plates; then the sharp vapor of the vinegar or urine ignites it, which comes from the overly-ignited sulfur. Because of this, the light earthy moisture joined to it, which is ignited, takes on that greenness, much like the hottest and worst bile which physicians call the "rust of copper." Since at first the vapor is not as sharp as the vapor of joined wine, it does not induce such an intense redness, and so the gold color remains pleasant. Orpiment, however, is excellently "burning," and so when it approaches a substance colored this way, it burns the small amount of moisture in it; then what remains is the earthy opacity. This is the same way that burnt bile leaves behind a "melancholic ash," according to medical experience. Thus, so much has been said concerning the nature and effects of copper.

# Rubea autem metalla in colore admixtione diuersa sunt a dictis: sicut satis ostendimus cum de coloribus metallorum ageret. 

Habet autem ferrum secundum se specialem determinationem extra alia elementa. Dicamus igitur eris compositionem supponentes que iam dudum probata sunt omne metallum ex sulphure componi & argento viuo. Ponamus igitur argentum viuum esse bonum non feculentum siue lutulentum, no[n] tamen ab humore extraneo omnino purgatum: substantiam sulphuris esse feculentam & adurentem & in parte accensam: sicut argento viuo per substantiam & qualitates commisceri. nunc enim absque dubio conuertit ipsum in ruborem & non poterit eidem propter utriusque non plenam subtiliationem bene misceri / tunc efficiet es quod non est omnino bone mixtionis. propter quod multa fer inde resoluitur / & multum euaporat in igne quia cum sulphur in parte incensum est. ideo quedam partes argenti viui amplius quam alie purificatur & consumit in eis superfluum humidum & in illis partibus videbitur habere venas auri. In alijs autem ubi minus digestum est erit scalosum & ignobile & terrestre propter adustionem / & hanc diuersitatem in cupro quod inuenitur in theutonicis partibus in loco qui <margin>Goslaria</margin> goslaria vocatur expresse inuenimus. & ideo etiam hoc cuprum melius omnibus alijs estimatur tanquam venas auri habens immixtas / & non est improbabile quin sulphur illi eris sit mictu cum arsenico rubeo in aliqua quantitate. & ideo sit magis adurens sulphur illius metalli quam alterius.

<margin>Cupru[m] i[n] auricalcu[m] vertit[ur]</margin>
Nunc igitur scimus materiam eris / quoniam est metallum ex argento viuo plusquam oportet aliquantulum habens per commixtionem adurentis sulphuris ad formam ruboris deducti / ex qua autem natura sulphur sit adurens in precedentibus satis determinatum est. Arsenicum autem calcinatum sit quidem nigrum ex rubeo / sed postea & sublimatum in alutel quod est vas opertum cum collo alto vt sepius diximus reuertitur album ad instar niuis / & si sepius iterentur talis calcinatio & sublimatio tunc efficitur multum album & acutissimum / & ex acumine eri coniunctum liquando penetrat in ipsum & conuertit in candorem. si tamen diu stet in igne es expirabit arsenicum & tunc redit pristinus color cupri sicut de facili probatur in alchimicis. Hi autem qui in cupro multum operantur in nostris partibus parisius videlicet & colonie & in alijs locis in quibus fui & vidi experiri uertunt cuprum in auricalcum per puluerem lapidis qui calamina vocatur. & cum euaporat lapis adhuc remanet splendor obscurus declinans aliquantulum ad auri speciem. Vt autem albius efficiatur & ita citrinitati auri magis sit simile immiscet aliquantulum de stagno. propter que etiam auricalcum multum de ductibilitate cupri amittit. Et illi qui decipere volunt & splendorem similem auro inducere ligant lapidem: ita quod diutius remanet in ere in igne no[n] euaporans cito ab ere. 

Ligatur autem per oleum vitri tostatur enim fragmenta vitri & conuertuntur in puluerem & spargitur in testam super es postquam immissa est calamina / & tunc vitrum piectum enatat super es & non sinit euaporare lapidem & lapidis virtutem: sed reflectit vaporem lapidis in es. & sic dumque fortiter purgat es & adurunt in eo materie feculente. Tandem tamen euaporat etiam oleum vitri. & tunc euaporat virtus lapidis / sed auricalcum efficitur multo splendidius quam esset sine illo. Qui aut[em] adhuc amplius assimilare auro intendit. has purgationes per opesum & vitri oleum sepius iterat / & loco Auricalci stagni ponit argentum & immiscet auricalco. Et hoc efficit ita rutilum cum colore citrinum quod multi credunt ipsum esse aurum cum in veritate adhuc remaneat sit in specie eris. 

<margin>Hermes</margin>
Hermes autem dicit quod si eri liquefacto tuchia puluerizata siue sit tuchia alba siue rubea quod ipsum in colorem auri conuertit. Quid autem sit tuchia in sequenti libro ubi de medijs aget dicetur. sed hic sufficiat est quod tuchie adustione assumitur terrestreitas & purgat ab ere superfluum humidum ipsius. & ideo tunc erit pulchrius. tamen & virtus tuchie euaporat per ignem si diu steterit in igne. & ideo nisi aliud medicamen fuerit euaporabit tuchia. & tunc erit pristinus color cupri. Dicit etiam Hermes cum quo concordant experta. quod si es tale aspersum super acetum vel vrinam pueri masculi virginis locet penetrabit virtus urine siue aceti substantiam eris & conuertet ipsum in virorem. Si autem iterum per se solum es locetur super racemos expressos solo vapore vini conuertetur in optimum colorem viridem plucentez. Si autem huic colori auripigmentum siue arsenicum approximatur & precipue adustum condemnando destruit virorem & inducit colorem fuscum terrestrem ad opacitatem declinantem. Huius causa autem ex dictis facile manifestatur. est enim sal aperitiuum / & ideo aperit cupri substantiam seque si in tenues laminas deductum sit / & tunc vapor acetus aceti vel urine incendit ipsum: quod tamen est a sulphure nimis accenso. propter quod humidum terrestre adiunctum leue quod est ignitum in ipso virore accipit sicut colera calidissima & pessima que est sicut erugo eris vt dicunt medici. Quoniam autem primo vapor non est adeo acutus sicut vapor vini coniuncti / tunc non ita intensam inducit rubedinem. & ideo manet auri color placidus. Auripigmentum autem est excellen[ter] adurens & ideo cum hoc approximat substantie sic colorate comburet modicum humidum quod est in ipso. & tunc manet quod est terrestre opacum. per eundem modum quo etiam colera adusta relinquit cinerem melancolicum accidentalem calidissime melancolie secundum experta medicine. Tanta igitur de eris natura & effectibus dicta sunt.

He shifts from discussing the skepticism of the audience to explaining the specific administrative circumstances that led to him standing in the speaker's chair today: the primary official, Johannes Cornerus, is incapacitated by illness.</meta>

<header>Dissertation on loathing & hatred</header>

For, against my will—I do not lie—and **beyond expectation and hope** <note>Greek original: καὶ παρὰ δόξαν καὶ ἐλπίδα</note>, contrary to hope and opinion, I am drawn forward, I who by no means deemed myself worthy of such **HONOR**. For I know, and know well, nor do I deny, that those who now preside over this University and its Colleges, who exercise the public and professorial tongue with praise, and who have offered their services to this present proceeding, could have brought more reason and authority to persuasion, more weight and efficacy to moving the heart, and more elegance and beauty to delighting the ear. I do not deny it, I say; I praise this judgment willingly and **with both thumbs** <note>original: "utroque pollice," a Roman idiom meaning to give full and enthusiastic approval, derived from the amphitheater where spectators used their thumbs to signal a gladiator’s fate</note>; indeed, I do not blush to add my own opinion to this; I do not refuse it.

But since the Reverend, Most Distinguished, and Eminent Man, Lord **JOHANNES CORNERUS** <note>Johannes Cornerus (1597–1680) was a prominent theologian and official at the University of Jena</note>, Doctor of Sacred Theology, Dean and Canon of the same Faculty and of the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Keeper of the Seal and primary Executor for the Most Reverend Archbishop of Mainz and Prince-Elector, our most merciful Lord, and Ordinary Vice-Chancellor of this our University—who, due to adverse health, is now attending to a **serious illness** <note>original: "morbum sonticum," a specific legal and medical term for an illness so severe it legally excuses a person from fulfilling their duties or appearing in court</note>, and for that reason is unable to perform himself what would otherwise be his duty—has seen fit that something be granted to me also in this proceeding; and since the Philosophical College—whose leaders I once felt to be my own teachers, and whom I still cherish with a mindful and grateful spirit—has commanded me to grant the **PETITION**, and has ordered that I should make the Candidates (whom I love for their singular gifts of mind) masters of their **WISH**; the Will of this man has now been a law to me. His Authority has stood for my reason. Both of these so stirred me in my idleness and pushed me in my hesitation that, although I am conscious of my own insignificance and well know how **scanty is my furniture** <note>original: "curta supellex," a metaphor from the Roman satirist Persius referring to a lack of mental resources or learning; literally "a short supply of household goods"</note>, I nevertheless did not hesitate to ascend this chair and carry out the duty entrusted to me. <meta>This page continues the biography of the physician and alchemist Nicolas Barnaud. It follows a discussion of the satires and theological accusations leveled against him, specifically regarding the authorship of controversial works during his time in Geneva.</meta>

### 5. Nicholas Barnaud,

which was published under the title *The Genevan Ape* <note>original: *Le Magot Génévois*</note> in 1613. However, since this work—as Marchand proves—is a satire on the Synod of Montpellier and the Reformed <note>Protestant</note> church in general, it deserves no credit. Meanwhile, it is certain that Barnaud was in close contact with Faustus Socinus <note>a prominent Italian theologian and founder of Socinianism, which rejected the Trinity</note>, who also dedicated his *Defense of his Disputation on the passage in the seventh chapter of Romans* <note>original Latin: *Defensionem Disputationis suae de loco VII. Cap. ad Rom.*</note> from the year 1595 to him. At that time, Barnaud had already translated Socinus's work *On the Authority of Holy Scripture* <note>original Latin: *de auctoritate scripturae sacrae*</note> into French and published his translation in 1592.

He resided in Geneva between 1575 and 1599, but moved to Leiden in the latter year, and in 1601 to Gouda, where he presumably died. This is everything known about him, and his name would likely have been forgotten by posterity—neither remembered as a physician nor as a friend of Socinus—had he not kept his memory alive among the lovers of the **Great Art** <term>Great Art; a traditional name for Alchemy, specifically the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone</term> through various alchemical writings, which he seems to have written especially in the final years of his life. These, along with his other writings, are as follows:

*Wake-up Call for the French and their Neighbors* <note>original French: *Reveil Matin des François et de leurs Voisins*</note> by Eusebius Philadelphus, Cosmopolitan, in the form of a dialogue. Similarly, lead is turned into tin by granulating the lead, washing the granules often with false water <note>original: "aqua falsa"</note>, and cementing it with a moderate fire <note>original: "igni modico"</note>, and finally reducing it. Paracelsus, in book 7 of his work on the transmutation of things, teaches how to do this through the cementation of plates of <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> and <term>Oil</term> <gloss>alchemical symbol for oil</gloss>. Conversely, tin turns into lead by calcining the tin often and administering a strong fire to it so that it may separate more quickly and the dross may be removed. In the same way, it is not very difficult to change LEAD into COPPER by way of cementation with vitriol; our friend performed an experiment of this matter not long ago and gifted us with a portion of this artificial copper.

Finally, and in conclusion of this chapter, we wish to append the words of an anonymous author, which are found in Chapter 14 of the <term>Magia Naturalis</term> <gloss>Natural Magic</gloss> by Wolffgang Hildebrandus, New Edition, page 764, under the title: "A non-entity in the transformation of metals / is the reversal of imperfect metals into other imperfect ones / such as iron into copper et cetera," since they are diametrically opposed to the other authors contained in this chapter; the same words are as follows:

Grind the antimony small and sublime it with half as much <term>salarmoniac</term> <gloss>sal ammoniac</gloss>. Put what has sublimed into a glass retort and drive it over into a receiver for a third time. Separate the <term>feces</term> <gloss>dregs</gloss> from it each time. Finally, sweeten the <term>salarmoniac</term> well away from it and <term>reverberate</term> <gloss>roast/calcine</gloss> the material of the antimony in a well-sealed vessel with a gentle fire, not driven too strongly, until it becomes like cinnabar ore. When that has happened, pour a strong distilled wine-vinegar over it and extract its <term>rubedinem</term> <gloss>redness</gloss>. Draw off the vinegar until a powder remains at the very last. This must happen in a <term>bad unser lieben Frauen</term> <gloss>bain-marie/water bath</gloss>. Then extract it again with <term>spiritu vini</term> <gloss>spirit of wine</gloss> so that the <term>feces</term> come away from it; then you have the extraction clean and clear.

When that has also happened, put this <term>spiritum vini</term> into a glass flask along with the extraction, add a little of the <term>tincturæ corallorum</term> <gloss>tincture of coral</gloss> and the <term>quintæ essentiæ</term> <gloss>fifth essence</gloss> of rhubarb. Give a person three or four drops of it. It provides gentle <term>sedes</term> <gloss>stools/bowel movements</gloss> and purges without any tearing, provided you have handled it rightly in the preparation. It makes for a lightness of the spirit and is a good medicine for all those who desire subtle bowel movements.

However, it might well astonish a physician how this medicine could provide gentle <term>sedes</term>, because antimony is otherwise a penetrating, tearing substance, and rhubarb is added to it, which by itself also has a purging power. Let him not be astonished, then, for the antimony is killed by such means

Antimonium, das reibe klein, und sublimire es mit halb so schwer Salarmoniac, was sublimirt hat thue in eine Glaß-Retorten, und treibs herüber in eine Vorlage zum dritten mahl, die Feces scheide jederzeit davon, letzlich süße das Salarmoniac wohl davon ab, und reverberire die Materiam des Antimonii wohl verschlossen mit gelindem Feuer nicht zu starck getrieben, biß sie werde wie ein Cinnober-Erz; wann das geschehen, so geuß einen starcken destillirten Wein-Eßig darauf, und extrahire seine Rubedinem, den Eßig zeug ab, biß zum letzten ein Pulver bleibet, das muß im Bad unser lieben Frauen geschehen, dann mit Spiritu Vini abermahls extrahirt, daß die Feces davon kommen, so hast du die Extraction rein und klar.

Wann das auch geschehen, so thue diesen Spiritum Vini in einen Glaß-Kolben, mit samt der Extraction, thue darzu ein wenig der Tincturæ Corallorum, und der Quintæ Essentiæ von der Rhebarbar, gieb einem Menschen davon ein drey oder vier Tropffen, giebt gelinde Sedes, und purgirt ohn einiges Reissen, wann du recht damit bist umgangen in der Präparation, macht Leichterung des Gebüts, und ist eine gute Artzney allen denen, so da begehren subtile Stuhl-Gänge.

Es möchte aber wohl einen Artzt verwundern, wie diese Artzney gelinde Sedes geben könte, weil das Antimonium sonsten eine durchdringende reißende Materia ist, und die Rhebarbar ihm zugegeben wird, welche per se auch eine purgirende Kraft hat, der lasse sich nicht wundern, dann das Antimonium wird durch solch Mittel also getödtet,

These are the practical social and moral virtues like justice and temperance used in daily life.</note> of which we are capable.

<margin>On the Topic of Virtues</margin>
For him, essence is solely "being," because of the absence of all form and the essence of that which is; but perfection through that which is formed comes from God. For as you are of the First Being, so you are not of the first good of the same. For rather, essences and virtue are from this; but only essence according to the **progression** <note>original: "proodon." In Neoplatonism, this is the process of the One overflowing or "proceeding" into the lower levels of reality.</note> from it, which is present to all from God. But perfection is according to the **return** <note>original: "epistrophen." This is the soul's movement back toward its divine source after its descent into the material world.</note> to it. Nor does he demand to be perfected, for he alone is, unless he is a beginning toward the earthly. Therefore, just like one painting from a model, or otherwise taking the prescribed **archetype** <note>original: "archetypian," a primary pattern or blueprint in the divine mind.</note> for the imitation, if he did not keep it with him to record it, so too he who would sketch and color virtue within himself could not otherwise be assimilated to God through the divine, unless he had used that alone to record it. And because of this, my own self will be accurately fashioned after the prototype through the contemplation of the Reason and the model.

### On Virtues

One who possesses the **theoretical virtues** <note>original: "theoretikas aretas." These are virtues of pure contemplation and intellectual vision.</note> is called "God-fathered" <note>original: "theopator." A technical term for the highest level of Neoplatonic virtue where the soul becomes like the source of the divine.</note>. One who has the **purificatory virtues** <note>original: "kathartikas." Virtues that "cleanse" the soul of material attachments.</note> is called "daemonic" <note>original: "daimonios." This does not mean "evil," but refers to a spiritual or "spirit-like" being that bridges the gap between humans and gods.</note>. One who has the **civic virtues** is called "excellent" <note>original: "spoudaios." A term for the person who performs their human duties and social roles with moral excellence.</note>. He who is beloved of God is called "God-fathered," because the soul's state is toward what is called "divine" through theoretical virtue. It is necessary

<column-break/>

therefore, that which is darkened must be assimilated to God, changing from the "excellent" man into the "daemonic." If it becomes divine—which is again "God-fathered"—the one among us who is only "excellent" might at some point also change into vice. But perhaps the divine man is not [subject to change], namely the theoretical man. He who is beloved of God, the "God-fathered," who is seen to be entirely obedient to the divine, might at some point be transferred to the innate, being the very form of virtue from himself, and having become divine in color.

<margin>On Intellect</margin>
### On Intellect

Every **Intellect** <note>original: "nous." In this context, it refers to the higher, divine Mind that perceives truth directly and intuitively, rather than through step-by-step logic.</note> holds its essence, its power, and its activity as eternal. For its whole essence is present all at once. It neither increases nor decreases; nor was it not present yesterday. Its essence alone is similar to itself; for it thinks the whole and the all as a complete whole together. It neither sees the past nor knows the future as something yet to be, but knows everything as it is in the "now." It is not moved, nor is it embellished, nor does it reason through syllogisms <note>original: "syllogizomenos." The Intellect does not need to argue from point A to point B; it simply "sees" the truth.</note>—which is like an echo where the soul reaches a conclusion by placing perceptions. Instead, all knowing is found in its very being. For being unmoved, it could not be measured by time, neither in its essence, which is in its **indivisibility** <note>original: "amereian." A state of being that cannot be split into parts.</note>, from which its essence is unmoved. But the intermediate and middle of these is like an eternal power that has been allotted its substance.

<margin>On Number</margin>
### On Number

Numbers are an essence, indivisible. For that which has no parts is not of the same body. That which is unmoved is entirely **indivisible**. Everything that is divided is divided either by magnitude or by quantity. But if it is eternal in every respect and I assume a certain body, it is therefore indivisible. The translator notes that this page addresses the unusual inclusion of this hymn in the Homeric collection, given its stylistic similarities to later "Orphic" hymns.</meta>

# 323

## TO ARES.

Hymn 65; while Ares is asked there to pause in his deeds and turn to works of peace, the poet here prays for a peace-inclined heart. The lust for war is called (line 12) "bitter wickedness" <note>original: *kakotēs pikrē*</note> and (line 13) "the soul’s deceptive impulse" <note>original: *psychēs apatēlos hormē*</note>, while the laws of peace, by contrast, are "harmless" <note>original: *apēmones*</note> (line 16). Throughout the entire first half, the hymn is indistinguishable from the Orphic hymns <note>A collection of late-antique hymns attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus, known for their philosophical and mystical tone rather than the narrative style of Homer.</note>.

It is therefore quite remarkable how this hymn could have found its way among the Homeric ones. According to *Baumeister* (p. 103), it was included as Homeric by the compiler of our collection out of ignorance. However, since it is established from the introduction to the hymns that the Alexandrian scholars <note>The librarians and scholars of the Great Library of Alexandria who standardized the Greek literary canon.</note> were already familiar with the smaller Homeric hymns, at the very least a subsequent addition to the collection must be assumed. *Bücheler*, on the other hand (p. 1), and *Guttmann* (in his critical history, p. 43) attribute its inclusion to a scribe’s error. The former believes the hymn entered our collection at the time when the Homeric hymns were combined with the Orphic ones. Yet, since this connection between Homeric and Orphic hymns is not consistent, *Bücheler’s* assumption remains just as uncertain as *Baumeister’s*.

1. **"Exceeding in strength"** <note>original: *hypermeneta*</note>, like **"savior of cities"** <note>original: *polissos* (vs. 2)</note> and **"livelihood"** <note>original: *biotēs* (vs. 10)</note>, are words found only in this hymn. — Ares is also called **"heavy-charioted"** <note>original: *brisarmatos*</note> in Hesiod's *Shield of Heracles* 441; Athena is called **"golden-helmeted"** <note>original: *chryseopēlēx*</note> in Callimachus 5, 43.

3. **"Strong-handed"** <note>original: *karterocheir*</note> appears otherwise only in the very late *Palatine Anthology* 9, 210. — **"Mighty with the spear"** <note>original: *dorysthenēs*</note> was already used by Aeschylus in *The Libation Bearers* 158.

Die Kriegslust heifst (12) κακότης πικρή und (13) ψυχῆς ἀπατηλὸς ὁρμή, die Gesetze des Friedens dagegen sind ἀπήμονες (16). In der ganzen ersten Hälfte unterscheidet sich der Hymnus in nichts von den orphischen.

Es ist daher merkwürdig genug, wie dieser Hymnus unter die homerischen gelangen konnte. Nach *Baumeister* (p. 103) wäre er von dem Hersteller unsrer Sammlung aus Unkenntnis als homerisch aufgenommen worden, da aber soviel aus dem, was in der Einleitung zu den Hymnen gesagt ist, feststeht, daſs die Alexandriner auch die kleineren homerischen Hymnen schon kannten, so müfste zum mindesten eine nachträgliche Ergänzung der Sammlung angenommen werden. *Bücheler* dagegen (p. 1) und *Guttmann* (h. cr. p. 43) schieben seine Aufnahme einem Schreiberversehen zu. Der erstere meint, der Hymnus sei zu der Zeit in unsre Sammlung geraten, wo die homerischen Hymnen mit den orphischen verbunden wurden. Da aber diese Verbindung der homerischen und der orphischen Hymnen keine ständige ist, so bleibt die Vermutung *Büchelers* ebenso unsicher als die *Bau-meisters*.

Nuperrime autem G. Koertius de ea parte Cynegetici quae technica dicitur lucubrationem instituit, quam priusquam ad finem perduxisset morte est interceptus. Primum exposuit non modo dispositionem incommodam esse, sed ipsam doctrinam adeo mancam et obscuram ut venatoribus vix utilis esse posset. Et id quidem iure eum contendisse fatendum est: sed confirmat coniecturam nostram de huiusce libelli origine. Xenophontis enim heres, homo studiorum certe rhetoricorum haud rudis, sed in scribendo parum habilis, rerum seriem, sicut in volumine sibi tradito perscriptam invenerat, integram servavit nec regulis ex sua scientia addere quidquam ausus est quod illustraret aut in ordinem idoneum redigeret.

At multa, inquit Koertius, in hac parte operis ita falsa sunt praecepta ut nullo modo a viro vere venandi perito conscripta esse potuerint. Quam sententiam quominus pleno exemplorum numero exponeret et stabiliret fatis est prohibitus. Sed nonnulla saltem quae vituperavit aut vituperaturus erat controversa potius quam falsa esse dixerim. Suadet enim Cynegetici scriptor ut leporem, ubi a catulis captus sit, iis discerpendum tradat venator. Quod consilium reprehendit Koertius tamquam plane absurdum. At id ipsum commendat Blanius, vir haud minus quam Koertius artis venatoriae gnarus. Quid? In libro de Re Equestri Simonem laudat Xenophon quod pedum bonitatem in equo sonitu prodi docuerit: id quod perspicue falsam esse declarant Bourgelatus et Berenger. ### PREFACE

The age and authenticity of the *Cynegeticus* <note>On Hunting</note> are subjects of debate following the work of Fischer and Valckenaer. For my own part, I believe only this: the little book as we now read it was not written by Xenophon himself. But, to state immediately what seems to me to have some appearance of truth, I suspect he left behind a <term>σύγγραμμα</term> <gloss>treatise</gloss> in which he had committed to writing a series of rules for the use of young hunters, a eulogy and defense of the art of hunting against Aristippus, and an extemporaneous <term>κατηγορίαν</term> <gloss>accusation</gloss> against the sophists, compiled from the wisdom of Antisthenes. This material, however, Diodorus his son—or whoever it was into whose hands it fell—decided to publish, altering the style of writing to his own fashion, yet retaining the name of Xenophon. Although many have detected in our little book many signs of Xenophon's own studies and learning, no one, I think, has even attempted to refute those very weighty arguments of Rademacher, by which he demonstrated that its style is entirely alien to the custom of Xenophon. And as for Herbert Richards, who was inclined to vindicate the authority of the whole book on account of certain words and locutions peculiar to Xenophon, I fear he has not sufficiently weighed how many and how great are the arguments brought to the contrary.

<summary>The preface addresses the scholarly controversy surrounding the authorship of the 'Cynegeticus', suggesting it is a heavily edited compilation rather than an original work by Xenophon.</summary>

# CYNEGETICVS

### PRAEFATIO

Cynegetici de aetate et fide post Fischerum et Valckenaerium ambigitur. Equidem hoc tantum sentio, libellum nostrum qualem nunc legimus non ab ipso Xenophonte scriptum esse. Sed, ut statim dicam id quod mihi veritatis aliquam speciem habere videtur, haud scio an *σύγγραμμα* reliquerit in quo regularum seriem in usum venatorum iuniorum, artis venatoriae et laudationem et defensionem contra Aristippum, *κατηγορίαν* sophistarum extemporalem litteris mandasset, compilata Antisthenis sapientia : id autem Diodorus filius, seu quisquis fuerit cuius in manus venerit, scribendi genere in suum morem immutato in lucem edere statuerit manente tamen nomine Xenophontis. Quamquam enim multi multa Xenophontis ipsius studiorum et doctrinae indicia in nostro libello detexerunt, nemo, opinor, gravissima illa Rademacheri argumenta ne conatus est quidem refellere, quibus demonstravit omnino alienum esse eius stilum a Xenophontis consuetudine. Et Herbertus Richards, qui ob verba et locutiones quasdam Xenophonti proprias, ad vindicandam totius libelli auctoritatem propensior fuit, vereor ut satis ponderaverit quot et quanta in contrariam partem adlata sint.

**Νοήμονος**.

# Νικοσθένης — νιφετός

**Nicosithenes** is a proper name.
<margin>a</margin> **Nicostratus** the comic poet. Athenaeus mentions him in the second book of the *Deipnosophistae*, and says that his plays are *Pandrosos*, *Antyllus* (which also seems to be by Philetaerus), *Hierophantes*, *Clene*, as well as *Abra*, *Hesiod*, *Diabolus*, *Anterosa*, *Hecate*, *Mageirus*, *Otis* <note>or perhaps *Patriotae*</note>, *Plutus*, *Syrus*, *Apelaunomenos*, *Pseudosegmatias*, and *Tocistes*. I found these listed in a collection.
<margin>b</margin> **Nicostratus** the Macedonian rhetorician. He was ranked among the ten lesser rhetoricians, a contemporary of Aristeides and Dion Chrysostomus. He lived during the time of the Emperor Marcus Antoninus. He wrote a *Decamythia*, *Icones*, *Polymythia*, *Thalatturgos*, and many other works, as well as eulogies for Marcus and others.

**Nicophon**, son of Theron, an Athenian comic poet, contemporary of Aristophanes the comic poet. Among his plays are these: *Coming Up from Hades*, *Birth of Aphrodite*, *Pandora*, *Encheirogastores* <gloss>Hand-to-mouthers</gloss>, *Sirens*.

**Nicochares**, son of Philonides the comic poet, an Athenian comic poet, contemporary of Aristophanes. Among his plays are *Amymone*, *Pelops*, *Galatea*, *Heracles Marrying*, *Heracles Choragus*, *Cretans*, *Laconians*, *Lemnians*, *Centaurs*, *Cheirogastores* <gloss>Hand-to-mouthers</gloss>.

**Nicuris** is a place name.

**Nikōen** <gloss>may they conquer</gloss> and **nikōē** <gloss>may he conquer</gloss> are optative forms.

**Nicon**. This man, having won victories in boxing, wrestling, the pancratium, the footrace, and other events at Olympia, Nemea, the Isthmus, and other games, received, as they say, fourteen hundred wreaths. After he departed from among men, one of those who had hated him while he was alive approached his statue and whipped it, until the statue fell and struck the offender. The children of the man pursued the statue for murder, and the Thasians cast it into the sea, in accordance with the law of Draco the Athenian, which mandates exile for inanimate objects that kill. When the Thasians were suffering misfortune, the Pythian oracle commanded them to bring it back. While they were at a loss as to how to raise it, fishermen who had cast their nets for fish brought up the statue. The Thasians then set it up where it had originally been. *Pausanias* 6.11, concerning Theagenes.

**nin** <gloss>them/her/him</gloss> <note>original: "νίν"</note>; "If the people here were to speak of them..." (Sophocles, *Oedipus at Colonus* 43). "You are the one who..."

<column-break/>

"...speaks of them, not I: for you are the one performing the deed, and deeds find their own arguments" (Sophocles, *Electra* 624).

**Nineveh**, a city, and **Ninevite**, one from that same city.

**Niobe** is a proper name.

**Nireus**, the handsome and well-formed.

**Nisa**, a city. And **Nisaea**, a city.

**Nisaea**, a harbor of the Megarid.

**Nisaeum**, a place in Persia where the swiftest horses are produced, called Nisaean. Others (Herodotus 7.40) say it is a large plain in Media, named Nisaeum. This plain, therefore, bears the large horses. **Nisaeus** is a proper name, and refers both to the citizen and the horse.

**Nisibis**, genitive *Nisibeōs*, is the name of a city. **Nisibenian** is the citizen.

**Nisus** is a proper name. "And to Nisus fell the Megarid."

**nissomenos** (Homer, *Iliad* 13.186), returning, and **nissonto** (13.119), they were returning.

**nitarion** and **bitarion**, diminutives used toward women. *Nitarion* is like "little nestling," that is, a young girl. Symmachus says, "Nitarus" is often used as a reproach for softness, and "Batos." They also called small, female vessels *batylai*, and there is a play by Theopompus titled *Batyle*. Others say these are types of plants; he wishes to say, therefore, that he held me like flowers. Aristophanes (*Plutus* 1012): "And by Zeus, if she noticed me feeling sad, she would use the pet names *nitarion* and *bitarion*."

**Nitarius** is a proper name.

**Nitereion**, a promontory.

**Nitria**, a place.

**Nitron** <gloss>natron/soda</gloss>.

**Nitocris** is a proper name.

**Niphades** <gloss>snow-flakes</gloss>; "And words like snowflakes" (Homer, *Iliad* 3.222).

**niphei**, it is snowing, and **niphomena**, being snowed upon.

**Niphetos**, snow falling in fine particles. There are four types of freezing of the watery moisture in the air: above the earth, to a lesser degree, is snow, and to a greater degree, hail; on the earth below, to a lesser degree, is frost, and to a greater degree, ice. *Niphetos* is not a freezing, but rather this quality concerns a different coloring. "As the land of the Scythians is often sprinkled with snow, and it is impossible for them to live without a cold climate."

Νικοσθένης ὄνομα κύριον.
<margin>a</margin> Νικόστρατος κωμικός. τούτου μέμνηται Ἀθήναιος ἐν β' Δειπνοσοφισῶν, λέγει δὲ ὅτι δράματα αὐτοῦ ἐστὶ Πάνδροσος καὶ Ἄντυλλος, ὃς καὶ Φιλεταίρου δοκεῖ εἶναι, καὶ Ἱεροφάντης καὶ Κλεινή, ἔτι δὲ Ἄβρα καὶ Ἡσίοδος καὶ Διάβολος καὶ Ἀντερωσα καὶ Ἑκάτη, Μάγειρος, Ὦτις <note>an Πατριῶται</note>, Πλοῦτος, Σύρος, Ἀπελαυνόμενος, Ψευδοσιγματίας καὶ Τοκιστής. ταῦτα ἐν παραθήκῃ εὗρον κείμενα.
<margin>b</margin> Νικόστρατος Μακεδὼν ῥήτωρ. ἐτάχθη δὲ ἐν τοῖς κριθεῖσιν ἐπιδευτέροις δέκα ῥήτορσι, σύγχρονος Ἀριστείδου καὶ Δίωνος τοῦ χρυσοσόμου· ἦν γὰρ ἐπὶ Μάρκου Ἀντωνίνου τοῦ βασιλέως. ἔγραψε δεκαμυθίαν, εἰκόνας, πολυμυθίαν, θαλαττουργὸς καὶ ἄλλα πλεῖστα, καὶ ἐγκώμια εἴς τε τὸν Μάρκον καὶ ἄλλους.
Νικοφῶν Θήρωνος Ἀθηναῖος κωμικός, σύγχρονος Ἀριστοφάνους τοῦ κωμικοῦ. τῶν δραμάτων αὐτοῦ καὶ ταῦτα, Ἐξ Ἅδου ἀνιών, Ἀφροδίτης γοναί, Πανδώρα, Ἐγχειρογάστορες, Σειρῆνες.
Νικοχάρης Φιλωνίδου τοῦ κωμικοῦ, Ἀθηναῖος κωμικός, σύγχρονος Ἀριστοφάνους. τῶν δραμάτων αὐτῷ Ἀμυμώνη, Πέλοψ, Γαλάτεια, Ἡρακλῆς γαμῶν, Ἡρακλῆς χορηγός, Κρῆτες, Λάκωνες, Λήμνιαι, Κένταυροι, Χειρογάστορες.
Νικυρίς ὄνομα τόπου.
νικῷεν καὶ νικῴη εὐκτικά.
Νίκων. οὗτος πὺξ καὶ πάλην καὶ παγκράτιον καὶ δρόμον καὶ τἄλλα ἐν Ὀλυμπίᾳ καὶ Νεμέᾳ καὶ Ἰσθμοῖ καὶ ἄλλοις ἀγῶσι νικήσας ἔλαβε στεφάνους, ὥς φασι, χιλίους καὶ τετρακοσίους. ἀπελθόντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων, τῶν ἀπεχθανομένων τις ζῶντι αὐτῷ παρεγίνετο ἐπὶ τὴν εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐμαστίγου αὐτήν, ἐς ὃ πεσοῦσα ἐκείνη ἠμύνατο τὸν ὑβριστήν. τοῦ δὲ οἱ παῖδες ἐπεξῇεσαν φόνου τῇ εἰκόνι, καὶ οἱ Θάσιοι καταποντοῦσιν αὐτήν, κατὰ νόμον Δράκοντος Ἀθηναίου ὑπερορίζοντος φονεύοντα καὶ τὰ ἄψυχα. ταύτην δὲ ἡ Πυθία ἔχρησε κακῶς Θασίοις πράττουσιν ἀνενεγκεῖν. ἀπορούντων δὲ περὶ τῆς ἀναγωγῆς, οἱ ἁλιεῖς τὰ δίκτυα χαλάσαντες ἐπὶ ἰχθῦς ἀνήνεγκαν τὴν εἰκόνα. καὶ ἔστησαν αὐτὴν οἱ Θάσιοι ὅθι καὶ πρῶτον ἦν. Pausan. 6 11 de Theagene.

εὐνοίας ἔχειν αὐτοὺς καὶ μάλιστα οἳ ἂν κατὰ τὴν πόλεως
συνέρχονται. συνέρχεται τὸν πόλεμον ὧδε ἂν οὗτοι πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἠυτομόλησαν
τοὺς δὲ εὐτελεστέρους αὐτῶν ἐπαγεῖν σὺν πολέμων ᾗ καὶ
ρασιγαὶ εἰσὶν ᾗ καὶ κροτηθεὶς γένοι τὰ σήματα ὡς δεῖ σᾶς
τὰ πολλῶν ἰδίων αὐτῶν πεποιθότας χρὴ δὲ οὐμονοῦ ἐνδουλεύειν
ἡμῖν προσαβι δωρεὰν πεμπάνων οἱ πολέμιοι. ἵνα καὶ πέρας
ποτε τριακοντίους αὐτοὺς ἐν ἀγωγῇ δουλῶσι δωρεὰν σίλαντες
δι' αὐτῶν τὴν πόλιν παρελαβόν.

ᾗ τῶν καταλίκων ἐπινοηθέντα ῥᾷα ὡς δι' αὐτῶν ὀρθανόμενος
τὰ τῶν ἐναντίων σφαλοβλεῖ ἡμῖν τὸ εἰδέναι ᾗ πρὸς αἵρεσιν

<margin>Hoc caput in Celsis legationum ab Hoeschelio 1603 in auguda ed. praefatione vice: nulla facta authoris mentione dicitur: ha titulo: πῶς δεῖ πρεσβεύειν καὶ πρεσβεύεσθαι. In longuis illis contenditur: que huc asferantur.</margin>

εἰς τὴν πολεμίαν φεύγειν τοὺς αἰχμαλώτους οὐ μόνον διὰ τὴν ὑποψίαν ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ μὴ ἀναγνωρισθῆναι. οὐκοῦν ἕνεκα πολλὰ δὲ τῶν πολεμίων τυγχάνοντες τῶν μὲν πονηροτέρων καὶ φρονιμωτέρων τάχιον ἀπαλλάττεσθαι τοὺς δὲ ἀγαθοὺς καὶ ἀκριβεῖς καὶ τὸν τρόπον ἀκαλῶς γνωρίζειν τε καὶ πρὸς αὐτοὺς μεταλνεῖν.

Περὶ πρέσβεων
Ἐν πρέσβεσι ἡ παρ’ ἡμῶν ἡ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀποστέλλονται. καὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀποστέλλονται χρὴ φιλοτίμως τε καὶ δεξιῶς τούτους ὑποδέχεσθαι. καὶ γὰρ τιμῶσι αὐτοὺς τοὺς δὲ ἐπιμελῶς ὑπὸ αὐτοῦ δὲ ἀσφαλῶς ἔχειν εἰς σιωπὴν διδάσκειν ἐπερωτώμενοι αὐτὸν κἂν γε τῶν λίαν ἀπρεπῶν πρέσβεων ὦσιν ὠφελεῖσθαι ἐκείνων τε καὶ ἡμῶν εἶναι ἵνα τῶν ἐθνῶν ἐμφανίζῃ αὐτοῖς τὴν ἡμετέραν σπουδὴν ἀσφαλῶς ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ οἱ πλησιόχωροι ἡμῶν καθιστάμενοι. ἔνθεν δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν ἔχουσι δύναμιν. εἰ δὲ μάλα πολὺ ἡμῶν διεστηκόσιν ὧδε πλῆθος στρατὸς εἴη ἀνδρεῖος. χρὴ γῆλε πᾶντον ὑπ’ ἐς γυναῖκαν καλλῇ ἐμφανίζειν αὐτοῖς πλῆθος δὲ ἀνδρῶν καὶ ὅπλων εὐσχημίαν καὶ τύχην ὑψηλά. οἱ δὲ παρ’ ἡμῶν πρέσβεις ἀποστέλλονται χρὴ τούτους πρῶτον μὲν ἐπ’ εὐσεβείᾳ γνωρίζεσθαι καὶ μὴ ἐπ’ ἐκκλησίᾳ κατηγορηθέντες ποτὲ δημοσίᾳ κατακρίνωνται. εἶναι φρονίμους τὴν φύσιν, εὐνοοῦντα κοινὰ ὧδε καὶ πρὸς ἀρνοῦντες ὅθεν σωτηρίων κάθ’ ἕρ ἡ γουλίο. καὶ τὴν ἀποστολὴν προθύμους ἀλλὰ βεβαιώσεως καθάπερ οἱ ἀγωνίαις ἰατροί. ὁ μὲν παρὰ παρχηδονίοις δεβυοῦται καὶ πρὸς ρωμαίους περὶ εἰρήνης πρέσβευον ἀπεσταλμένος ὁμοῦσιν ἐπανελθεῖν προϋπέθετο. τῶν ρωμαίων τὴν εἰρήνην οὐκ ἀπεδέξαντο. ὁ δὲ πρὸς ρωμαίους ἀφίκετο ἀπαγορεύειν τὸν ρωμαίων ῥήτορα ἀσύμφορον αὐτῶν οὐδὲν πειθὼ δ’ αὐτοὺς ἐπανελθεῖν πρὸς παρχηδονίους τὸν ὁρῶν φιλόμενος. ὅτε μὲν ἐς βαβυλῶνα τῆς αἰγύπτου τὸν πέρσην ἀνηγέας τὰ αἰγυπτίων διέλουσιν χρὴ δὲ τοὺς πρέσβεῖς παραχωρεῖν, πρὸς οὓς ἀποστέλλονται φαίνονται ἐπιχαρῆσε. μεγάλο φύγωσι ἄμφω δὲ οἱ οἰκεῖα τάδε τῶν πολεμίων ἐκείνῳ ποιοῦντες ἀλλαγῇ.

for those things that are necessary for existence, so that he might enjoy the future state of his own youth <note>original: "νότητος", likely referring to spiritual renewal or vigor</note>, he did not make a judgment. He says what kind of end follows after the neglect. For these people, the tyranny arises from the very things that are more useful and leads toward this sacred servitude. For the sinners, there will be food that remains wretched; but for the righteous, there is an abundance apart from accusations. For them, the suffering is in no way able to represent the manner of life in a tragic way. For through the working of the secret things of Christ <note>original: "χριστοῦ"</note>, Christ is found in my own affairs. Some things, having his body <note>original: "σῶμα"</note> and an end that has a hard appearance, he provided from his own flesh and blood. In this way, he might offer grace <note>original: "χάριν"</note> to them. But the garments of grace he hews with iron and they are cut into small pieces. He leads the way, rather, by dividing the stones with naked ash. He himself will point out the paths to those who work the mines. The entire work is divided by the cutting of atoms <note>original: "ἀτόμων", referring to indivisible particles or small fragments</note> and according to this manner. For they themselves and they alone, by the grace that sparkles in their own words, do not cut from the stones, but from themselves; and they cut through the breeze. They undermine a multitude, not immediately, but the body of Christ which is from him alone and of stone. But the body of the choir; and again from them a portion on the left hand, in which there also, in a similar way, they define a broken and similar portion to those of the wicked. These alone, with stones bound to those who act afterward, competing with stone-cutters, as if seating the stone like a bark or shell; and having transformed the foundations of the body in many ways. And the fragments, rather, fall to the ground, not according to their own appearance and power, but toward the eye upon the sun's rebuke, with no one permitting it. But the men and

<meta>This page continues the transition from Proclus’s mathematical discourse on the World Soul toward the physical application of these principles. Having established that the universe is bound by geometric and harmonic proportions, he now examines how these "powers" manifest in material bodies and the human form, using the analogy of a physician to explain how Nature maintains the "health" or balance of the cosmos.</meta>

# Commentary on Plato’s Timaeus

<page-num>288</page-num>

...common in **power** <note>original: "dynamei" (δυνάμει). In this context, it refers to an inherent faculty or potentiality that allows a body to act or be acted upon.</note>. Bodies also have certain causes; some kinds are manifest to us, while others are the causes themselves. For among these, some are understood to have an intellectual power, while others have different sorts. This is the case with our own bodies: while some things are visible, it is not always clear why all bodies are subject to the forces that compel them. For within the body, the passage of time is seen in the changes of their composite parts. Since a middle-ground mastery exists over all the **elements** <note>original: "stoicheia" (στοιχεία). The fundamental building blocks—fire, air, water, and earth—which Proclus views as being governed by higher spiritual principles.</note>, the underlying essence uses them, though they are clearly part of Nature itself. It performs its work according to this principle. And therefore, it is composed of presences, the phases of which are counted in number. For while some are able to act through numbers, natural things follow after. The whole universe is seen by those who look, but regarding the elements, these things are not the same. We possess the powers of bodies, both those that synthesize and those that are functional; for bodies were given to us, yet the state of their powers is not judged solely by the senses, nor are they all the same, so that all things are even now part of the same bodies. It is composed of power even in its parts.

For you might say that something in the senses is infinite compared to other bodies, as it has become the means for diagnosis, and is the cause of all these same things. Or perhaps this power has been put forward as either a theoretical science or a medicinal one, like the nature of health. For if bodies do not all become a certain thing by nature, it happens through the causes of **physicians** <note>original: "iatron" (ἰατρῶν). Proclus frequently uses the doctor as an analogy for the Demiurge or Nature, both of whom "prescribe" order to chaotic matter.</note>; for they provided the active causes and some power, or perhaps the entire synthesis of the body is brought toward this. Or if they are made through the ways of the **flesh** <note>original: "sarka" (σάρκα).</note>, it is not possible to define them as indivisible. Just as one might wish for all powers to be authoritative, they each arise specifically in their own way. We speak of the advantage and the division of the beginning of bodies; they would surely incline toward where a certain body of the generations is compared. It is necessary to say that they are as wretched and pitiable as we can imagine.

Natural philosophy teaches the truth. And it is simply this: we see some of their powers as desirable, while another power was composed of all the parts that fulfill such a thing. According to the appearance of communion and the **symmetry of bulk** <note>original: "onkou symmetrias" (ὄγκου συμμετρίας). The mathematical balance of physical volume or mass.</note>. And as far as the sensory perceptions are concerned, these things are common to all; to be ignorant of them is to lose them. There is a method for these things to relate the part to the whole of the subject matter. For instance, things known by us would not have this order of theirs through this method, even if the first orders are from the **connatural** <note>original: "symphyton" (συμφύτων). Things that are grown together or share an innate nature.</note> bodies. Such a world is for us a governing principle. Because we have known whether it exists and what its particularity is, and the seasons themselves; but one must not be so bold as to treat them as a desert. Even if a certain opinion from them was mistaken until the end. Since there are certain—

<column-break/>

<page-num>289</page-num>

—on the other hand, acting as an opponent to everything through the **harmonies** <note>original: "harmonion" (ἁρμονιών). Referring to the musical and mathematical ratios that Proclus believes hold the physical universe together.</note>. From this, the cause or the path arose and continued. These are the distinguishing marks of how things come to be; for they were innate to the universals, and exist through the world, both in the parts and the whole. It appeared as though the things within the ruins were moving into the world. The cause is most similar toward the external. And so all things, if one understands that all these things are fitted together, are positioned as the seat of the **Eternal** <note>original: "aidiou" (αϊδίου). The timeless, unchanging realm of the divine.</note> itself. Therefore, all things have been joined together through its own nature and remain undivided, just as the scripture stands. There is also something indivisible, and the **demiurgic reason** <note>original: "demiourgikon logon" (δημιουργικὸν λόγον). The creative blueprint or "word" of the Creator that organizes the cosmos.</note> itself is handed down as that which is without disposition, even within natural things. Such is the nature of the intentions within the creator. I say these things exist through the bond of these elements. And indeed, such things are unsubstantial due to their nature, yet they are synthetic; for this is the nature of the whole world, that it be extended, and the one seat of all things leads out from the messengers.

The nature of the gods is in those things in which both being and the divine exist. Insofar as the sovereignty of the Eternal has begun, the world is also eternal. There is also that which is governed by the lowest things, such as the virtue of the whole, or even the physician that exists within it. For there is a certain utility in it... or a darkness. For health <unclear>...</unclear> indeed, what we call nature exists in us as living beings. And those things which exist through other bodies. It is appropriate that it is thus in power. However, those who look toward the fluid and whatever color it may be, participate in it, and insofar as it is given through heat, a part sleeps there, and the composition of this is far from the peak. These things, then, we reasonably know to be small, because the harmony of this consists either in its lack of passion or its removal. But the other things within us, such as **loves** <note>original: "erotes" (ἔρωτες). Not merely romantic love, but the cosmic force of attraction that draws the soul toward the divine.</note>, are blamed for such things or for the nature of the divine. Most of all, such things are strengthened by this, and by the attraction that might occur through the holy temple. For it is known through sensory things. For those things which seemed then to be distinguished by a lack of passion were composed in the same way. Already the preparation is fulfilled or composed. It possesses a power close to that of the cause. Or why do we speak of God as the divine cause, seen as a concern that proceeds into him? It seems right to name it thus. The description of the whole world is by nature; we name it, as if nature is the leader of the manifest causes. Through the one who created, we seek the things that are known, or we name the distinction of the ancients which is least contradictory. And so the **Eternal One** <note>original: "ho aionios" (ὁ αἰώνιος). The timeless principle of the universe.</note> speaks. Our joy...

# Meditations
## On Grammar, Motion, and the Afflictions of the Mind

**Column 1**

There is a deception even regarding the name **apolic** <note>original: *apollikēn*; the term is obscure, possibly referring to a name that is "removed" or "distant" from its object</note>. What belongs to one, it says, but much is that which is equal to being. Among equals. A name was given to things that exist. The form is derived from these. This is what we say. A pretext <unclear>s'</unclear> of blame, for these are not those things by which they measure, from which we name things in some way. But those things of private victories. To seek a name in this way. In which also to remain. This was better said of common things. But the external, is it possible? The "splendid" used <term>catachrestically</term> <note>original: *katachrēstikōs*, the use of a word in a sense different from its proper one, like calling a "silver" cup "golden"</note> of common things. For the one who shares frequently tends to follow it.

And immediately after this: speak concerning **structure**; as many things as he sees regarding structure in a single way. And there is a humble thing of his, the steps. It is itself, and one will find it. It is equal. What kind of thing is the <term>pronoun</term> <note>original: *antōnymia*</note>, and its feminine form, "this woman." And "that man" and "that woman" for example. For it is not first for him. It is used <term>infinitively</term> <note>original: *aparemphatikōs*</note>. For the whole of... the whole, but no <term>pronoun</term> happens [to match]. It is <term>deictic</term> <note>original: *deiktikon*, pointing or demonstrative</note>. Or if it does not show more, "these things."

For example, "these men," or "these women," or "these men." And the <term>figure</term> <note>original: *schēma*</note> is to proceed. Rich. They do not differ poetically from the formation. Of these, on the one hand, whether it is still something or non-being. Those things, on the other hand, are brief. For example, or if they act. They make it clear. For even the Athenian things—the way of forming them—never once existed. For example: "this man," "herself," but the things regarding the same form do not belong to... for example, to these. And because "this man" is only...

...is. In <term>voice</term> <note>original: *phōnē*</note> it is the thing being said. And it is of the... and this... but all the **doubtful** <note>original: *aporētika*, things causing difficulty or questioning</note> things, they take the "or" in some way. If by **voice** the thing appeared. For it is [necessary] to see how they are. Which one? Adding... to swim. A **thought** <note>original: *noēma*</note> regarding the action here of the two, just as with animals. From which also... themselves are said more than a ship. But the sewing/seam... perhaps, not to go down to those who hear. That man. And that man already goes not, so that that woman would not...

<column-break/>

...other tender tracks. From the word "at the same time." What is this except [this]? So that the beautiful ones <gloss>themselves</gloss> do not always go around. They purify indeed. They always go around. They let go. They release. And they send forth. From the word for "I go" <note>original: *eimi*</note>, the third of the... they go. Whence they... they go. They enter <note>original: *isiasin*</note>, instead of "they go in."

They go out, they fly, they fly, they go down, they go up, they go through, they go towards, they go around, they go away. The "being about to" [future], the "all"... things of "hoping." The "to dwell," and "to remain," after... the "to stretch" <gloss>is transformed</gloss>. Let it not be thought of. Since even "to be afraid" are several things. And yet, you always hope to be; or simply, thus also themselves are of the...

...himself. Not by chance is he such. And it is the same of the **verbs** <note>original: *rhēmatōn*</note>; he heard, "you have ceased"; and the same to whom. So that you said: you fight. From where let us see also from <term>verbs</term> <note>original: *rhēmatōn*</note>. This creation: toward some honor for us through... from which the "made thing" is likely the **wandering**, or **deception**. Instead of "he will go," or "in a trick." A <term>well</term> <note>original: *phreas*</note>. Regarding being springs. Or a well. Just like a well. Where [one is] not in some well. And a well. The thing that flows. Those through a bitter...

...on the one hand, **madness** <note>original: *aponoia*, literally a loss of sense or desperation</note>. "Feed the leaves." The ancient... having placed... water, and every... and... they are the **instruments of the voice**. From which also the sounds of the <term>voice</term> <note>original: *phōnēs*</note> [arise]. Just as for one who speaks much with words, it is **madness** <note>original: *mania*</note>; but the many limbs [of a sentence]. **Melancholy** <note>original: *melancholia*</note>. Of the ancient word, **madness** <note>original: *mania*</note> is common. Or grief. A poetic thing. And the [act of] madness... terrible. The thing that spoke. Or having leaped away. ...and you will have the double mercury of the sages <note>a classic term for the Philosopher's Stone or its primary material</note>, which lacks nothing except to be cooked and reduced into projection powder. As for the white liquor that comes out of the oil of gold, it is an animated mercurial spirit that has the aurific principle. It serves to multiply and to ferment the double mercury from before when it is reduced to powder.

Proceed thus: take one ounce of the double mercury reduced to powder, put it into an egg-shaped vessel with half an ounce of the white liquor, seal it, and cook it at a regulated fire until reduced to powder. Take this powder and mix it with half its weight of the white liquor, cook as before, and reiterate this work as much as you judge appropriate. This is called "inceration" <note>the process of softening or making a substance wax-like</note>; it multiplies the powder in quality and quantity, and one can push it almost to infinity.

It must be noted that with this white liquor, one can make very lucrative ores with gold and mercury, and that promptly. One can make them with the aforementioned powder, and it is good to understand in passing that it is from this single trunk and this root that all the particularities and all the transmutatory branches start.

Take the projection powder from before and mix it with ten times its weight of common mercury, cook the whole together in a matrass for 40 days, then add ten times the weight of this common mercury and cook everything as before. Take the cooked mass and divide it into two, melt one part, and you will find good gold that stands every test, and with the other part, join its weight of common mercury and cook for a month, and thus you will be able to draw half every month to melt.
