<meta>This page continues the discussion on the early life and character of Pythagoras. The previous page ended with a footnote quoting Iamblichus regarding Pythagoras's divine reputation. This page details his interaction with the aging philosopher Thales of Miletus and provides further citations from classical and early modern scholars concerning his nearly divine nature.</meta>

...this could be shown by the consensus of many writers, if I did not have to keep this work brief. Thales of Miletus was still living at that time. He remains a great name in the history of philosophy today. In that era, he was venerable not only because of his diverse and extraordinary learning, but also because of his advanced age. Therefore, at the very start of his youth, Pythagoras went to him among others for instruction <meta>fe</meta>

*...that he was the same person.* <note>original Greek: αὐτον εἶναι</note> *Now that his father was dead, he grew up endowed with the most honorable and temperate character and became a man. Indeed, even while still quite a young man, he was treated with every kind of honor and reverence, even by those who were most advanced in years. Whenever he spoke, everyone who saw and heard him turned their eyes toward him. To anyone he looked upon, he seemed so miraculous that it was rightly claimed by most that he was the SON of GOD. This is how Arcerius translated this passage. Apuleius, in Florida, Book 2, page 18, says: A man of massive talent and surely possessed of a mind more majestic than human capacity. You will find more things of this kind here and there in the works of Iamblichus and Porphyry, regarding whom the commentary of Rittershusius should be consulted. See also Justus Lipsius, On Stoic Philosophy, Book 1, dissertation 6, page 750, and the dissertation by Schiltius on Pythagorean discipline...*

### LES EXPÉRIENCES MAGIQUES DU GROUPE INDÉPENDANT D'ÉTUDES ÉSOTÉRIQUES.

En 1889, nous avons fondé à Paris le *Groupe indépendant d'études ésotériques*, destiné à contrôler les expériences concernant les forces encore inconnues en action dans l'homme et dans la nature.

Les premiers mois furent consacrés à la propagande et les travaux purent être fructueusement poursuivis dès le début de l'année 1891. A ce moment le groupe était divisé en sections techniques dont l'une s'occupait de Magie pratique. Personnellement nous avions fait quelques expériences suivies de succès, ainsi que notre ami F. Ch. Barlet ; mais ces expériences avaient besoin d'un contrôle que la suite des études pouvait seule fournir. L'année 1891 fut consacrée aux études préliminaires, et au commencement de 1892 plusieurs essais, accompagnés d'entraînement végétarien et concernant la vision des élémentals, furent entrepris et couronnés de succès, principalement en ce qui touche les expériences de M. Delfosse. Au milieu de l'année, des faits rapportés dans les grimoires furent soumis à un contrôle expérimental et M. Michelet, un des commissaires, put même certifier le fait que le diamant pur empêchait le passage de l'action magnétique de l'aimant. Ce fait rapporté par Agrippa et inconnu des physiciens modernes est familier aux marchands de diamants, ainsi qu'il fut constaté. En même temps, une expérience d'évocation consciente fut tentée par M. M. H. et, malgré des oublis et des fautes nombreuses, cette expérience donna des résultats très curieux et très instructifs. Nous en rapporterons les principaux détails d'après les opérateurs eux-mêmes.

Au mois de mars 1892, en période de lune croissante, MM. H. et K., membres d'une commission d'enquête des phénomènes magiques, tentèrent l'expérience suivante qui fut conduite dans le secret le plus absolu :

Après 12 jours d'entraînement triple : végétarien <unclear>...</unclear>

<meta>This page continues the historical account of the Frankish kings, transitioning from the general expansion of their power to the specific Italian campaigns of Charlemagne and his relationship with the Papacy.</meta>

# S Y N O P S I S

->Events were conducted with great vigor;<- the fame of Charles, King of the Franks <note>better known to history as Charlemagne</note>, was celebrated, and his power was no less impressive. Regarding him, see *Sigonius’s Kings of Italy, the Bavarian Annals by the Reverend Father Brunner (part 2), the Anonymous Saxon Poet, Eginhard in Reuber’s collection, Hector of Aachen, and the Annals edited by Pithou.* 

For after the war in Aquitaine was completed, having been requested by Hadrian, the Roman Pontiff <note>Pope Hadrian I, who reigned from 772–795 AD</note>, he came into Italy with an army. Just as his father, Pepin, had crushed Aistulf, the King of the Lombards; so too did Charles capture Aistulf's successor, Desiderius, who had been a heavy burden to Italy and Hadrian. After a long siege of Pavia, Charles took him prisoner, cast down his son Adalgis from the throne, and expelled him from all of Italy. In this way, he gained possession of the entire Kingdom of the Lombards. *See Regino (book 3), Guagninus (book 4, chapter 1), and Aemilius of Verona’s History of the Franks (book 2).*

Furthermore, Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle* that once Pavia was captured, Charles returned to Rome. In a Synod of 153 bishops <note>original: "Antistitum"</note> celebrated by Pope Hadrian, the right of choosing the Roman Pontiff <note>original: "jus eligendi Romanum Pontificem"</note> was granted to him. It was also established that Archbishops and Bishops throughout the individual provinces were to receive <term>investitures</term> <note>investiture: the formal ceremony where a ruler grants a bishop the symbols of their spiritual and temporal power, such as a staff or ring</note> from him. *See Chapter "Hadrian," distinction 65, and the works of Lord Goldast.*

<meta>catchword: dast.</meta>

In the time of the emperor Theophilus, Scholasticius the door-keeper was chamberlain, and in the time of Michael, son of Theophilus, the patrician Damian was chamberlain and after him, in the same reign, Basil, the Christ-loving emperor, was chamberlain. In the time of Basil, the Christ-loving sovereign, there was no chamberlain during all his reign. In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Samonas was chamberlain, and after him, in the time of the same emperor, the patrician Constantine. In the time of Alexander the emperor, the patrician Barbatus was chamberlain; and in the time of Constantine, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Constantine, mentioned before in the time of the sovereign Leo, was chamberlain again; and in the time of the sovereign Romanus, the patrician Theophanes; and in the second reign of Constantine, the patrician Basil.

In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving and ever-memorable emperor, lived the late Ktenas, an aged cleric of great wealth, who was precentor of the New Church and was skilled in singing as was no other at that time. This same Ktenas besought the patrician Samonas, who was at that time chamberlain, to intercede for him with the emperor so that he might be made protospatharius and wear the shirt and go in procession to the Lausiacus and take his seat as protospatharius and receive a stipend of one pound, and in respect of this remuneration might give the emperor forty pounds. But the emperor could not bring himself to do this, saying that it was out of his power, and «to the great disgrace of my imperial majesty if a cleric becomes protospatharius». On hearing this from the patrician Samonas, this same Ktenas added to the forty pounds a pair of ear-rings valued at ten pounds, and a silver table with animals on it in gold relief, also valued at ten pounds. And the emperor, besought by the request of the patrician Samonas, the chamberlain, took the forty pounds of gold and the pair of ear-rings and the table with its gold on silver relief work, so that the total gift of the same Ktenas amounted to sixty pounds. Then the emperor made him protospatharius, and he received a stipend on that occasion of one pound. After being honoured with the rank of protospatharius this same Ktenas lived two years and then died; and he received a stipend of one pound for each of the two years.

It should be known that in the time of the emperor Theophilus, Scholasticius the door-keeper served as chamberlain. In the time of Michael, the son of Theophilus, the patrician Damian served as chamberlain, and after him, in the same reign, Basil, the Christ-loving emperor, served as chamberlain. In the time of Basil, the Christ-loving sovereign, there was no chamberlain throughout his entire reign. In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Samonas served as chamberlain, and after him, in the same emperor's reign, the patrician Constantine served. In the time of the emperor Alexander, the patrician Barbatus served as chamberlain; in the time of Constantine, the Christ-loving sovereign, the aforementioned Constantine, who served under the sovereign Leo, served again as chamberlain; in the time of the sovereign Romanus, the patrician Theophanes served; and in the second reign of Constantine, the patrician Basil served again.

<margin>235</margin> It should be known that in the time of Leo, the Christ-loving and ever-memorable emperor, there was that old man Ktenas, a very wealthy cleric, who was also a <term>domestikos</term> <gloss>official or leader</gloss> at the New Church, and was an expert in singing, such as there was no other at that time. This same Ktenas begged the patrician Samonas, who was chamberlain at that time, to intercede for him with the emperor so that he might become a <term>protospatharios</term> <gloss>first sword-bearer, a high court rank</gloss>, and wear the <term>epikoutzoulon</term> <gloss>a specific cloak or garment of rank</gloss>, and proceed to the Lausiacus <note>A ceremonial hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople</note> and sit as a <term>protospatharios</term> and receive a stipend of one pound, and for such a favor he would give the emperor forty pounds. The emperor, however, would not agree to do this, saying that it was impossible, and stating: "It is a great disgrace to my imperial majesty for a cleric to become a <term>protospatharios</term>." Upon hearing this from the patrician Samonas, the same Ktenas added to the forty pounds a pair of <term>scholarikia</term> <gloss>earrings or jewelry</gloss> valued at ten pounds, and a silver table with gold relief work, also valued at ten pounds. Being swayed by the request of the patrician Samonas, the chamberlain, the emperor accepted the forty pounds of gold, the pair of <term>scholarikia</term>, and the gold-relief silver table, so that the total gift of the said Ktenas amounted to sixty pounds. Then the emperor made him <term>protospatharios</term>, and he received a stipend of one pound at that time. The same Ktenas lived for two years after being honored as <term>protospatharios</term> and then died; he received a stipend of one pound for each of those two years.

<summary>This page records the succession of chamberlains from the reign of Theophilus through Constantine VII and details the purchase of the rank of protospatharios by the cleric Ktenas.</summary>

# Ancoratus 105, 8 to 106, 8

And he did not have the foreknowledge of the one who spoke to the satyr acting as a goat, who first found fire and approached <margin>P 109 D 209</margin> to kiss it: "Do not touch it, goat, for if you touch it, you will burn your beard." There have been many named Athena, not just one. One was a wanderer roaming around the Tritonian lake; another was the daughter of Ocean; another the daughter of Cronus; and many others.

There are many named Artemis. One is the Ephesian, another the daughter of Zeus, and likewise many others. And there are multiple <note>interpolated: "figures of"</note> Dionysus: the Theban one, another who is the son of Semele, the one associated with the Corybantes, and the one torn apart by the Titans, whose <term>myein</term> <gloss>initiation</gloss> involves the <term>kreonomia</term> <gloss>distribution of raw flesh</gloss> of the Curetes. Then there is Hercules, the one called the <term>alexikakos</term> <gloss>averter of evil</gloss> among them. I will remain silent about all his deeds and show only one from among them all that is perhaps praised by them. It will be enough for him to have undergone this labor so that salvation might come to life. For if he had not corrupted fifty virgins in a single night, how would the world have been saved? Rather, it would have perished. I simply confess to you, I am weary of recording their evil deeds in prose. Furthermore, very cruel kings and tyrants, having had certain favorites and having buried them in the earth, had nothing more to grant them since they themselves were mortal like those they loved. Out of their goodwill, they handed over their tombs to be worshipped as gods by their own subjects, under a wicked pretext, leading to the error of life.

<note>Scholarly note: The story of the satyr and the fire is a common fable used to illustrate lack of foresight. Epiphanius continues the theme of "plurality of gods" to undermine their divinity, listing multiple Athenas and Artemises. The criticism of Hercules refers to the myth of the daughters of Thespius. The final section attributes the origin of pagan gods to the deification of deceased favorites by powerful rulers.</note>

# Thanksgiving.

He who stills the wars in all the world, breaks the bow, shatters the spears, and burns the wagons with fire.

Be still, and recognize that I am God. I will be honored among the heathen, I will be honored upon earth.

The Lord of Hosts is with us, the God of Jacob is our protection, Selah.

## The LXX. <note>original: "LXX." refers to Psalm 70</note> Psalm.

<note>An ornamental initial 'E' begins the text of the 70th Psalm.</note>

Hasten, God, to save me; Lord, help me.

They must be ashamed and confounded who seek after my soul.

They must turn back and be humiliated who wish me evil.

So that they must again be confounded, those who cry out over me, "There, there!"

They must be joyful and glad in You, who seek You and who love Your salvation; let them always say: "Highly praised be God."

I, however, am miserable and poor; God, hasten to me, for You are my helper and savior; my God, do not delay.

Therefore, it is to be suspected that because we had an early warm Spring, when the wine sprouted early, and beautiful warm weather occurred from the middle of June until the 20th of July, the wine will have a good flowering time. And then, because a warm Autumn follows this, we have hope for a good drink of wine this year.

Around the 12th, cool rain with fog will manifest, followed around the 16th by a thunderstorm with heavy downpours. Finally, however, this month will hold out to the end with warm weather and fruitful rain.

October will also still give fine warm weather, but with many strong south and northwest winds.

In November, the weather will also still be fairly tolerable, generally having much rain mixed with snow, and will begin with this around All Saints' Day <term>Alle Heiligen</term> <gloss>November 1</gloss>.

Around Advent, the mild weather will end, and the sharp winter cold will set in.

With a blast, O Lord, with the sound of the shofar:
The Lord, with the sound of the shofar, a voice from heaven upon the holy mountain and upon 
Jerusalem, and <note>original: "או כנת ימינך"</note> may the setting of Your right hand be as it was planted from the beginning.
God has ascended with a blast, the Lord with the sound of the shofar:
The Lord, with the sound of the shofar, revealed the end and the appointed time when He will blow, and He will walk 
in the storms of the south <note>Teman, often associated with divine manifestation in Hebrew poetry</note>, and the kingdom of wicked Greece shall then be 
laid bare: God has ascended with a blast, the Lord with the sound of the shofar:
The Lord, with the sound of the shofar, on the holy mountain He shall blow, the abode of Zion 
shall be smoothed, and Mount Seir shall be cleft, and broken, and removed, <note>the structure</note> that was blown: 
God has ascended with a blast, the Lord with the sound of the shofar:
The Lord, with the sound of the shofar, the Unique One riding <note>the heavens</note>, to His multitude 
He will cause to be heard good tidings, He will sing, and will renew the kingdom 
of the nation <note>Israel</note> by which we were saved. His holy oracle He will build, and will reveal the end 
of salvation: God has ascended with a blast, the Lord with the sound of the shofar:
The Lord, with the sound of the shofar, shall proclaim liberty in the land to gather 
His people from the four corners of the earth, and He will cause the prince of Edom to fall, 
and they shall hear from the ends of the earth: "Thus said the Lord God 
to Edom, a rumor <note>of judgment</note>": God has ascended with a blast, the Lord with the sound of the shofar:
The Lord, with the sound of the shofar, shall blow from the heavens, and the lost 
in the land of Assyria and the outcasts in the land 
of Egypt shall come, and they shall bow down to the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem, 
for my strength and song is the Lord, and He became my salvation. God has ascended, etc.

seed: [The matchmaker] says, "Hey, matchmaker, you tell them: the time has arrived. Prepare the incense, flowers, fruits, and a thousand strips of paper candles. Bring the altar, the bow and arrows, the five grains, and the <term>cuncao</term> <gloss>short grass, a symbol of filial piety</gloss>. By now, the new top scholar must be waiting to come." Bai Minzhong, dressed in official robes and accompanied by attendants, stops. He recites a poem: "Official brocade and palace flowers leap upon the purple steed; I boast of my official rank during the three-day tour of the Phoenix City. I do not know which lady in the decorated tower will be the first to throw the embroidered ball." [Bai Minzhong speaks:] "I, little official Bai Minzhong, who would have thought that today would come? I arrived at the Examination Hall, submitted my papers, and the Sage personally tested me in the Golden Hall. My eyes never shifted, and I answered a hundred essays. The words of the Sage are equal to those of the Hanlin scholar Li of the previous dynasty. With one examination, I, this young student, became the top scholar. In one day, I was promoted thirteen ranks, reaching the position of Hanlin Academician. Now, I obey the Sage's command to go to the residence of Minister Pei to become his son-in-law."

But if you cannot restrain that desire which you have persuaded yourself to reach toward truth by reason, many and long detours must be tolerated by you, so that reason does not lead you except by that which alone should be called reason, that is, true reason, and not only true, but so certain and alien to any semblance of falsehood, if it can indeed be found by man at all, so that no false or plausible disputations can lead you astray from it. Nothing is desired more prosperously. Let reason act and lead where it will, provided it leads correctly. God will do this, who must be invoked through such things alone, or certainly through these. But let us return to the matter I had instituted. For if it is known to you what a line is and what a figure is, tell me, I ask you, whether you think that figure can be made if the line is led to infinity from one side or the other? I affirm that this can be done in no way. What must be done so that I may make a figure? What else but that that line not be infinite and be led in a circle so that it reaches itself from the other side? I do not see how any space can be enclosed by one line unless it is done according to your description; it will not be a figure. If you wish to make a figure with straight lines, can it be done, or can it not be done from one line? By no means, nor from two. What about three? I see it can be done. Well then, you know and hold that a figure is to be made with three straight lines, and it cannot be done with fewer than three; if anything should oppose you, this reasoning will recall you to the truth. Clearly, if someone showed me this, there is nothing I would trust that I could know. Now, therefore, answer me how you will make a figure with three lines. When they join themselves at the ends. What, where they join themselves? Do you not see that angles are made? It is so. How many angles, therefore, does this figure consist of? The same number as the lines, M. Did you constitute the lines themselves as equal or unequal? D. Equal. M. What about the angles? They are patent. Or is one different from the other, either larger or smaller? Furthermore, I see that they themselves are also equal. Can it be made so that in a figure which is made with three equal straight lines, the angles are unequal or not?

...they rot. Once these conditions have taken hold, patients wish to be cured by medicines with a powerful, driving force, such as <term>nitre</term> <note>original: "niterum"; saltpeter or sodium carbonate, used here as a cleansing or caustic agent.</note>, <term>calcitis</term> <note>original: "calcitum"; a copper-bearing mineral used for its drying and astringent properties.</note>, <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmentum"; arsenic trisulfide, a highly caustic mineral used to "eat away" dead flesh.</note>, and <term>sandarac</term> <note>original: "sandaraca"; red arsenic sulfide.</note>, and other such things that can burn like fire and consume the putrefaction. If these medicines fail to help such wounds at all, physicians apply actual fire <note>cauterization</note> to dry out the humors and to thin the <term>pterygium-like growth</term> <note>original: "pterigillaginem"; likely referring to a film, scale, or callous growth on the skin or wound edge.</note>.

### Chapter 11. On carbuncles and other such things.

With these and similar medicines, they treat <term>anthrax</term> <note>original: "antracas"; from the Greek for "coal," referring to the black, burnt appearance of carbuncles.</note>, which is the same as a carbuncle. They drive out the suppressed [infection]. That is, where the place is putrid, they apply the medicine only at the junction where it is wounded so that it may "eat" <note>consume the diseased tissue</note>. However, using the <term>Androto</term> or <term>Musa</term> <note>Specific names for medicinal troches (pastilles) named after their inventors in the Greco-Roman tradition.</note>, or the other <term>troches</term> <note>original: "trocisci"; small medicinal lozenges or tablets intended to be dissolved or applied topically.</note> mentioned above, they smear the areas around the wound with sweetness <note>likely a sweet syrup or honey-based preparation</note>. They also rub the dry and red areas with the juice of <term>plantain</term> <note>original: "plantagini"; a common herb used to cool inflammation.</note>. But if the size of the swelling is great, they should apply a liniment with wine or a preparation for that purpose, and then with vinegar. They also use a <term>cataplasm</term> <note>a poultice</note> made of flour, vinegar, and honey, so that nothing stands in the way or hinders the healing. Soon at the beginning, blood should be drawn, or a treatment made according to the strength of the person and the severity of the cause. All these things should be done quickly at the start, as I said, to strike down the darkening [sore].

However, the physician should consider each limb and part in its differences: which parts of the body are naturally dry, which are moist, which are hot, which are dense, which are porous, which are strong, and which are weak. He must know how long a treatment should be held or how much a part can endure the strength of the medicines; some parts are naturally moist and hot. From this, they can know in their treatments how long something should be applied, and whether a part needs to be cooled, heated, moistened, or dried. For just as we know the whole body, so we must know each individual limb. For the limb itself will teach us its own cure.

I know that the ancients were not ignorant of which limbs or places of the body are naturally fleshy. If they suffer a <term>phlegmon</term> <note>original: "flegmonem"; a hot, red, painful swelling or inflammation.</note> (that is, some feverish heat), they should not be dried out completely. Those places that are "venous"—that is, abundant in small veins—and even more so those members where the arteries are, should be dried out the least of all. Especially those that are "nervous" <note>In 12th-century medicine, "nervous" (nervosa) often included tendons and ligaments.</note>, such as cartilaginous and bony parts. And until the part that suffers returns to its original nature, it should not yet be considered fully cured; and the work it performs as its office should be performed as it was before. For these medicines are very drying and are exceedingly cold in their power, and they must be consolidated certainly according to their own virtue. For often, if they are applied poorly or in the wrong place, these medicines do harm when applied.

It should be noted that the quality of the limbs varies the mode of treatment. For we treat the heat of the eyes in one way, the ears in another, and whatever else we care for in another. For who would dare to apply <term>nard oil</term> <note>original: "oleũ nardinũ"; a fragrant, warming oil from the spikenard plant.</note> or anything else of that nature to the heat of the eye, as we are accustomed to do for the ears? Or do we not pour sheep's milk into the eye, such as fresh woman's milk? But who would dare [to do that to the ear?]...

The ignorant do not have less of it; the wise do not have more.
Nature is stored within; <term>Qing</term> <gloss>Emotions</gloss> are expressed without.
Grief, fear, joy, anger, desire, hatred, and love.
Just as a spring must flow, just as a trunk must have branches.

When moved by a stimulus, this is called the <term>Ji</term> <gloss>incipient stirrings</gloss>.
The name of these stirrings is where good and evil are distinguished.
When they break out, that is evil; when they hit the mark of moderation, that is good.
The feelings of commiseration, shame, deference, and right or wrong.

> *He carried the same around his comrades three times with pure water,*
> *Sprinkling with light dew, and a branch of budding olive,*
> *And purified the men.*

Where Servius says: He carried around, that is, purified with water; it is an ancient word. Thus Plautus: I will carry you around as if you were possessed, that is, I will purify you. For lustration is so called from the carrying around of a torch or sulfur. Thus Servius reads in the Plautine passage, though he did not specify in which comedy it appears; so that in common editions, one seeks it in vain because of the varied reading. Thus, lustration through air, water, or fire was most frequent; that by a dog or puppy, and its leading or carrying around the human body, was rarer, with "purifying women" also being employed for this purpose.

<margin>l. iii.</margin>
Whence those whom Theophrastus calls <term>hiereias</term> <gloss>priestesses</gloss>, are called <term>apomaktriai</term> <gloss>wipers-off</gloss> by Pollux in the *Onomasticon*, and <term>perimaktriai</term> <gloss>those who wipe all around</gloss> by Plutarch, from the term <term>perimattesthai</term> <gloss>to wipe all around</gloss>. Everything has come to nothing like running water. Similarly, I also, most miserable, have been reduced to nothing, and I did not know it, for my days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like hay. For we are dust, and man is like hay; his days shall flourish like the flower of the field, for the spirit will pass through it, and it will not stand, and he will know his place no more. Behold now, consider that man is a fragile thing, a thing enduring for a small time, like the flower that grows in the field. Whence Isaiah 40: "All flesh is hay, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. Truly the people is hay. The hay has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains forever." And therefore why does man, who is like the hay of the rooftops which has withered before it is pulled up, boast? Whence it is written in Tobias: "Flesh is a vessel of clay, a lamentable vessel, withered hay, a fragile clod, a sack of stench. The life of the flesh is labor; the conception of the flesh is menstrual decay; the end is putrefaction, the origin is mud. First it is sperm, now a stinking sack, later food for worms in the tomb. For what does man boast so much?" Likewise Bernard, in his book of *Meditations*: "Whence does man boast, whose conception is guilt, birth is pain and labor, life is the necessity to die? After the man is the worm, after the worm is stench and horror. Thus every man is turned into a non-man." Attend therefore, and see the beginning of your life.

## ABSOLUTIO

<margin>11.</margin>Quæritur: Quænam ex verbis absolutionis: *Ego te absolvo a peccatis tuis in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti*, pertineant ad essentiam formæ, & sint necessaria ad valorem sacramenti?

Resp. Quamvis DD. inter se pugnent, & alii scripserint, hæc verba: *a peccatis tuis* esse solum de necessitate præcepti, & ad essentiam formæ non spectare, ac sufficere doceant ista: *absolvo te*: tamen negari non potest major probabilitas sententiæ dicentis, verba illa, *a peccatis tuis* spectare quoque ad essentiam formæ; nam ea est plurium opinio, & colligi videtur ex *Trident. sess. 14. cap. 3.* Maxime, quia illa verba: *absolvo te*: sunt indifferentia ad absolutionem a *peccatis, & censuris*; ergo ut significent determinate absolutionem a *peccatis*, debent determinari per hæc: *a peccatis tuis*; cum itaque tutior sit ista sententia, proculdubio qui ea omittit, exponit Sacramentum periculo nullitatis, quia dum agitur de Sacramentorum valore, semper sunt tutiora sequenda juxta decretum *Innoc. XII. damnantis prop. 1.*

<margin>12.</margin>Quæritur. An absolutio a peccatis possit conferri absenti, qui per Epistolam, vel per nuncium confiteretur?

# PROPOSITION
## The Principal.

While there are indeed various questions in the whole epistle, and individual passages have their own proper proposition, nevertheless, nothing prevents calling everything back to one general statement, which in a certain way contains the <term>ὑπόθεσιν</term> <gloss>hypothesis/subject matter</gloss>. Let that general proposition be therefore:

It is the duty of the <term>Corinthians</term> in every way, with dissensions and the corruption of morals removed, to cultivate agreement in doctrine and morals by every kind of virtue, so that the image of God may be restored in them and perfected for the coming of our Lord <term>Jesus Christ</term>.

# DIVISION OF THE WHOLE EPISTLE
## into certain parts.

From the end, the whole epistle can be distributed into two parts. For first, he corrects the dissensions risen from the emulation of teachers, which generally pertain to the restoration of sound doctrine. Then, he amends corrupt morals, so that the innocence of life might be restored among them, by which they might walk without offense to the brethren. Furthermore, the restoration of sound doctrine and the innocence of morals are regarded as the ends in the whole epistle. But because the division is concise and treated sporadically in the epistle, let us add

Whoever dies in his love has attained every goal.
How much healing from illness, how much he cleared from darkness!
How many favors he has for those present and the absent!
How many places are there where tears were shed
in his mind when he was called in love for my master.
I am infatuated with him, rising in his proximity.
My Lord, hasten it for me, so the drink may become clear for me.
How many generous acts he has, how many gifts he bestowed!
How many reliable people narrated from him every obligatory knowledge.
Excellent is that Chosen One, and chivalry, and loyalty.
The virtue of Ahmad is not hidden in the east or the west.
O Messenger of God, O best of all the Prophets,
save us from an abyss, the one that makes me grow <note>possibly a poetic reference to a trial or the self</note>.

renew the submission after the Yathribi Prophet <note>the Prophet from Medina</note>.
Upon him, grant peace as long as a branch sways in the sanctuary,
or the full moon of the sky appears in the beauty of the gleaming one.
The Prophet, may God's blessings be upon him, and He will attain his blessings.
Everyone who prays upon him, the answer is [there].
O most generous of God's creation, I have no one to seek refuge with
other than you when the general calamity occurs.
And the status of the Messenger of God will not be narrow for me
when the Generous reveals Himself by the name of the Avenger.
For from your bounty is this world and the next,
and from your sciences is the knowledge of the Tablet and the Pen.
O soul, do not despair of a slip that has become great,

## IN LUKE.

there was a lack of wood for a cross.

<margin>To whom he wrote.</margin>
I have advised briefly concerning the author; let us also say to whom he wrote. Matthew is said to have written to the Hebrews; the other three to the Gentiles, and therefore Jerome affirms that Luke wrote to the Greeks. And Nicephorus, book 6, chapter 16, says: he was concerned to write to the Gentiles, through Paul by Luke.

<margin>Who Theophilus is.</margin>
Luke himself testifies that his writing pertains to Theophilus, and even if we grant that this man was of the senatorial order, nevertheless, in his person, all the faithful are not incorrectly understood; for whoever has true religion at heart, and loves God seriously, he can be called a <term>theophilus</term> <gloss>friend of God</gloss> in reality, and for that reason Luke dedicated his writings to all the faithful.

Regarding the matter of the writing, the third and last point remains. We said in the preface to Matthew what the Gospel is and how it is received in the sacred scriptures; from there those things should be repeated. But here special things pertain, such as the occasion, the genre of speech, the proposition, the parts, etc.

<margin>The occasion of writing, which was Luke's.</margin>
The occasion was offered to him, and indeed imposed by necessity. Whether this task was enjoined upon him by Peter, as Dorotheus wants, or by Paul, as Nicephorus, who in book 2, chapter 45, writes that he was ordered by Paul to write, just as Mark was by Peter, and in book 5, chapter 16. Certainly the authority of such great men was necessarily to be followed by him.

<summary>This page explores to whom Luke addressed his Gospel, interpreting Theophilus as a representative of all the faithful, and discusses the various apostolic influences behind the composition of the work.</summary>

That I have adapted my Saturnian System to the Copernican System, no one, I think, can rightly reproach me. Yet since Fabrius interdicts it for all Catholics, I wonder why he does not pronounce that all my inventions are to be rejected on this name alone. But he saw, I believe, that I could easily substitute the Tychonic system for the Copernican. For whether I use one or the other matters very little as far as the phenomena are concerned. But the truth of the matter is explained no differently than by following Copernicus; whose opinion our Saturnian System also recommends not a little.

I do not understand, however, how Fabrius can assert so confidently that this opinion about the motion of the Earth is to be held only by heterodox Aristarchians. For as often as I confer with Catholics (namely, Roman ones) about it, they profess that they are by no means bound by the decrees issued to the contrary, whether they proceeded from the Cardinals or from the Supreme Pontiff himself. To whom they do not attribute so much in the interpretation of the meaning of Sacred Scripture that one must necessarily stand by them even in controversies of fact, as they call them: and clearly, they think the rest of the Earth is to be established by reasons rather than sanctioned by edicts. Furthermore, it is certain that in France the Copernican System is defended everywhere not as a hypothesis, but as liquid truth, and that by the Ecclesiastics and Priests themselves, who teach that doctrine publicly in entire volumes, with Rome, as far as I know, saying nothing to the contrary. Weighing all these things, I long ago believed that, beyond those ignorant of astronomy and the unskilled multitude, only some Cleanthes, among whom is Fabrius, still adhere to an ancient error and struggle in vain against the motion of the Earth.

Ratio prioris est: quia subjicibile, qua tale, non est praedicabile, ut per se constat; ergo cum Logicum sit Universale praedicabile, subjicibile, qua tale, non erit universale Logicum. Atqui cum universale metaphysicum nec in praedicabilitate, nec in subjicibilitate situm sit; sed in inexistentia unius in multis, sicut subjicibile, qua tale, potest adhuc esse unum aptum esse in multis, ita etiam poterit esse universale metaphysicum. Ratio posterioris est, quia Genus, quod est subjicibile, (verbi gratia animal respectu viventis,) est etiam praedicabile respectu rationalis, & irrationalis.

VII. Q. *An Genus in communi, univoce predicetur de Genere entis realis, & entis rationis?* Respondeo. Haec duo Genera secundum suas partes materiales tantum convenire inter se analogice; quia Ens tantum analogice potest praedicari de ente reali, & ente rationis. At vero si in esse generis, & prout sunt considerationis Logicae accipiantur; cum utriusque idem prorsus sit artificium Logicum, & conceptus, dubium non esse, quia univoce inter se conveniant.

VIII. Q. *Cum Genus summum ab infimo aeque multum distet, quam Genus infimum a Specie; cur Genus infimum aliud est universale, quam species; & Genus summum non aliud, quam genus infimum?* Respondeo. Diversitatem istam non petendam esse a majori vel minori distantia, quam universalia habent in linea praedicamentali; sed ab eorum conceptu quidditativo. Cum itaque & Genus summum, & Genus infimum praedicentur ut pars materialis; species vero, ut tota essentia; dubium esse nullum potest, quin species a Genere infimo plus differat, quam hoc a summo.

IX. Q. *An conceptus definiens Genus signatum sit conceptus faciens formaliter Genus exercitum?* Respondeo. Cum conceptus faciens Genus in actu exercito debeat etiam facere universale in actu exercito; universale autem fieri non possit per conceptum simplicem non abstrahentem a multitudine; & conceptus definiens Genus signatum non abstrahat a multitudine; sicut est conceptus simplex, ita non est conceptus faciens Genus in actu exercito. Per definitionem itaque Generis definitur Genus signate, non autem fit exercite.

X. Q. *Quid sit species in communi sumpta?* Respondeo. Etsi certum sit, speciem metaphysicam sumptam in communi recte posse dici, *Unum aptum inesse multis ut tota essentia*; ingens tamen inter hanc & speciem Logicam cum sit discrimen, non immerito quaeri posset, an cum Logicum universale sit praedicabile, Speciei Logicae dari possit definitio in communi? Hinc de hac definitione apud autores altum ubique silentium, semper definientes speciem vel praedicabilem tantum, vel tantum subjicibilem. Censemus itaque Speciei in communi sumptae, prout includit Praedicabilem, & subjicibilem, non posse aliam meliorem hac (*Unum aptum ut totam essentiam terminare propositionem*,) definitionem dari. Nolumus tamen asserere, alios male egisse, dum speciem prius diviserunt, & divisam primum definierunt. Nam

cùm species subjicibilis in esse Universalis, et speciei Logicæ, non conveniat univocè cum Prædicabili ; quæ autem univocè inter se non conveniunt, priùs debeant juxta Aristotelem dividi, et postmodum definiri; constat Autores agentes de specie tantùm Logica, hoc est prout est unum ex prædicabilibus, rectè divisas tantùm species definivisse.

XI. Quæstio. *Qua ratione definienda sit species Prædicabilis, et subjicibilis?* Responsio. Speciem Prædicabilem esse *Unum aptum ut totam essentiam prædicari de multis.* Subjicibilis verò est, *Quæ subjicitur generi, Vel quod idem est Unum aptum, ut tota essentia esse subjectum propositionis.* Cùm enim hic sermo tantùm sit de propositione naturali; si prædicatum latiùs patet subjecto, quod est species, tunc debet hoc ipso esse genus; ergo in præsenti, idem est esse subjectum propositionis, et subjici generi.

XII. Quæstio. *An præter dictas species nulla alia restet?* Responsio. Specierum adhuc aliam esse subalternam, aliam Infimam, ut vult communis sententia. Infima est, *Unum aptum ut totam essentiam prædicari de pluribus numero tantùm diversis.* verbi gratia homo, qui de Francisco, Petro, Paulo et cetera Differentibus inter se tantùm numero prædicatur. Subalterna autem est : *Unum aptum ut tota essentia subjici; et ut pars materialis prædicari.* Quia scilicet ipsa est, ut Porphyrius capite secundo inquit, Genus et species, sed diverso respectu.

XIII. Quæstio. *An ad hoc, ut differat Genus à specie, sufficiat, hanc ut totam essentiam; illud verò ut partem materialem prædicari: cùm vivens verbi gratia genus sit, et species, et eadem constitutiva, nempe corpus animatum includat?* Responsio. Inter Genus et speciem materialiter sumpta, sufficere prædictum discrimen, non tamen inter Genus et speciem formaliter sumpta. Nam conceptus faciens speciem formaliter debet esse complexus ita concipiens *corpus animatum* ut genus et differentiam, ut vi illius conceptus evadant hæc duo *unum aptum ut tota essentia prædicari de pluribus.* Quòd si autem conceptu simplici concipiatur *corpus animatum*, tunc idem erit, ac *vivens*, quod est Genus, et non species formaliter accepta. Quin etiam reperitur differentia inter conceptum facientem subalternam, et infimam, nam objectum conceptûs facientis speciem subalternam non potest ita præcisè dari à parte rei. verbi gratia nullum datur objectum, quod sit præcisè *corpus animatum*. Objectum autem conceptûs facientis speciem infimam datur, à parte rei, verbi gratia *animal rugibile*.

XIV. Quæstio. *Cùm pars de toto nequeat formaliter prædicari; Genus autem sit pars speciei, quæ totum est; quomodo dici potest Genus formaliter prædicari posse de specie?* Responsio. Partem quidem non posse formaliter de toto prædicari sumptam in abstracto; at bene in concreto. Hinc licèt formaliter non bene dicam: *homo est animalitas*, rectè tamen dico: *homo est animal*.

XV. Quæstio. *Cùm species infima prædicabilis sit tantùm de individuis, intelligi non potest, nisi constet, quid sit Individuum; quid igitur nomine Individui intelligitur?* Responsio.

How, however, can it happen that the same thing extends more and less broadly than itself; is above and below itself? Answer. It is clear from the response to the previous question. The Genus defined here does not contain, as a dividing member, the genus of the definition; for the defined Genus is the whole concrete which we call Genus; but the genus of the definition is only the material part of this concrete; therefore the defining genus is not contained by the defined Genus, and consequently is not below it; but only above it, since it is a universal in common, which is predicable of each of its species. Nor does it hinder this doctrine that a universal is concrete: for although the defining genus is concrete, which is called *universal*, it is not, however, the concrete which is called *Genus*. And the reason is: because that alone is defined by some definition with which the definition is convertible; but the definition of Genus is only convertible with Genus, which is concrete, or the first dividing member of the Universal; therefore, etc.

V. Question. *Since not all things that are predicable in "what it is" of things different in species stand in the same way; what, and how many dividing members of the defined Genus should be assigned?* Answer. Because there are some Genera that can indeed be predicated, but not be subject <note>original: "subjici", meaning to be used as a subject of a proposition</note>; some, however, both to be subject and to be predicated; some, finally, only to be subject; therefore some are Most General Genera, others Subaltern, others finally Lowest <note>original: "Infima"</note>. The most general genera are those that obtain the highest place in any Predicamental table. The lowest, however, are those which are placed before things differing only in species. Those finally that are intermediate between these are called Subaltern. The Most General Genus, however, is defined: *That which is only predicable of inferiors as a material part.* The subaltern, however: *That which is predicable of many differing more than in species, and is at the same time subjectible along with others differing even more than in species from itself.* The lowest, finally: *That which is predicable as a material part of many differing only in species among themselves.* And because one Lowest Genus is such simply, another however only in a certain respect, we say that the Lowest Genus simply is: *That which is equally predicable of many differing among themselves only in species.* The other Lowest Genus is: *Predicable of inferiors, of which one cannot be divided into many different in species, but another can.* From which definitions it appears that a Lowest Genus not such simply is only lowest with respect to one inferior; with respect to another, however, it is a subaltern Genus. Furthermore, those Genera, *one of which contains another as a potential part*, are called subordinated; for example *substance, body, living*, etc. Those, however, of which one does not contain the other, will be called Disparate Genera; for example *fish, bird, plant*.

Constare ex responsione ad superiorem quæstionem. Genus hic definitum non continere, tanquam membrum dividens, genus definitionis; nam Genus definitum est totum concretum, quod vocamus Genus; genus verò definitionis tantùm est pars materialis hujus concreti; ergo genus definiens non continetur à Genere definito, et consequenter non est ipso inferius; sed tantùm superius, cùm sit universale in communi, quod de singulis illius speciebus est prædicabile. Nec huic doctrinæ obest, quòd universale sit concretum: nam licet genus definiens sit concretum, quod *universale* dicitur, non tamen est concretum, quod *Genus* vocatur. Et ratio est: quia illud tantùm est definitum alicujus definitionis, quócum definitio est convertibilis; sed definitio Generis est tantùm convertibilis cum Genere, quod est concretum, sive primum membrum dividens Universalis; ergo et cetera.

V. Quæstio. *Cùm non omnia, quæ de pluribus specie differentibus sunt prædicabilia in quid, eodem modo se habeant; quæ, et quot membra dividentia Genus definitum sint assignanda?* Responsio. Quia sunt quædam Genera, quæ prædicari quidem possunt, non tamen subjici; quædam verò et subjici, et prædicari; quædam denique tantùm subjici; ideo alia sunt Genera Generalissima, alia Subalterna, alia denique Infima. Genera generalissima sunt illa, quæ in quavis tabula Prædicamentali supremum locum obtinent. Infima verò quæ specie tantùm differentibus præponuntur. Quæ denique inter hæc media sunt, Subalterna vocantur. Genus autem Generalissimum definitur, *Quod tantùm prædicabile est de inferioribus ut pars materialis.* Subalternum verò, *Quod est prædicabile de pluribus plus, quàm specie, differentibus, et simul cum alijs plus etiam, quàm specie à se differentibus* subjicibile. Infimum denique, *Quod est prædicabile ut pars materialis de pluribus specie tantùm diversis inter se.* Et quia Genus Infimum aliud est simpliciter tale, aliud verò tantùm secundùm quid. Ideo dicimus, Genus Infimum simpliciter, esse, *Quod est æqualiter prædicabile de pluribus specie tantùm inter se differentibus.* Alterum verò Genus Infimum est, *Prædicabile de inferioribus, quorum aliud non possit in plura specie diversa dividi, aliud autem possit.* Ex quibus definitionibus apparet, Genus Infimum non simpliciter tale, esse tantùm respectu unius inferioris Infimum; respectu verò alterius esse Genus subalternum. Præterea illa Genera, *Quorum unum continet alterum tanquam partem potestativam*, vocantur subordinata; verbi gratia *substantia, corpus, vivens* et cetera. Quorum autem unum non continet alterum, Genera dicentur Disparata; verbi gratia *Piscis, avis, planta*.

VI. Quæstio. *An Genus subjicibile (idem dicendum de specie subjicibili) sit Universale; cùm non sit prædicabile?* Responsio. Genus subjicibile sumptum reduplicativè non esse Universale Logicum, at bene Metaphysicum: sumptum verò specificativè esse

Logicum verò *Quod de uno tantùm potest prædicari*. Quæ definitio bona est, sive accipiatur in sensu negativo (*quod de nullo alio potest prædicari*) sive in sensu positivo, scilicet, *Quod de seipso præcisè, saltem identicè, potest prædicari*.

XVI. Quæstio. *An hæ definitiones etiam constent genere, et differentiâ?* Responsio. Circa definitionem Individui Logici non posse esse dubium, quin illa constet genere (quod exprimitur per τὸ prædicabile) et differentiâ expressâ reliquis definitionis verbis. At fuêre, qui in definitione Individui metaphysici non invenientes genus et differentiam, eam putarent esse superfluam, et sufficere, si dicatur, *Indivisum in se*. Qui sanè non rectè sentiunt, cùm distinguere deberent inter Individuum formaliter, et individuum tantùm materialiter. Nam ut dixi quæstione 1. parte 1. de Uno, *Indivisum in se* est genus Unius, sive individui formaliter sumpti: quod etiam convenire posset mihi, si conjunctus essem corpori verbi gratia equino. Quo tamen casu non essem Individuum formaliter (nisi per Individuum intelligere quis velit totum complexum) præcisè ideo, quia non essem divisus ab omni alio.

XVII. Quæstio. *An hæc Individui definitio: Cujus collectio proprietatum in nullo alio est reperibilis: aut Cujus proprietates sub eadem combinatione non possunt alteri naturaliter convenire; sit essentialis?* Responsio. Ex duabus quæstione superiore datis definitionibus rectè deducitur, istas duas, quæ in re sunt una, non esse essentiales. Ratio est: quia ad hoc, ut aliqua definitio sit alicui essentialis, requiritur, ut, si non verificaretur de aliquo, hoc aliquod non posset dici illius definitum. Atqui, si unius verbi gratia Ovi A. omnes proprietates ponerentur esse etiam in Ovo B. de his ovis non verificaretur proposita definitio; et tamen, quia utrumque eorum esset *Indivisum ab omni alio*, et *Prædicabile tantùm de uno*, forent illa ova Individua, et consequenter definitum illius definitionis; ergo et cetera.

XVIII. Quæstio. *An re ipsa fieri possit, ut inter duo individua nulla prorsus detur discernibilitas?* Responsio. Mihi multò probabiliùs videri, nullum individuum esse possibile, quod non saltem à DEO discerni possit ab altero. Nam ponamus, DEUM simul in eodem loco, eodem tempore, ejusdem figuræ, ejusdem formæ producere duo ova; etsi per has circumstantias non possent hujusmodi ova discerni, possent tamen adhuc per alias discerni: nam cùm ovum A. non possit produci nisi per decretum volens producere ovum A. Ovum B. verò per decretum volens producere ovum B. Et decretum volens producere ovum A. debeat ipsum producere in determinatis aliquibus circumstantijs, quibus hoc decretum extrinsecè discriminatur quasi, (idem suo modo dicendum de decreto volente producere ovum B.) conficitur hinc, Ovum A. dicere respectum ad decretum volens producere ipsum in his circumstantijs; quem respectum ovum B. hoc ipso dicere non potest, quòd ovum B. dicat respectum ad decretum volens ovum B. producere in his etiam circumstantijs. ### Oleum Cicinum.

GELISCO, nouae Hispaniae prouincia, oleum seu liquor quidam adfertur, cui, oleum ficus infernalis, Hispani nomen indiderunt, eo quod ex arbore cum fructu, tum foliis simili Ricino, sed in maiorem altitudinem, ob soli ubertatem, excrescente, elicitur.

Eadem uero ratione hoc oleum Indi eliciunt, quam docuit Dioscorides lib. 1. cap. 30. hoc est, contuso semine, deinde in aqua cocto, postremum oleo innatante cochlearibus excepto. Hec eliciendorum oleorum ratio e feminibus & fructibus, Indis admodum familiaris est, quippe qui nullam expressionem norint: sed etiam hoc oleum isto modo quam expressione facilius elicitur.

<header>TACAMAHACA.</header>

<margin>Stomachic plaster.</margin>
From this, with a third part of storax and a moment of amber, a plaster is made that is most useful for the stomach: for it strengthens it, excites the appetite, aids digestion, and dispels flatulence. Applied to the brain in the same way, it strengthens it and removes pains. It has great efficacy in pains of the hip and every disease of the joints, especially if it arises from cold or mixed humors: since, besides the power of resolving, it also participates in astringency, for which reason it strengthens the parts in a wonderful manner.

Applied alone to wounds of the joints or nerves, it heals them: for it immediately brings them to suppuration and prevents spasms. I mix in a third part of wax, since it is applied more easily.

In short, its use is so celebrated that the common people know no other remedy for any pain, provided they are not highly inflamed; but it is very useful even in these cases, in the decline of the disease, for dispelling the remaining humor. It is hot at the beginning of the third degree, participates in much astringency, and is dry in the second.

Caraña.

<margin>Caraña.</margin>
From the interior part of the continent, through Cartagena and Nombre de Dios, a resin is brought, similar in color to Tacamahaca but more splendid, more liquid, and denser, called Caraña in the Indian language, a name it has also retained among the Spaniards, with the smell of Tacamahaca but heavier. It is fatty and oily, and therefore tenacious without much agglutination and melting. It is a new medicine, which was first brought here ten years ago.

<margin>Properties of Caraña.</margin>
The Indians use it for tumors and pains of all kinds. It is praised for the same diseases that Tacamahaca is accustomed to cure, and it exerts its powers in a shorter space of time: such that Caraña heals those whom Tacamahaca has not cured. We saw an example in someone who, due to a torture of the shoulder, could not move his arm for a long time, even though he had used Tacamahaca: but after he began to use Caraña, he was restored to health in three days.

Its power in pains of the joints is wondrous: for when applied, it easily cures them, provided there is no cause of hot humors.

<margin>Emplastrum stomachicū.</margin>
Ex ea, Styracis tertia parte, & Ambari momento, fit emplastrum stomacho longè utilissimum: siquidem illū roborat, appetitū ciet, concoctionem iuuat, & flatus discutit. Eodem modo cerebro imposita, eū roborat, & dolores aufert. Magna est efficacia in doloribus coxendicis, & omni articulorum morbo, praesertim si ab humoribus frigidis aut mixtis proue-niat: quoniā praeter resoluendi facultatē, etiā adstrictionis particeps est, qua de causa mirū in modum partes roborat.

Sola iuncturarum aut neruorū vulneribus imposita, ea curat: nā statim suppurat & spasmum prohibet. ego tertiā parte cerae admisceo, quoniā facilius inducitur.

In summa, adeò celebris est eius usus, ut plebs ad qualemeumque dolorem aliud remedium non norit, modò non sint inflammationes admodum calidae: sed & in his admodum utilis est, in morbi declinatione, ad discutiendum, qui supererat, humorem. Calida est initio tertij gradus, multae adstrictionis particeps, & sicca in secundo.

Caraña.

<margin>Caraña.</margin>
Ex Continentis parte interiore, per Carthaginem & Nome Dei, defertur resina colore Tacamahaca, sed splendidior, liquidior, ac densior, lingua Indica Caraña dicta, quod nomen etiam apud Hispanos retinuit, odore Tacamahaca, sed grauiore. Pinguis est & oleaginosa, ideoque tenax sine multa adglutinatione & colliquatione. Medicamentū nouum est, quod decem annis elapsis primùm huc illatum est.

<margin>Carañae facultates.</margin>
Ea utuntur Indi in tumoribus & omnis generis doloribus. Ad eosdem morbos laudatur, quos Tacamahaca curare solet, & minore temporis spatio vires suas exerit: sic ut quos Tacamahaca nō curarit, Caraña sanet. Exemplū vidimus in eo qui ob humeri cruciatiam multo tempore brachiu mouere non poterat, tametsi Tacamahaca usus esset: sed postquā Caraña uti coepit, triduo sanitati restitutus est.

Mira est eius vis in iuncturarum doloribus: nā imposita, facilè illos curat, modò nulla sit calidorū humorum influxio.

### XXXVII.

Sed hic dubium occurrit, quis dicatur Prodigus? An is cui interdictio fit sola lege? ita quidem voluit Donellus *liber 12. commentariorum juris civilis caput 22.* Fachinaeus *2. controversiarum 63.* an vero is cui decreto magistratus interdicitur administratio? quae sententia posterior cum sit receptior, et textibus ac rationi juris magis consentanea, mihi quoque arridet.

Quilibet etiam ex singulari ratione inutiliter pecuniam mutuam dat adolescenti luxurioso, quem scit pecuniam perditurum. *lex 12. paragrapho 11. Digesta mandati lex 24. paragrapho 4. I gave a dish, or a mass of gold or silver, so that you might sell it, and use the money, and you have sold it, and accepted the money redacted from it as a credit. *law 11, beginning, Digest on this title, law 19, in the beginning, Digest on prescriptive words.*

### XXIII.

But if, however, that dish, or mass of gold or silver, has perished by accident before it was sold, it must be thought that it perished at the receiver's risk, unless the one handing it over had previously intended it for sale: for in this case it does not perish for the creditor otherwise than if he had given it to be sold to another, who was not going to use the money. *law 4, in the beginning, the said law 11, in the beginning, Digest on this title, law 34, in the beginning, near the end, Digest on mandate.*

### XXIV.

Similarly, also here a singular mode of giving a loan for consumption has been received, if to you requesting a loan for consumption from me, I shall order my debtor to give you the money owed to me. *law 15, beginning, Digest on this title, law 34, in the beginning, verse: item that, Digest on mandate.* It is another thing if, to you requesting money as a loan, I shall order my debtor to promise, and you shall have stipulated from him as from another's debtor: for in this case you are held to me not by an action of loan for consumption, but by a <term>condiction</term> without cause. *law 32, Digest on this title.*

### XXV.

In which and similar cases, since the substantial elements that are required for a true and proper loan for consumption are lacking, (such as enumeration for the cause of a loan for consumption: money or a thing consisting in weight, number, or measure: and ownership of the money) a strict loan for consumption cannot exist. Since, however, in these cases money is sought as if it were a loan for consumption. *law 9, § last, law 19, Digest on prescriptive words, law 15, Digest on this title,* it is a consequence that this has been received benignly and singularly, because of the frequency of this contract, and its daily use. *law 9, § 8, Digest on this title.*

### XXVI.

But since all law is constituted for the sake of men. *law 2, Digest on the status of men, § last, Institutes on the Law of Nature, of Nations, and of Civil Law,* it will be little to know what and how fourfold a loan for consumption is, if the persons who can give and receive a loan for consumption are ignored. To these, therefore, I proceed, intending to act first concerning those who can give a loan for consumption.

### XXVII.

But all who can consent can give a loan for consumption *law 1, § 3, verse: but so much, Digest on pacts, law 32, Digest on this title,* and have the faculty of alienating. *law 1, 2, § 4, Digest on this title, law 2, Code if a certain thing is sought, and etc.*

### XL.

Sed quid juris sit si filiusfamilias contra SCtum de facto mutuatus sit, atque ex causa illa mutui postea pecuniam paternam solverit, quaeritur? Distinguendo respondendum: Aut enim pecunia adhuc extat, aut est consumpta. Priore casu cum pecunia alienata & creditori verè soluta non fuerit, quippe sine patris voluntate numerata, pater istam absque metu exceptionis vindicare poterit, secundùm l. 14. ff. h. t. Posteriore casu, si scilicet pecunia fuerit consumpta, ita distinguendum: aut filiusfamilias peculij alienationem non habuit, adeoque nec reverâ solvit, & tum competit patri condictio per l. 9. §. 1. ff. de SC. Maced. aut peculij alienationem habuit, cùm ex patris forsan voluntate solvit d. l. 9. §. 3. vel pater ratum habuit quod solvit l. 7. §. 15. ff. d. t. ac propterea reverâ solvit: & hoc casu patri condictio non competit. d. l. 14. in fin. ff. h. t.

### XLI.

An autem si filiusfamilias mutuatus pecuniam, peculium adventitium in solutum dederit, pater etiam eius repetitionem habeat, quaestionis est? Distinguendo: aut pater habet usumfructum in ijs rebus & filius eas non potest in praejudicium patris alienare. l. ult. §. 5. vers. filijs autem familias C. de bon. quae liber. aut pater usumfructum non habet: & jus nullum repetendi ei ex persona sua competere potest. Neque priori distinctionis membro obstat: quod ususfructus earum rerum quae usu consumuntur, tantùm legato constituatur: id enim cum communi schola negandum videtur. Dn. XXXIII. De Tempore Imaginario idem judicamus, quod de spatio Imaginario, scilicet ipsum præter durationes rerum intrinsecas, fundantes di- uersas relationes distantiæ et propinquitatis, re ipsâ nihil esse.

XXXIV. Postremò Duratio alia est creata, alia increata. Increata est propria solius DEI, diciturque Æternitas; et definitur à Boëtio: *Intermi- nabilis vitæ tota simul et perfecta possessio.* Duratio creata alia est temporaria, a- lia perpetua. Temporaria est, quæ et principium habet et finem. Perpetua, quæ saltem finem non habet. Velut duratio Angelorum et Animæ rationalis, quæ et Aevum dicitur, et communiter definitur, *Permanentia rei in esse aliquando ac- cepto interminata.*

### DE QVANTITATE.

XXXV. Quantum describit Aristoteles hîc lib. 5. tex 18. *Quod est divisibile in ea, quæ insunt, quorum utrumque vel unumquodque unum quid, et hoc aliquid aptum est esse.* Id est (ut quidem P. Suarez interpretatur) quorum v- trumque aptum est naturâ suâ per sese, ut unum quoddam totum, ab alijs separatum, manere, et quidem quantum est ex vi quantitatis, eodem modo di- visibile, divisibilitate scilicet Physicâ, et naturali, vi cuius unum Corpus naturaliter expellit aliud, vel partes eius à loco, quem ante occupabant.

XXXVI. Est sententia, ut ait P. Suarez, inter Thomistas satis vul- garis, primarium quantitatis effectum formalem esse distinctionem par- tium integralium; ita ut sine quantitate nec Materia prima, nec ulla alia entitas materialis aliquas partes integrantes habeat. Thomistas ex Nostris secutus est P. Vasquez tom. 3. in 3. p. d. 190. à n. 20. Sed contrà 1. Nam sicuti vnaquæque res per se ipsam est ens, ita per se ipsam est vna, et conse- quenter divisa et distincta à quovis alio. 2. Quia aliàs procedendum foret in infinitum. Nam si vna res est distincta ab aliâ per aliam entitatem tertiam, ergo ab illâ tertiâ debebit iterum distingui per aliam quartam, et sic in infini- tum. 3. Quia Materia supponitur ad quantitatem cum totâ suâ entitate. Ergo non potest accipere partes ab illâ: cùm enim totum nihil aliud sit, quàm omnes partes, quod supponitur cum totâ entitate, debet etiam supponi cum partibus. Non potest ergo primarius effectus formalis quantitatis consistere in distinctio- ne partium.

XXXI. The duration of a thing is not distinguished from its productive action. The reason is: 1. If the duration of primary <term>materia</term> <gloss>prime matter</gloss>, for example, were distinct from its production, it would follow that primary matter is a cause and is not a cause of its duration. It would be: because that duration would not be created, but would be drawn out from the potentiality of the matter. And it would not be: because matter cannot be prior by nature than its own duration. For it would have to be supposed and understood as existing in this instant, before it had that by which it formally exists in this instant. Which involves an open contradiction. And do not say, with Father <term>Arriaga</term> <gloss>Rodrigo de Arriaga, a Jesuit philosopher</gloss>, that for "prior by nature" nothing is understood except only the entity of the matter with indifference to existing in this or that time. For to be prior by nature says to be prior to another in this real instant. Therefore, primary matter cannot be understood as "prior by nature" with indifference to existing in this or that instant. 2. If duration were distinguished from the productive action of a thing, the conservation of no act would be formally free. Because the action itself, through which an act is produced, and insofar as it precedes the mode of duration, is not conservation, nor is it a new exercise of freedom; however, the mode of duration itself, which follows such an action, is not formally free, but necessarily results from the entity of the thing. And so, conservation as such would never be formally free; which does not seem to be something to say. For that which has new laudability and merit must have new freedom. But the conservation of a good act has new laudability and merit.

XXXII. It seems more probable that an indivisible created duration is not possible, which would correspond, in and of itself and essentially, to several parts of time. The reason is: 1. Because no creature can be given which, antecedently and from the intrinsic, is <term>inannihilabilis</term> <gloss>incapable of being annihilated</gloss> for any time, since this indeed seems to be against the supreme subjection of the creature, by which it ought, for any instant with respect to GOD, to be able both to be and not to be. 2. If such a duration were possible, it would have to exist in fact in Angels and in the rational soul; for since these entities are by their own nature indefectible, they would most especially require such a mode of duration; which, however, they do not have in fact, as is evident from the Holy Scriptures and the Fathers; by whom all things are said to be annihilable by GOD at any moment, so that no created thing can in any way resist him. Therefore, it is a sign that such a mode of duration is not possible.

XXXI. Duratio rei non distinguitur ab actione productivâ illius. Ratio est. 1. Si duratio Materiae primae v. g. esset distincta à productione illius, sequeretur Materiam primam esse causam, & non esse causam durationis illius. Esset: quia illa duratio non crearetur, sed educeretur ex potentiâ Materiae. Et non esset. Quia Materia non potest esse naturâ prior, quàm ipsius duratio. Deberet enim supponi & intelligi existens in hoc instanti, antequam haberet id, per quod formaliter in hoc instanti existit. Quod apertam contradictionem involvit. Neque dicas cum P. Arriagâ, pro priori Naturae nihil intelligi, nisi solam entitatem Materiae cum indifferentiâ ad existendum in hoc vel illo tempore. Nam esse prius naturâ, dicit, esse prius altero in hoc instanti reali. Ergo Materia prima non potest pro priori naturae intelligi cum indifferentiâ ad existendum in hoc vel illo instanti. 2. Si duratio distingueretur ab actione rei productivâ, conservatio nullius actûs esset formaliter libera. Quia actio ipsa, per quam producitur actus, & prout praecedit modum durationis, non est conservatio, neque est novum libertatis exercitium; ipse autem modus durationis, qui talem actionem consequitur, non est formaliter liber, sed necessariò resultat ad entitatem rei. Itaque conservatio ut talis nunquam esset formaliter libera; quod non videtur dicendum. Nam quod novam laudabilitatem habet ac meritum, debet habere novam libertatem. Sed conservatio actûs boni habet novam laudabilitatem & meritum.

XXXII. Videtur probabilius, non esse possibilem durationem creatam indivisibilem, quae correspondeat, per se & essentialiter pluribus partibus temporis. Ratio est 1. quia non potest dari creatura, quae antecedentiter, & ab intrinseco sit pro aliquo tempore inannihilabilis, cum hoc quidem videatur esse contra summam subjectionem creaturae, per quam debet pro quocunque instanti respectu DEI posse esse, & non esse. 2. Si talis duratio esset possibilis, deberet de facto esse in Angelis, & animâ rationali: cum enim hae entitates sint naturâ suâ indefectibiles, talem durationis modum, vel maximè exigerent: quem tamen de facto non habent, uti ex SS. Litteris & PP. constat; à quibus passim omnia dicuntur quovis momento à DEO annihilabilia, ita ut nihil creatum possit ipsi ullo modo resistere. Ergo signum est, talem durationis modum possibilem non esse.

## CXXXIX. CURETES.

> *After Ops gave birth to Jove from Saturn, Juno asked that she yield him to her, since Saturn had cast Orcus under the Tartarus, and Neptune under the waves; because he knew that if any were born from her, he would deprive him of the kingdom. When he asked Ops, that it might be whatever she had brought forth, she showed a stone wrapped up, which Saturn devoured. When he sensed this, he began to seek Jove through the lands: Juno, however, carried Jove away to the Cretan island. Adamantaea, the boy's nurse, hung him in a cradle on a tree, so that he would not be found in heaven, nor on earth, nor in the sea. And so that the infant's wailing would not be heard, she summoned the beardless ones, and gave them small bronze shields and spears, and ordered them to clatter while going around the tree, who are called Curetes in Greek, others are called Corybantes: these are however called Lares.*

Causam hujus rei hanc reddunt Hebræorum magistri in Talmude Hierosolymitano tractatu Megilla, (x) quod Moyses die quinto hebdomadis ascenderit in montem ad recipiendas tabulas Legis, die vero secundo descenderit. Quæ si quis cum decantatissimis quarta et sexta feria (*) Jejuniis singulis hebdomadibus in Ecclesia Romana suscipi solitis contendat, Pharisæismi non obscura indicia deprehendet. Quare et in Ecclesia puriori nunquam hæc jejunia usitata fuerunt. Quanquam enim Tertulliani (y) nobis objiciant auctoritatem: evictum tamen jamdudum est à Rigaltio (z) per Stationes ibi non intelligi jejunia, sed conventus istos orandi causa institutos, assentiente ipsomet Petavio. (a) Illud vero quod ex Epiphanio et Clemente Alexandrino (b) opponunt erudite discussit Dallæus (c) Restat proinde ut adhuc illud disquiramus, an id quoque jejunii nomine Hebræis venerit, quando à carnis esu sibi quisque temperavit. Nec multum abest, quin illud asseram, quandoquidem in Massechet (d) Avoda Sara ממוני לתעניתא pisciulorum jejunio destinatorum mentio injicitur. Infederat quippe jam eo tempore multorum animis perversa hæc opinio, ac si non aliter quam evitatis carnibus, refrænari voluptates, ac libido coërceri posset. Prorsus aliter ac Pythagoras (e) docebat, qui symbolo suo ἰχθύων μὴ γεύεσθαι ad luxum deliciasque supervacaneas piscium pertinere esum judicabat. Propagatus iste error fuit, non solum in Montanistas et Tatianos (f) sed et Romanenses à Judæis hæreditario quasi jure illum acceperunt. Tandem et illud prætermittendum non est, quod Gabriel Albaspinæus (g) refert: fuisse olim moris, ut nemo tempore jejunii osculo exciperetur, quod etiam Ordo Romanus cæterique rituum scriptores confirmant. ### לו בשפה רפה ובכובד ראש.

*Non adeo frequentes sunt (die jejunii) salutationes inter virum & amicum ejus. Discipuli autem sapientum prorsus neminem salutant, sed tanquam objurgatione digni & separati à DEO incedunt. Si igitur eos ex plebejis quisquam salutaverit, salutem ipsis eqvidem reddunt, sed voce submissâ & gravi vultu. Hisce vero immorari diutius haud licet, cum argumenti amplitudo aliorsum nos ducat.*

### §, III.

Si vero quicquam aliud, Jubilæa sanè hunc ornant locum: quæ quinquagesimo quoque anno mancipiis libertatem, Dominis vero amissas venditasque possessiones restituebant. Legemque istam divinitus præscriptam, summâ religione usque ad Sanctuarii prioris desolationem observarunt. Postquam vero longa dies fatalem istum temporis orbem perfecerat, & Judæi in suas redierant sedes, nunquam revocata illa fuit, nec Jubilæorum solemnia celebrata.

By "superpositions," however, is understood that kind of fast which Dionysius of Alexandria, in his Epistle to Basilides, calls <term>hyperthesis</term> <gloss>a postponement or continuous fast</gloss>, the reason for which Henricus Valesius accurately explains <note>(i)</note>. From all these things it is concluded that those fasts were only established by the Roman Church at a time when it had already fallen away from the truth of the faith and the integrity of morals. Nor is it without cause that one might suspect it passed into the camp of the Jews, if one weighs the testimonies of so many authors of good repute. Justin <note>(l)</note>, the most faithful epitomizer of Trogus Pompeius, is authority that Moses consecrated the seventh day, called the Sabbath after the custom of the nation, to a fast for all time.

Nothing, indeed, could be said that was more inconvenient, or that was more repugnant to the custom of the Hebrews. For they never indulged their genius on the Sabbath otherwise, and it was the greatest offense if anything were lacking on that day in the way of splendor and luxury. Hence Kimchi: <note>original: "מצות עשה לענוג הגוף ביום השבת במאכלים ערבים וטובים שמתוך שישנהו משאר ימים לטוב יזכור מעשה בראשית ושהוא חדשהו מאין ושבת ביום השביעי ומתוך כך ישבח לאל ויפארהו בפיו ובלבבו"</note> "It is an affirmative commandment that every person should delight his body on the Sabbath with pleasant and good foods, so that he may establish a distinction between the remaining days and the feast; he shall remember the work of creation, and that God created it from nothing, and rested on the seventh day, and for that reason he shall praise God and glorify Him with his mouth and his heart."

Prodit in arenam purpurata fraudum Magistra regalis thori Augusta consors: prodit supremus bellorum Imperator Porphyrius, binis militum stipatus cohortibus: Prodit Augustus Orientis Imperator Maximinus, facundiâ et majestate, mellea voluptatum illicia, blanditias, et lenocinia omnibus ad persuadendum tormentis potentiora tenellæ Virgini propinat. Quid ad hæc CATHARINA? Brevi sed argutâ dictione Augustam Maximini conjugem, invictum regalis Exercitûs Imperatorem Porphyrium, Impietatis armis exuit, loricâ induit justitiæ et salutis galeâ, in obsequium fidei captivavit. Narrat ingeniorum phœnix Virgilius oleaginam Herculis arborem, temporis iniquitate exsuccam, nullarum feracem frondium, nullo præditam virore, Lauro sociatam sectis caudicibus repullulâsse, diffusam in ramos, crispatam in folia, opacam viatoribus umbram præbuisse. Tantùm profuit sociari Lauro. E fabularum cortice veritatis nucleum eruamus A.A. Augusta Maximini Conjux, quæ in sterili gentilitatis aruerat arenâ, coronatæ Sociata Lauro CATHARINÆ, orthodoxæ fidei virorem induit, crispatur in folia, diffunditur in ramos, exuberat in fructum fortitudinis Christianæ, coronata victrici Lauro contra Maximini fulmina, Tiberij Cæsaris turbato cœlo Laurum gestantis gloriam sepultura, sumit à minarum fulmine Heroam fortitudinem, à flagellis animum, à rota stimulos, ab ensibus robur; Incursantes plumbatorum Aquilones ramorum umbone retundit, ramis umbrantibus et stillantibus veræ fidei succum emortuis infundit stipitibus, animat in vitam, in virorem induit et gloriæ ornatum. Verùm à Stygijs ignibus in Maximini pectore furoris recrudéscente incendio Catenis Laurum onerat effera Tyrannis: Nescis proceram Xerxis arborem ab infibulatis per catenas nexibus honorari non onerari? Carbones Lauro subjicit ardescens Tyranni rabies: Nescis pluribus à flammarum radijs Laurum fulgere illustriorem? Nescis Hammonij nemoris Laurum ardentissimis Poli subjectam incendijs, in frondium virorem exuberare? Nescis Byzantinam oleam flammeo irroratam imbre, novis germinantem folijs, altiùs explicare verticem? Nudate Laurum, exuite corticem, truncate cervicem: Cervix lactea niveos lactis emanabit rivulos, et muricatis venarum fontibus stillabit purpuram, ut ardentem Tyranni sitim restinguat Sanguine; Lacteáque Virginei candoris lilia purpureis Martyrum cognata rosis, coronatæ agnata Lauro luculentè manifestet Victrix Laurus CATHARINA. Jubet coronatam Laurum lictoris ferro decuti Tyrannus. Procumbit coronata laurus, prostrata corpore, erecta vultu, sublimis animo, terris altior in terram ruit, ut premat corpore, conculcet pedibus, eludat pectore, quidquid fluxæ telluris redolet vanitatem. Quodque Lauro proprium est, inservit cæsa triumpho militantis in terra, triumphantis in cœlo

Ecclesiæ: Et (a.) parte superstes vivit suis in filijs (quos Christo genuit) profuso lacte animat ad constantiam, stimulat in pugnam, solidat ad victoriam, componit ad triumphos. O fœcunditatem felicissimam coronatæ Laurûs CATHARINÆ, quæ tot beata fructibus arbor fæcundos sequacium germinum traduces posteritati transmisit. Arborem vitæ dixeris hanc Laurum, cujus immortalis vigor in flore mortali, feracium adhuc florum spem viridem ostentans, à sæculis egressus in sæcula progreditur, nec temporis vetustate venustatem, nec hostilium procellarum turbine virorem amissurus, per ipsa florum funera vitam immortalem negotiatur : Fructus sui morsum indulsit sanguinis Helluoni Maximino, ut voracem ejus ingluviem satiaret. Maximini ferro primos dimittit surculos, ut per succisa Martyrum germina, cælestibus hortis inferatur. Lacte manat & purpurâ, ut mori non erubescat, aut certè dulciùs se mori ostendat (dulcissimum enim est mori triumphantem) quàm Tyrannus vivat. Vernat adhuc Laurus coronata, congestos inter nivium cumulos, frondescit inserta, flectitur in arcus, assurgit in colossos, in trophæa excrescit. Quid ampliùs? Diffluit in rivos lactis & sanguinis, ut niveo-purpureas sapientiæ baccas candido-purpureis Austriæ Philosophis propiner, funditur in succos, liquescit in remedia, desudat in balsamum, stillat in aquam vitæ. Inservit cæsa triumpho coronata Laurus CATHARINA, quando corpus truncum in latera, ramos in remos, comam in vela, in rudentes assamenta commodat, ut felicibus Austris ad portum Sapientiæ vestra naviget oneraria Neophilosophiæ: nisi malitis chartas pro carbasis, Porphyrij arborem pro malo navali, calamos pro remis, intellectûs acumen pro acu nauticâ, pro Saburrâ pulverem scholasticum, pro clavo clavam Philosophici Herculis clavini scientiarum exercitationem substituere, nè ad infamem à tot spectatis ruinis Arcadiæ pontem, naufragium incurratis. Hac sub Lauro coronatâ quiesce coronarum parens Austria, & imminentia barbari Martis fulmina (quæ Avernalis hærefeos tempestas in Austriæ minatur interitum) objectâ Lauro faciliùs eludes. Vive novo victoriæ ferto coronata Vienna; Vive coronatæ Lauro devota semper Austria, & quemadmodum Rhean Numitoris Albanorum Regis filiam, jovemque tenellum filium ab implacabili furore, ab inexplebili ingluvie Saturni, Augusta Laurus vindicavit, paribus auspicijs noveris te ab instabili regnorum Helluone Austriacis inhiante Regnis, Lauri victricis ope liberandam. Quippe postibus (b). Augustis eadem fidissima custos Augustissimæ Domûs præfixa valuis, trisulca fulminantis impietatis tela feliciùs infringet. Cui dum vos A.A. festivium accinitis triumphum, ego gloriosas Austriæ Lauros, victoriæ geminatæ testes, secuturi triumphi prodromas in perennantis gloriæ coronam coronatæ Lauro appendo CATHARINÆ.
