power! O sublime height of the branches! O illustrious shadow of Wisdom! You might doubt whether that fertile Laurel CATHARINE, by overshadowing them, illuminated those most shining stars of the East, the fifteen Orators, or by illuminating them, more happily overshadowed them, emulating the Lycian Proclus, who, having embraced the radiating rivulets of light with a burning mirror, increased fire with fires; not otherwise did the crowned Laurel, through the illustrious mirror of its branches, drinking in the rays of wisdom emanating from the most divine sun, illuminate the fifteen philosophers sitting in the shadow of death, serenely restoring and increasing the fire of celestial love with new fires, and the light of divine knowledge with new light.

I had heard that Daphne, having been turned into a green Laurel <note>(a) Natalis in Mythology.</note>, masked and at the same time masking, lived though dead, spoke though tongueless, and played with the ears through the airs, testifying that a trophy inscribed for immortality with perpetual greenery had been erected over the triumphed-over Apollo: I had heard about the famous tree of the Dodonian grove <note>(b) Pliny book 15, chapter 30.</note>, which, at the fans of the flattering zephyr, poured forth voices with the neat throat of its branches, and emitted truer oracles to the consulting people, omens of happiness, and messengers of joyful things.

The crowned Laurel CATHARINE gives credit to these fabulous trees, for, blown by the celestial zephyr, she speaks by breathing, wins by speaking, and gains fifteen victims for GOD by winning. O the unexpected face of things, at which the very Future centuries will stand amazed. You know (cast your thought into the past times of effeminate antiquity) you know how the oracle of Wisdom, Socrates, hung as a student from the mouth of the philosophizing girl Diotima: You know that Pythagoras, the apex of sciences, whom he inscribed in the immortal calendars, submitted his volumes to the judgment of his sister Themistoclea: You know that, Aristippus the Father having yielded to the fates, the learned thoughts of his daughter Arethis were received by the fervent pens of Philosophers: But you do not know that by the torch of the arguing tender Virgin, Philosophers buried in blind darkness were excited to the light of faith, CATHARINE excited them: You do not know that the robed President of the Philosophers, the Emperor of the East, Maximinus, was defeated by a weak woman in a literary contest, CATHARINE defeated him: you do not know that among armed arrows, burning pyres, pointed wheels, among axes, the young girl triumphed securely, CATHARINE triumphed.

So much is there a certain partnership of female weakness with Divinity, that our Laurel not only equals the eulogy of Pliny, that it is always dedicated to triumphs, and does not succumb, shaken by no storm of persecution, no rains of calamities, no tempests of torments, but because it is then most flourishing, when it is covered with snows, and resonates when burned, when it offers an omen of future happiness to those besieged by crackling flames, the Poet supporting the claim: *The Laurel, foreknowing the future, brings signs of Salvation.* Therefore, the whole line of Sages having been triumphed over, the battle now looked toward the triarii, the most experienced in fighting and hitherto accustomed to victorious arms

Audieram virentem in Laurum conversam Daphnen (a.) personatam simul & personantem, vivere mortuam, elinguem loqui, perque auras ludentem aures illudere, virore perpetuo inscriptum immortalitati trophæum, de triumphato erectum Apolline, contestari: Audieram de famosâ Dodonæi nemoris arbore, (b.) quæ blandientis ad zephyri flabella, concinno ramorum gutture profudit voces, & consulenti populo veriora emanavit oracula, felicitatis omina, lætarum nuntia, rerum.

Fabulosis arboribus fidem adstruit coronata Laurus **CATHARINA**, quæ cælesti afflata zephyro, spirando loquitur, loquendo vincit, vincendo quinque Denas DEO victimas lucratur. O inexspectata rerum facies, quam ipsa Ventura sæcula obstupescent. Novistis (in elapsâ effæminatæ antiquitatis tempora cogitationem emittite) novistis quonam pacto Sapientiæ oraculum Socrates ab ore philosophantis puellæ Diotimæ pependerit discipulus: Novistis apicem scientiarum Pythagoram, quæ fastis immortalibus inscribebat, volumina sororis suæ Themistocleæ judicio subjecisse: Novistis, cedente fatis Aristippo Patre, Filiæ Arethis erudita sensa præfervidis Philosophorum calamis fuisse excepta: At non novistis tenellæ Virginis argumentantis face, cæcâ sepultos caligine Philosophos ad fidei lucem excitatos, excitavit **CATHARINA**: Non novistis trabeatum Philosophorum Præsidem, Orientis Imperatorem Maximinum, ab imbelli fæmina in literario certamine fuisse victum, vicit **CATHARINA**: non novistis inter armata spicula, pyras ardentes, cuspidatas rotas, inter secures securam triumphâsse fæmellam, triumphavit **CATHARINA**.

Usquè adeò quoddam imbecillitatis fæmineæ cum Divinitate consortium est, ut non solum Plinij elogium adæquet Laurus nostra, quod 6. semper dicata triumphis, nullo persecutionis turbine, nullis calamitatum imbribus, nullis tormentorum procellis labefactata succumbat, verùm quòd tùm maximè vireat, cum nivibus operitur, resonet usta, cum crepitantibus obsessam flammis, secuturæ præbet omen felicitatis suffragante Poëta, *Præscia venturi Laurus fert signa Salutis.* Triumphatâ igitur universâ Sapientum acie, pugna jam ad triarios spectabat bellandi peritissimos & victricibus armis hactenus assuetos

And to the child of the King, the money was then given, and the woman who was a messenger sent a sign of life, covering the seal <note>the letter</note>. Likewise, immediately, the ministers brought it and walked back to the country to face the King. All the news of the greatness and the wisdom from both the seal and the messenger, after the letter from his child was read, the King and Queen were very happy. After some time, the decree of Allah Ta'ala came to Sultan Mughal, who became very ill. He was growing sicker and yearning for his child.
<column-break/>
He then expressed his desire, "Go you to the land of Damascus to call my child, for I am very ill and yearn for him." The minister then took the order and walked to the land of Damascus, without stopping, day and night. When he arrived, he went to face the King. He saw King Burhan al-Arifin sitting in the audience, attended by all the ministers. He bowed, "Your Majesty, I have been sent by the Queen, for the King is very ill and awaits you." After the King's son heard this, he immediately went to face his father-in-law.

*Ancient Relations of the Indies and of China by two Muhammadans who went there in the ninth century, translated from the Arabic into the French language with Notes and Dissertations by Mr. Eusebius Renaudot, and rendered into Italian by an Anonymous author. This time our Extract will turn upon three things, that is, concerning the primary Editor of this work, who is Mr. Renaudot, concerning the Relations themselves, and concerning the Notes and Dissertations added to them, with saying in the end something about the merit of the present version. And as in lutes and flutes, and in song itself, a certain concert must be maintained from distinct sounds, which learned ears cannot bear to be changed or discrepant: and that concert is made from the moderation of the most dissimilar voices, a concord and harmony: so from the highest and lowest and intermediate orders, as from sounds, a city consists by the consent of the most dissimilar in a moderate way: and what is called harmony by musicians in a song, that is in a city or republic, concord, the tightest and best bond of safety in any republic, which cannot exist by any pact without justice.

9 But justice cannot attain its effect unless from the authority of someone who holds supreme power: whence Cicero says, without supreme justice, a republic cannot be governed. And there are as many supreme powers as there are republics, each one one, just as in one physical body, one soul which commands, not two: in the world, one god, who moderates it by his discretion. It would be a monster, nay, impossible, for there to be two equal supreme powers in one and the same republic. For that which is supreme, in its own order, does not admit a superior, unless it is subordinated to something. If you constitute two, the civil body must now be divided, and two republics be made. But that supreme power sometimes admits administrators and distributors, two, three, or more: but those three or more separately do not each have supreme power in their hands, but all together one, as happens in aristocracy and democracy. But in a monarchy, the sum of all power is in the hands of one, from whom the rest, who moderate the republic or principality or kingdom under him by parts entrusted to them, depend: nor are they said to have anything of their own, and therefore they expedite committed business not in their own name, but that of the prince or as his delegates or officers. And just as the hand is not weaker because it is divided into fingers, but is more agile for performing tasks; so supreme power is not diminished when explained by many: and business communicated to many in the republic is more easily accomplished. For supreme power is not committed such that the fingers are separated from the hand, nor the hand from the arm, nor the arm from the body, or the body from the head. But just as the virtue of the soul diffused through the whole body and members executes its mandates through its instruments: so supreme power exerts its authority through the ministries of those placed in charge. And thus the subordinated powers of magistrates, dukes, counts, and the like, do not use supreme power, which cannot be communicated any more than unity can, but they use the authority of him who holds the same, with effect. As from unity, other numbers follow, two, three, and the following, so that unity is not a number, but the principle of number, as a point is not a line, but the principle of the line, which arises from the points following it.

10 But because words that are incorrectly added do not make up the description, they warn us that society and community are placed as the genus, the rest as differences, from that general natural society of men. The society of things and life demonstrates the matter of the republic:

14 Constat itàq; hæc respublica, materia & forma, quæ paucis per speciem protheoriæ seu præuiæ speculationis, ante oculos proponere debemus. pro materia sunt res ipsæ publicæ circa quas versatur forma administrationis & publici seu reipublicæ.

Res istæ publicæ, in summa, vel corporales vel incorporales, diuinæ & humanæ sunt. inter corporales publicas & ad rempub. pertinentes, sunt ciuitates, oppida, regna, imperia. & in illis, ædes sacræ, theatra, viæ publicæ, maria, flumina, castra, & similia. plura quæ vtilitati comuni seu publicæ populi destinata sunt, vt vectigalia & reditus public.

Inter incorporalia publica & communia, religio, iura, mores, leges, & similia.

Inter res, & personæ publicæ sunt: vel cum authoritate propriæ potestatis, vt principes, etiam sacrosancti reges, monarchæ, imperatores, summus pontifex, sacerdotes, & similes. vel cum authoritate executionis potestatis publicæ, gerentes habentium potestatem personarum, quales sunt magistratus ecclesiastici & seculares, iudices, legati, vicarij, vicem regum agentes, toparchæ, scribæ & notarij publici, & similes.

Ad res quoq; pertinent, actiones quæ publicæ tantùm sunt, cōsilia publica, comitia, bella, induciæ, iudicia publica, & ipsa potestas & authoritas iudicādi, aliáq; munera seu officia publica, vel realia, vel personalia, vel mixta, put ad causa publica respiciūt & reip. vtilitate.

Rursum personarum & actionum publicarum ministeria, cura & solicitudo, non solùm publicam causam: sed etiam, authoritate publica tamen & eadem potestate, disponunt causam priuatarum personarum. Separatum enim quidem est dignitate & potestate publicum à priuato: sed quia publicum sine priuatorum muneribus & personis esse non dicitur, ideo & coniunctum priuatum publico: vt publicum per se quidem considerari possit, tamen non nisi imperfecte, quia, vt dixi, sine priuato esse nequeat, &, nisi authoritate publica, priuata dirigantur, & compellantur suos tenere ordines vt conuenit societati, breui tempore respublica dissoluitur. Quare diligenter cum publico & priuatum in administratione reipublicæ curandum est: sed magis publicum omnium, quàm aliquorum singularis ratio procuranda. Vt medicus primum, dum membrum hominis ægrum est, propinat quidem pharmacum quod ex toto corpore malos humores educere possit: sed ibi non subsistit, quin etiam loco affecto singularia adferat remedia: & si videat membrum aliquod incurabile, cuius etiam morbus serpendo alia sana membra inficere possit, vt salua alia membra conseruet, sæpe abscindi membrum putidum iubet. ## XV.

<margin>Geilfusius Controversiae Physica 8. §. 1. 4.</margin>
Face hac praevia sponte jam elucescit, quid et quomodo simplicia à mixtis differant; Tum etiam, quod elementorum neque formae, neque vires in mixto aboleantur, sed ita modificentur ac gubernentur, ut sub liberrimâ mixti servitute munia sibi concredita peragere, actionesque proprias ad formae suae imperatricis nutum conformare non recusent. Patet insuper; quod nec ex solis quatuor elementis mixtum componatur. Liquet denique; quod ex illorum et qualitatum varia temperie, omnes mutationes et generationes Physicas deducere, labor sit frustraneus. Facessant itaque pulverulenta ac trivialia isthaec bella, quae Galenus, Aristoteles, Avicenna, Averroës et alii, naturalis Philosophiae regno intulerunt. Ea enim si taediosè ac curiosè nimis persequamur, haud rarò majorem temporis, veritatis, solidaeque eruditionis jacturam, quam de ignorantia et falsitate victoriam allatura sunt. Quanquam antiqui illi Philosophiae conditores, non illico ob aliquot naevos contemptim habendi, sed potius perenni gloriâ digni sint, quia obstetricantem dextram, paternamque adhibuere curam, ut vagientem è cunis Philosophiam susciperent, ejusque ad floridam juventutem robur adaugerent. Atque hic ille est miscibilium ordo, quem de iisdem ratione, ut loquuntur, ratiocinante separatis, et per genesin potissimum investigatis intellectum volumus.

Cum autem nulla materiâ, nullumque corpus formae expers sit, inquirendum itaque quaenam corpori perfectè mixto naturaliter dicata sit. Quisquis ergo specificam atque determinatam petit formam, illi ad ipsas mixtorum species, tam intermedias, quam ultimas descendendum erit. Atque sic in regno minerali formam inveniet ejusdem nominis adhuc communem: Velut in vegetativo & animali regno, animam cum vegetativam tum sensitivam, eas tamen omnes non nisi intermedias agnoscimus. Determinatiùs idcircò, in infimis speciebus, ultima & specifica forma erit quaerenda, cui omnes sive immanentes sive transeuntes insint facultates & actiones. Hinc alia forma essentialis est auri & carbunculi, alia lauri & roris marini, aquilae alia & leonis, alia etiam hominis forma est. De quibus tamen omnibus res nobis eatenus, qua constituentem duntaxat subjecti sui causam agunt, cujus quoque merito species à speciebus diametrali essentiae ratione distant.

### XVII.

Praeter hasce specificas, *formae etiam subordinatae* non sunt praetereundae, quae elementis quibusque seorsim ac indicibili adhuc modo insunt, ita ut neutra alteram, in minima etiam atque intima illa miscibilium περιχώρησιν, immutet, inque naturae suae commercium rapiat. Eo tamen modo in uno eodemque subjecto existunt, quo species visibiles, radiique lucidi recti, obliqui ac transversi, per universum aërem aequè latè diffunduntur, neque tamen confunduntur. Partiales insuper formae, heterogeneis mixtis non sunt denegandae, juxta quas partes à partibus; uti species à speciebus suum fortiuntur discrimen. Sed & *accidentarias* formas non eliminamus, quia pro rerum extra ordinem sese admifcentium varietate, tanquam comites & advenae haud rarò se agglutinant, à quibus introductae individuis qualitates idiocraticae & insolitae plures originem ducunt.

### XVIII.

Hae denique omnes, potissimum autem *specifica forma*, pro immediato existentiae suae radicalis subjecto, *calidum nativum* deposcunt, quod est focus & officina Naturae, in qua custoditur ignis, ille formalis ac divinus, qui primus omnium mixti facultatum & functionum motor est. Alterum verò subjectum sive organum potius, quod operationibus debetur, sunt spiritus rerum influentes radiique corporei, queis mediantibus forma ex centro suo, quasi in apricum prodit.

are the only parts of the universe, or if you please, three elements, which those wise men admitted; for this reason, they depicted Jupiter armed with a thunderbolt. This triad of the ancients, however, implicitly and in reality exhibits a quaternary, which even today is most accepted and most true. But some ascend to a <term>quinary</term> <gloss>a group of five</gloss>, and even those of the quaternary; the leader of these, Aristotle, ignorant of revealed creation, added the heavens with the stars as a fifth element. But indeed, entities ought not to be multiplied beyond necessity; for heaven encompasses the air, while the stars themselves are not simple, being fixed to the heavens on the third day, after the creation of the elements and vegetation.

### XIV.

From these mixables, before the mixed body itself is constituted, it is necessary that the essence and virtue of all of them flow together into a certain seminal mass. Unless this were done, nature would have to be accused of a certain leap committed out of order, while it might produce a body too prematurely and lazily, and one that does not cohere, from elements not yet converted into a seminal rudiment and modified by the first digestion. This mass is therefore still rude and indeterminate, like sperm, covered in an elemental garment, kindled by celestial fire, and imbued with a radical spirit: or, to explain more openly, it is nothing other than **Limus** <gloss>Slime/Mire</gloss>,
<margin>Physica restituta, canon 69.</margin>
*which is the proximate matter of all generated things; for it is as it were chaos, in which all things reside confusedly and by virtue of the elements. From slime was created the first parent of the human race; every generation thereafter proceeded from slime. In the generation of animals, slime is made from sperm and menses, thence the animal. In the production of vegetation, seeds first pass through putrefaction into a subtle slime, then are hardened into a vegetable body. In the generation of metals, slime issues forth from sulfur and mercury perfectly mixed and resolved into a fatty water, from which metallic bodies are hardened through long decoction. In the philosophical solution of metals and the creation of the arcanum of the philosophers, slime is first educed, with the seed of both parents purged and mixed.* Moreover, that universal slime, as the most noble deposit of GOD and Nature, and an inestimable treasure of blessing, from which, as if from Noah's ark, every genus of living thing proceeds, exhibits to us a specimen of that ancient confused mass, or prime matter, and contains within itself the harmonic marriage of the whole universe. ### XIX.

<margin>Physica restituta canon 206.</margin>
Quibus omnibus tandem unitim coalitis corpus emergit *mixtum, partim corporea, spiritualis partim ac mediæ naturæ.* Corpus quod palpabile est terram refert, spiritus qui invisibilis, est formalis aut astralis. Vaporosa denique & aërea substantia inter utrumque ambigit. Cum autem quodlibet à nobiliori denominationem suam obtineat, sciendum est, quod *mera mixtorum natura spirituales sint, corpora verò earum cortices & tanquam testacea vasa, quibus illæ custodiuntur; neque enim aliter mare istud inferum transfretare, & in hoc abyssi centro hospitari potuissent sublimes illæ naturæ, nisi corporeis elementis alligatæ eorum pondere sisterentur: illæ per corpora sentiuntur, corpora per illas moventur & agunt; sic mutuas sibi præstant operas. Homericæ Iunonis arcanum illud est, quam incudis pondere pedibus adjecto Iuppiter demisit.*

<margin>Physica restituta canon 224.</margin>

# PRAXIS

If, however, it is desired to find the area of a mountainous surface, consider the circuit of the summit, and similarly that of the base, and of the ascent. Then join the circuits of the base and the summit, and take the half of the product. Multiply this by the ascent, and the product will show the sought quantity. For example, let there be a mountain whose summit circuit is 300 feet, the base circuit is 1000 feet, and the ascent is 800 feet. The total area will be 520,000 feet.

If the mountain differs greatly in the circuit of its summit, middle, and base, such that it ascends in the shape of a pyramid, you will discover its area in this way: Collect the sum of the circuits of the base, the middle, and the summit into one total. Multiply the third part of this by the ascent, and the sought area will be clear. For example, if the base circuit is 2500 feet, the middle circuit 1600 feet, the summit circuit 100 feet, and the ascent 2000 feet, the area will be 2,800,000 feet.

If the mountain is uneven in its ascent and likewise in its circuits, its area must be investigated by another way. Join the circuit of the base to the circuit of the summit, and take the half of the product. Multiply this by the other half, and the product will give the area. For example, let there be a mountain whose summit circuit is 200, the base circuit 1400, the longer ascent 850, and the shorter ascent 750. The area will be 640,000.

### Division of surfaces into <term>actus</term> <gloss>a Roman measure of length/area</gloss> or <term>iugera</term> <gloss>acres</gloss>.

Whatever surfaces you may know, if you wish to divide them into <term>actus</term> or <term>iugera</term> or other measures, multiply the length and width of the measure you are holding by themselves, and you will have the feet or the area of the measure whose sides you multiplied. If you divide the feet of the surface to be divided by this, the quotient will show the sought amount.

One who possesses such heroism is called a Bodhisattva <gloss>Enlightenment Being</gloss>. Through that enlightenment, they know the aspects of all phenomena, yet they have no obsessive attachment to those phenomena. It was asked: If they know the aspects of all phenomena, what are those phenomena toward which they have no obsessive attachment? It was said: They know the aspect of form, yet have no obsessive attachment to it. Likewise, they know the aspects of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, yet have no obsessive attachment to them. Applying this as before, they know the aspects up to the sense bases, yet have no obsessive attachment to them. Likewise, they know the aspects of the elements, yet have no obsessive attachment to them. Likewise, they know the aspects of the applications of mindfulness, yet have no obsessive attachment to them. Applying this further, up to the eightfold noble path, and likewise the ten powers of a Tathagata <gloss>Thus Gone One</gloss>, and applying it up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they know their aspects, yet have no obsessive attachment to them. It was asked: Venerable Subhuti, what is it for a Bodhisattva Mahasattva <gloss>Great Enlightenment Being</gloss> to know the aspects of all phenomena and yet have no obsessive attachment to them? It was said: Venerable Sharadvatiputra, by whatever aspects, whatever signs, and whatever marks—

<leaf-break/>

—up to the eightfold [path], the ten powers of a Tathagata, and likewise up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they have gone beyond; therefore, it is called the Perfection of Wisdom <note>original: "prajnaparamita"</note>. Because they have gone beyond the knowledge of all things, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, it is called the Perfection of Wisdom. Venerable Sharadvatiputra, by that enumeration, it has gone beyond; therefore, it is called the Perfection of Wisdom. Venerable Sharadvatiputra, as for what was asked regarding what is called "close observation," here, Venerable Sharadvatiputra, when a Bodhisattva Mahasattva practices the Perfection of Wisdom, they do not closely observe form as "pleasant." They do not closely observe it as suffering, nor as neither suffering nor pleasure, nor as permanent, nor as impermanent. Applying this as before, they do not closely observe form as self, nor as non-self, nor as empty, nor as non-empty, nor as having signs, nor as signless, nor as having wishes, nor as wishless, nor as peace, nor as non-peace, and up to being secluded or not secluded. Likewise, they do not closely observe feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a self.
stored.83:
Continuing from the previous leaf, apply it up to the point of being secluded or not secluded. Likewise, it should be applied to the Perfection of Generosity and up to the Perfection of Wisdom. Likewise, it should be applied from inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities. Likewise, it should be applied to the applications of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, the ten powers of a Tathagata, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Likewise, it should be applied to all phenomena, to all doors of meditative concentration, and all doors of dharani <gloss>incantation/retention</gloss>. Likewise, they do not observe the knowledge of all aspects as permanent or impermanent, nor as pleasure, suffering, or neither suffering nor pleasure, nor as self and non-self, empty and non-empty, having signs and signless, having wishes and wishless, peace and non-peace, up to being secluded and not secluded. Venerable Sharadvatiputra, when a Bodhisattva Mahasattva practices the Perfection of Wisdom, they observe all phenomena in that way. When that was said, Venerable Sharadvatiputra—

<leaf-break/>

—the Perfection of Generosity is empty of the Perfection of Generosity. That which is emptiness is not the Perfection of Generosity; it is unarisen. Applying this as before, the Perfection of Ethics, the Perfection of Patience, the Perfection of Diligence, the Perfection of Concentration, and the Perfection of Wisdom are empty of the Perfection of Wisdom. That which is emptiness is not [the Perfection of Wisdom], up to the point that the Perfection of Wisdom is unarisen. Venerable Sharadvatiputra, by that enumeration, that Perfection of Wisdom is not the Perfection of Wisdom. Applying this as before, it should be applied extensively to inner emptiness as well. Venerable Sharadvatiputra, by that enumeration, that which is the non-arising of form is not form; it is also unarisen. Likewise, that which is the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness; it is also unarisen. Likewise, that which is the non-arising of the knowledge of all aspects is not the knowledge of all aspects; it is also unarisen. When that was said, Venerable Sharadvatiputra said this to Venerable Subhuti: Venerable Subhuti, why is it said that "that which is the non-diminishment of form is not form"?

པ་དང་། ལེན་པ་པོ་མི་དམིགས་ན། དེ་ནི་དེའི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཅན་དང་། སེམས་ཅན་མི་དམིགས་ན། དེ་ནི་དེའིི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཕ་
རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། བཟོད་པ་དང་བཟོད་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བཟོད་པ་ཅན་མི་དམིགས་ན། དེ་ནིདེའི་བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཡི་ན་ནོ། །བརྩོན་འགྲུས་དང་། བྱ་བའི་དངོས་པོ་དང་། སེམས་
ཅན་མི་དམིགས་ན། དེ་ནིདིའི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཡིན་། །བསམ་གཏན་དང་། བསམ་གཏན་པ་དང་། བསམ་གཏན་དུ་བྱ་བ་མི་དམིགས་ན། དེ་ནི་དེའ་བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་
ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་། །ཤེས་རབ་དང་། ཤེས་རབ་ཅན་དང་། ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་དོན་མི་དམིགས་ན། དེ་ནི་།དེའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཡིནཏེ། ཀཽ་ཤི་ཀ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་
སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པའི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིནཔ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དང་། བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱི་པ་དང་། བརྩོན་
འགྲུས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་དང་། བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་པྱིན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་འ་གྱུར་རོ། །ཀཽ་ཤི་ཀ་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུའམ་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་མོ་དེས་
དེ་ལྟར་མི་དམིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱི་པ་འདི་དོན་དང་བཅས། ཚིག་འབྲུ་དང་བཅས་པར་བསྟན་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་ཕ་རོལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དང་།
<leaf-break/>
ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལྟར་བཅོས་པ་སྟོན་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལྟར་ བཅོས་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་དག་མིག་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །རྣ་བ་དང་། སྣ་དང་།
ལྕེ་དང་། ལུས་དང་། ཡིད་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པར་ བྱེད་དོ། །གཟུགས་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པར་བྱད་དོ། །སྒྲ་དང་། དྲི་དང་། རོ་དང་། རེག་བྱ་དང་། ཆོས་རྣམས་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པརབྱེད་དོ། །སའི་
ཁམས་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་ པར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཚུའི་ཁམས་དང་། མེའི་ཁམས་དང་། རླུང་གི་ཁམས་དང་། ནམ་མཁའི་ཁམས་དང་། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའི་ཁམས་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོནཔར་བྱེད་དོ། །མིག་གི་
ཁམས་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་ སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །རྣ་བའི་ཁམས་དང་། སྣའི་ཁམས་དང་། ལྕེའི་ཁམས་དང་། ལུས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་དང་། ཡིད་ཀྱི་ཁམས་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟེན་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་
དང་། སྒྲའི་ཁམས་དང་། དྲིའི་ཁམས་དང་། རོའི་ཁམས་དང་། རེག་བྱའི་ཁམས་དང་། ཆོས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་བྱེད་དོ། །མིག་གི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའི་ཁམས་ མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་
པར་བྱེད་དོ། །རྣ་བ་དང་། སྣ་དང་། ལྕེ་དང་། ལུས་དང་། ཡིད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའི་ཁམས་མ་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །མིག་གི་འདུས་ཏེ་རེག་པ་མི་རྟག་གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད། རྣ་བ་དང་།
སྣ་དང་། ལྕེ་དང་། ལུསདང་། ཡིད་ཀྱི་འདུས་ཏེ་རེག་པ་མི་རྟག གོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་དོ།། །།གཟུགས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དང་། བདག་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དང་། མི་སྡུག་པའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་དོ།

པ་ཆེན་པོ་པའི་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུའམ་རིགས་ཀྱི་བ་མོ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྟོན་པ་ན། འདི་སྐད་དུ་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་ཁྱོད་ཚུར་ཤོག །ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་པ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྒོམས་ཤིག །དེ་ལྟར་བསྒོམས་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ

མི་མཉམ་པ་དང་མཉམ་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ལྡན་པ ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་བསོད་ནམས་མང་པོ་མངའ་བའི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་
པའི་མཆོད་རྟེན་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱེད་དེ ། དེ་ཙམ་མམ ། ཆུང་ཟད་ཙམ་མམ ། ཆུང་ངུ་ཞིག་གམ ། ངན་ངོན་ཙམ་ཞིག་གམ ། གསོག་ཙམ་ཞིག་གམ ། ཐ་ན་གློག་གི་རྒྱུན་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཀྱང་སྣང་བར་བྱེད་
དམ ། ཐ་ན་ཐེམ་སྐས་ཀྱི་གཞི་གཅིག་སྣང་བར་བྱེད་ན་ཡང་ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ་དེའི་རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་པ་ནི་ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སམ ། རང་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པར་མི་ནུས་སོ། ། ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ་གཞན་ཡང་
ལན་ལ་ནི་མི་རེ་ཞིང་དད་པ་དང་། དགའ་བ་དང་། དང་བས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཏང་བའི་རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་པ་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་པ་དེ་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་སྟོན་པར་སྤྱོད་དོ། ། ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ་གཞན
ཡང་དད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་གུས་པར་གནས་ཤིང་གཡོ་མེད་ལ་སྒྱུ་མེད་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལ་ངེས་པར་སེམས་པའི་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་འམ ། རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་མོ་དགེ་བའི་བསམ་པ་སྐྱེས་ནས་མར་མེ་ཆུང་ཟད་
ཙམ་མམ། ཆུང་ངུ་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཀྱང་སྣང་བར་བྱས་ཏེ་མར་མེ་སྣང་བར་བྱས་པ་གང་གིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་མཆོད་རྟེན་དེའི་ཐ་ན་ཐེམ་སྐས་ཙམ་སྣང་ངམ ། བསྐོར་ས་ཙམ་སྣང་ངམ ། སྨད་དམ ། གདུགས་
སམ ༏ ཐེམས་ཅད་སྣང་ངམ ། ཐ་ན་བར་སྐབས་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་ཞིག་སྣང་བའི་མར་མེ་དེ་མོད་ལ་མྱུར་དུ་ཤི་སྟེ ། རླུང་གིས་བསྐྱོད་པས་སམ ། ཆར་པས་སམ ། མར་ཟད་པས་སམ ། སྙིང་པོ་ཟད་
<leaf-break/>
ཙམ་དུ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་གྲངས་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་བཟུང་བར་གྱུར་པའི་དོན་དེ་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་མཁྱེན་ཏེ། ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ་མར་མེ་དེ་ཙམ་དུ་ཆུང་ངུ་ཕུལ་བའི་རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་པ་ཡང་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་ན། གང་གིས་དེ་བཞིན་
གཤེགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་མཆོད་རྟེན་ལ་མཆོད་པ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་བྱེད་དམ་བྱེད་དུ་འཇུག་སྟེ། སྤོས་སམ། མེ་ཏོག་ཕྲེང་ངམ། གདུགས་སམ། བ་དན་
རྣམས་སམ། གང་ཡང་རུང་བའི་མར་མེའི་ཕྲེང་བ་རྣམ་པ་མང་པོས་མཆོད་པ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་བྱད་དམ་བྱེད་དུ་འཇུག་པ་ལྟ་སྨོས་ཀྱང་ཅི་དགོས། ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ་གཞན་ཡང་ཆོས་འདི་བཞི་ནི་དད་པས་རྟོགས་
པར་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བཞི་གང་ཞེ་ན། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ནི་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་དད་པས་རྟོགས་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཆུང་ངུའི་རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་པ་ཡང་བདག་ཏུ་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་
བ་དད་པས་རྟོགས་པར་བྱ་བ། དཀོན་མཆོག་གསུམ་ལ་དད་པའི་ལས་མངོན་པར་འདུ་བྱེད་པའི་རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་སྟོན་པ་མཐོང་བ། ཉན་ཐོས་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་བསམ་
པའམ། ཡོངས་སུ་བསམ་པར་མི་ནུས་ན། འཕགས་པའི་རིགས་ལ་མི་གནས་པ་གཞན་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ལས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་པ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་ཤེས་པའམ། ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པར་ནུས་པ་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས་ཏེ་དེ་ནི་གནས་

Having understood the body that has an essence and the body that lacks an essence, I shall give it an essence." Recognizing that resources possess faults, one gives essence to essenceless resources—Shariputra, this is the first certainty of mind from making an offering to a stupa of the Tathagata. Shariputra, furthermore, one thinks: "By making an offering to the supreme recipient of gifts, the unsurpassed field of merit, I have no fear of the hells of sentient beings, nor the fear of birth as an animal, nor the fear of the world of Yama <note>Lord of the Dead</note>. My happy transmigrations are five: I shall either obtain the higher realms, or if not <note>meaning human birth</note>, I shall obtain a fine form, or obtain resources, or obtain enlightenment." Shariputra, that is the second certainty of mind obtained from performing an offering to a stupa of the Tathagata. Shariputra, furthermore, one who is perfectly established in the complete offering of a lamp to the stupa of the Tathagata knows: "I have given a gift. I have also performed merits. I have abandoned stinginess." And they think: "I am a giver, and I have given a gift..."

༄༅། །སེམས་ཅན་རྣམ་པ་ཐ་དད་པ་དེ་དག་ས་ཕྱོགས་རྣམ་པ་ཐ་དད་པ་དག་ཏུ་མདོ་སྡེའི་གཏན་ཚིགས་རྣམ་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་འདི་དག་གཅིག་ལ་གཅིག་བརྗོད་དམ། ཐོས་པར་
བགྱིད་དམ། གཏམ་བརྒྱུད་བརྗོད་ན། བཙུན་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ས་ཕྱོགས་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཤིན་ཏུ་མདངས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་སྣུམ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ས་ཕྱོགས་དེ་དང་དེ་དག་ཏུ་སེམས་
ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར། སའི་བཅུད་རྣམ་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་དང་ཡོ་བྱད་ཐམས་ཅད་རྒྱས་པར་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར། རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བར་འགྱུར། ཤིན་ཏུ་རྒྱས་པར་འགྱུར། སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཐམས་
ཅད་ཀྱང་བདེ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ནོར་ཆེ་བ་དང་། ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཆེ་བ་དང་། སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་མོས་པར་འགྱུར། དཀོན་མཆོག་གསུམ་ལ་མངོན་པར་དད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་པ་དང་།
བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་སའི་ལྷ་མོ་བརྟན་མ་ལ་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བཀའ་སྩལ་ཏོ། །སའི་ལྷ་མོ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་ལ་ལ་དག་གསེར་འོད་དམ་པ་མདོ་སྡེའི་དབང་པོའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་འདི་ལས་ཐན་ཚིག་
གཅིག་ཉན་ན་དེ་དག་མིའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་འདི་ནས་ཤི་འཕོས་ནས་སུམ་ཅུ་གསུམ་པའི་ལྷའི་རིས་ཀྱི་ནང་དུ་ལྷའི་རིས་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་ཞིག་ཏུ་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །སའི་ལྷ་མོ་སེམས་ཅན་གོང་ལ་ལ་དག་
གསེར་འོད་དམ་པ་མདོ་སྡེ་དབང་པོའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་འདི་མཆོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། གནས་དེ་དག་ལེགས་པར་བརྒྱན་པར་བྱེད་དམ། ཐ་ན་གདུགས་གཅིག་གམ། བ་དན་གཅིག་གམ། རས་བཅོས་བུ་

༄༅། །པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་འཚང་རྒྱ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་། སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བ་དང་། དུད་འགྲོའི་སྐྱེ་གནས་དང་། གཤིན་རྗེའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་
ཐམས་ཅད་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆད་པར་འགྱུར་བར་ལུས་མི་གདའ་བར་བགྱིས་ཏེ། དགེ་སློང་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་དེའི་རྐང་པ་ལ་ཡན་ལག་གི་དམ་པ་མགོས་བརྟན་པར་བགྱིའོ། །གསེར་འོད་དམ་པ་མདོ་སྡེའི་དབང་པོའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་
ལས༏ སའི་ལྷ་མོ་བརྟན་མའི་ལེའུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་བཅུ་པའོ།། །།དེ་ནས་གནོད་སྦྱིན་གྱི་སྡེ་དཔོན་ཆེན་པོ་ཡང་དག་ཤེས་གནོད་སྦྱིན་གྱི་སྡེ་དཔོན་ཆོས་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་བརྒྱད་དང་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཏུ་
སྟན་ལས་ལངས་ཏེ། གོས་ཕྲག་པ་གཅིག་ཏུ་བགོས་ནས་བུས་མོ་གཡས་པའི་ལྷ་ང་ས་ལ་བཙུགས་ཏེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ག་ལ་བ་དེ་ལོགས་སུ་ཐལ་མོ་སྦྱར་བ་བཏུད་ནས། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་འདི་
སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །བཙུན་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ད་ལྟར་དང་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་ན། གསེར་འོད་དམ་པ་མདོ་སྡེ་དབང་པོའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་འདི་གྲོང་ངམ། གྲོང་ཁྱེར་རམ། གྲོང་རྡལ་ལམ། ལྗོངས་སམ།
དགོན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སམ། རིའི་སྨན་ལྗོངས་སམ། ཕོ་བྲང་འཁོར་གང་དུ་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེར་བཙུན་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་གནོད་སྦྱིན་གྱི་སྡེ་དཔོན་ཆན་པོ་ཡང་དག་ཤེས་བདག་གནོད་སྦྱིན་གྱི་སྡེ་དཔོན་
ཆེན་པོ་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་བརྒྱད་པོ་དེ་དག་དང་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཏུ་གྲོང་ངམ། གྲོང་ཁྱེར་རམ་། གྲོང་རྡལ་ལམ། ལྗོངས་གསམ། དགོན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སམ། རེའི་སྨན་ལྗོངས་སམ། ཕོ་བཟང་འཁོར་དེར་མཆི་བར་བགྱིའོ། །ལུས་

གཅིག་གིས་གཡོགས་ན་སའི་ལྷ་མོ་རྟག་ཏུ་བརྒྱན་པའི་གནས་དེ་དག་འདོད་པ་ན་སྤྱོད་པའི་ལྷའི་རིས་བདུན་པོ་དེ་དག་ཏུ་ལྷའི་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྣ་བདུན་གྱི་གཞལ་མེད་ཁང་རྒྱན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ལེགས་པར་བརྒྱན་པ་དག་ཏུ་
གནས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །གང་གི་ཚེ་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་མིའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་འདི་ནས་ཤི་འཕོས་ཏེ། རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྣ་བདུན་གྱི་གཞན་མེད་ཁང་དེ་དག་ཏུ་སྐྱེ་བ་དེའི་ཚེ། སའི་ལྷ་མོ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྣ་བདུན་གྱི་བཞལ་མེད་ཁང་
རེ་རེར་ཡང་ལན་བདུན་བདུན་དུ་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ལྷའི་བདེ་བ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་ཡང་མྱོང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ་དང་། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་སའི་ལྷ་མོ་བརྟན་མས་འདི་
སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །བཙུན་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེས་ན་སའི་ལྷ་མོ་བརྟན་མ་བདག་དགེ་སློང་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྟན་ལ་མཆིས་པ་དེའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྟན་གྱི་འོག་ལོགས་ཀྱི་ས་ཕྱོགས་དེ་དང་དེ་དག་ཏུ་གནས་
པར་བགྱིའོ། །ཅི་ནས་ཀྱང་སངས་རྒྱས་བརྒྱ་སྟོང་དག་ལ་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་བསྐྲུན་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་གི་དོན་གྱི་སླད་དུ་གསེར་འོད་དམ་པ་མདོ་སྡེའི་དབང་པོའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་འདི་འཛམ་བུའི་གླིང་དུ་ཡུན་
རིང་དུ་གནས་ཤིང་མྱུར་དུ་ནུབ་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་དང་། སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱང་གསེར་འོད་དམ་པ་མདོ་སྡེ་དབང་པོའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་འདི་ཉན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་། མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་ན་བསྐལ་པ་བྱེ་བ་

"...Those various sentient beings, in various places, shall speak of these various logical points of the sutra to one another, or cause them to be heard, or tell the stories. Venerable Blessed One, all those places shall become very lustrous and very oily. In those various places, for the sake of all sentient beings, the various essences of the earth and all necessities will grow extensively. They will increase. They will flourish greatly. All those sentient beings will also be happy. They will possess great wealth, great enjoyments, and will be inclined toward generosity. They will have manifest faith in the Triple Gem." When she had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the Earth Goddess Dridha: "Earth Goddess, if any sentient beings listen to even one word from this King of Sovereign Sutras, the Holy Golden Light, when they die and pass away from this human world, they will be born into any of the divine realms among the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Earth Goddess, if any sentient beings, for the sake of worshipping this King of Sovereign Sutras, the Holy Golden Light, beautifully adorn those places, or even offer a single umbrella, a single banner, or a piece of cloth..."

<leaf-break/>

"...will become manifest, perfectly awakened Buddhas. All the sufferings of the hells, the animal realms, and the world of the Lord of Death <gloss>Yama</gloss> will be completely severed; my body will not be weary as I prostrate with the supreme limb, my head, at the feet of that monk who speaks the Dharma." This is the tenth chapter from the King of Sovereign Sutras, the Holy Golden Light, called the Chapter of the Earth Goddess Dridha. 

Then the great general of the Yakshas, Samjna <gloss>Perfect Knowledge</gloss>, together with twenty-eight Yaksha generals, rose from his seat. He draped his robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, in the present and in the future, wherever this King of Sovereign Sutras, the Holy Golden Light, appears in a village, city, town, province, wilderness area, mountain valley, or palace circle, there I, the great general of Yakshas, Samjna, together with those twenty-eight great generals of Yakshas, shall go to that village, city, town, province, wilderness area, mountain valley, or palace circle. My body..."

ཀུན། །སྒྱུ་མའི་དཔེ་བཞིན་སྣང་ཡང་རང་བཞིན་མེད། །ཆོས་ཉིད་ཆོས་སྐུ་མི་སྣང་རང་བཞིན་ཡོད། །ཡོད་པའི་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པས་མཚན་མ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་གནོན། །མེད་པའི་ཡོད་
པར་རྟོགས་པས་རིག་པ་རང་ས་ཟིན། །དེ་ཡི་ཆེད་དུ་རྒྱན་ཏིག་བཀོད་པ་བཞི་ལྡན་བསྟན། །ཀྱེ་ཀྱེ་གསང་བའི་བདག་པོ་རྒྱན་དང་རོལ་པ་གར་བྱུང་ཡང་། །ངས་དོན་གསལ་འདིར་སྨྲས་པ་
བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག །ཅེས་གསུངས་སོ། །སྤྲོས་བྲལ་དོན་གསལ་གྱི་རྒྱུད་ཆེན་པོ་ལས། རྒྱན་དང་རོལ་པ་བསྟན་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་བཞི་པའོ།། །།
དེ་ནས་ཡང་གསང་བའི་བདག་པོས་ཞུས་པ། ཀྱེ་ཀྱེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་རྡོ་རྗེ་འཆང་། །དེ་མཚོན་ཚིག་རྣམས་གསུང་དུ་གསོལ། །ཞེས་ཞུས་སོ། །སྟོན་པས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། ངས་བསྟན་
རྒྱུད་ལུང་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ། །ཆོས་ཉིད་ངང་ནས་ཆོས་སྐུ་གནས། །དེ་སྐད་བརྗོད་པའི་ཚིག་བྱུང་ན། །ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་ཆོས་སྐུས་བརྒྱན་པར་བཤད། །རིག་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ལྔར་བཤད་ཅིང་།
དེ་ལྔ་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལྔ་ཡི་མཚན་ཉིད་དང་། །དེ་ཡི་གདངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པ་ན། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་ཡེ་ཤེས་བརྒྱན་པར་བཤད། །ཡེ་ཤེས་འོད་ལྔ་སྐུ་རུ་རྫོགས་ལུགས་དང་། །རིགས་དང་ཁ་

stored.16:
is clarified. In that, the three bodies are spontaneously established. Know that this will arise extensively below." Thus he spoke. From the Great Tantra of Radiant Meaning Free from Conceptual Elaborations, this is the eighth chapter, presenting and identifying the Base in brief. Not contained by the crystal casket, the radiance of the stupa of the turquoise mandala was brought outside; this is the pith instruction on the arising of the five goddesses of the Base. <term>Abhita Jnanapancaprasara Prarakaladharu Ahara</term> <note>Sanskrit mantra transliteration</note>. At that time, the Teacher, Great Vajradhara, entered the meditative absorption of Radiant Primordial Wisdom. Also at that time, the Lord of Secrets requested: "That Great Appearance of the Base spoken of above is the non-sudden primordial wisdom; for the followers of the present and future, please speak on the meanings of primordial wisdom." Thus he requested. The Teacher arose from the intention of Radiant Primordial Wisdom and spoke: "Son of noble family, listen! I shall show the meaning of primordial wisdom in brief. I shall explain the essence of primordial wisdom, the definition of primordial wisdom, the divisions along with their enumerations, and apply them to illustrative examples. The essence of primordial wisdom is: radiant and non-conceptual. Furthermore, the naturally pure primordial wisdom of the abiding base is substantive-less and transparently penetrating. If joined with the 'Bodies,' it is the Truth Body. If joined with 'Awareness,' it is the Essence. Son of noble family, the mode of abiding resides as light,

<leaf-break/>
and because it does not appear as having cessation, it is the "Non-Abiding Primordial Wisdom." O wonder! Son of noble family, knowing in such a way is the "Primordial Wisdom of Self-Aware Awareness" because of awareness knowing itself. Because there is no creator in that, it is "Self-Arisen Primordial Wisdom." Because one does not deviate from its meaning, it is the "Primordial Wisdom of the Intent of the Moment of Death." To show the examples: the example for the "Primordial Wisdom of the Abiding Base" is like a jewel because everything arises from it. The "Primordial Wisdom of the Expanse of Reality" is like the sky. The example for "Mirror-like Primordial Wisdom" is like clear water or a polished mirror. For "Primordial Wisdom of Equality," the example of the equality of the three times is like a river. The example for "Non-Dual Primordial Wisdom" is like gold and its yellow color. The example for "Discriminating Primordial Wisdom" is like the stars and planets appearing in the ocean. The example for "All-Accomplishing Primordial Wisdom" is like the wind and the sun. The example for "Non-Abiding Primordial Wisdom" is like the moon in water. The example for "Primordial Wisdom of Self-Aware Awareness" is like a crystal and its light. The example for "Self-Arisen Primordial Wisdom" is like a diamond. The example for "Primordial Wisdom of the Intent of the Moment of Death" is like a queen abiding by the king's law, whom no man seeks to pursue. Thus he spoke. From the Great Tantra of Radiant Meaning Free from Conceptual Elaborations, this is the ninth chapter, showing the full identification of primordial wisdom.
stored.17:
Then the Teacher spoke again: "If one speaks of all activities arising from the Tantras and Transmissions I have taught, that is the Primordial Wisdom of the Abiding Base. If one practices in the emptiness of non-existence, that is the Primordial Wisdom of the Expanse of Reality. If one practices without cessation, that is the Mirror-like Primordial Wisdom. If one speaks without duality, that is the Primordial Wisdom of Equality. If one practices in an unmixed and perfect way, the words expressing distinct cognitive clarity are the Discriminating Primordial Wisdom. If one speaks of being without any obstruction, that is the All-Accomplishing Primordial Wisdom. Because one speaks of being free from extremes, it is the Non-Abiding Primordial Wisdom. By speaking of radiant awareness and by saying 'self-awareness,' it is the Great Primordial Wisdom of Awareness. Having spoken the diamond-like words 'unchanging' and 'unconditioned,' it is explained as the Great Self-Arisen Primordial Wisdom. Do not pass beyond; it is impossible to pass beyond; it is non-passing; press the syllables of the intent of the moment of death into the heart." Thus he spoke. From the Great Tantra of Radiant Meaning Free from Conceptual Elaborations, this is the tenth chapter, showing the words that symbolize primordial wisdom.

The pith instruction on the unceasing radiance within the Heart of the Sun. <term>Jnana Ah Shara Ratna Kala Prasahadu</term> <note>Sanskrit mantra transliteration</note>. At that time, the Blessed One dwelt in the intent of the power of compassion.

<leaf-break/>

"It abides in greatness. It abides in unimpeded, radiant transparency. Even the appearance of the two Form Bodies <note>the sambhogakaya and nirmanakaya</note> is completely pure, not appearing to oneself." Thus he spoke. From the Great Tantra of Radiant Meaning Free from Conceptual Elaborations, this is the eleventh chapter, showing the arising of the power of awareness and the complete purity of that power.

Then again the Lord of Secrets <note>Vajrapani</note> requested: "Please speak the words that symbolize that." Thus he requested. The Teacher spoke: "In all the Tantras and Transmissions I have taught, if the term 'power' <note>Tibetan: rtsal</note> appears, it is explained in this way: The power of awareness is the five primordial wisdoms. The power of those is the five colored lights. The power of the five lights is the five elements. The power of space opens the opportunity for clouds and mist. The power of wind is the roar of sound and movement. For water, it is the sound of rushing and the gathering of moisture. For earth, it is the appearance of form and providing a foundation. For fire, it is heat and the ripening of burning. From the white light come flesh and bone. From the yellow light come bile and lymph. From the red light come blood and warmth. From the green light comes breath. From the blue light comes the opening of the body's cavities. The power of the five elements arises individually; they are shown as both outer and inner. These are called the power of the outer and inner <term>bindu</term> <gloss>seminal points/spheres</gloss>. Appearing in that way, they are explained as the strength of capacity. By arising in that way, they are self-arisen."
stored.18:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Then the Lord of Secrets, having understood the intent, requested: "The single Body of Reality <note>Dharmakaya</note> appears as diverse. Please speak on the manner in which the power of awareness arises." Thus he requested. The Teacher spoke: "In the non-existent, transparent awareness, emptiness and unceasingness are indivisible. In that, why is discerning wisdom unobstructed? It is because it self-arises as the five primordial wisdoms. The self-radiance of the wisdom of the light of the expanse of reality is clear as blue from within the state of emptiness. The self-radiance of the mirror-like wisdom is clear as white from within the unceasing state. The self-radiance of the wisdom of equality is clear as yellow from within the indivisible state. The self-radiance of the discriminating wisdom is clear as red from within the state of knowing that. The self-radiance of the all-accomplishing wisdom is clear as green from within the unobstructed expanse. Those five arise in the expanse of reality; they are said to 'arise as the light of primordial wisdom.' Through realization, the bodies and primordial wisdom appear. Without realization, they arise as the two: the vessel <note>the external world</note> and the contents <note>sentient beings</note>. For example, though appearances occur in a pure mirror due to whatever conditions it meets, it is not stained at the time of appearance. Although there is no staining, it appears in that way. Likewise, in the awareness of the Body of Reality, various unceasing qualities arise. Even as they arise, they are clear as a single self-awareness. Abiding as one, there is no weariness. At all times and in all circumstances, it is non-existent and pure."

<leaf-break/>

"It did not arise from anything else; it arose from itself. Because the qualities have arisen, it is self-arising. Because it arises in that way, it is self-manifesting. That is what is meant by 'qualities.' All that arises, the total arising, and the many coarse arisings are the self-manifestation of the arising of awareness. The five bodies self-manifest as the five objects. Likewise, they appear as male and female bodhisattvas. Likewise, the activities of compassion appear. Similarly, various appearances manifest. When it is said to be 'like an illusion,' it means appearing while lacking inherent nature, and being radiant while lacking conceptualization. Thus, the power is explained as lacking inherent nature. Everything is self-appearance and self-manifestation." Thus he spoke. From the Great Tantra of Radiant Meaning Free from Conceptual Elaborations, this is the twelfth chapter, showing the arising of the power of awareness and the words that symbolize it.

Then again the Lord of Secrets requested: "Teacher, you who possess great compassion, what is the essence of this power? What is its definition and what are its divisions?" Thus he requested. "What are the examples that symbolize it?" The Teacher spoke: "The essence is unceasingness. As for the definition of power, because it possesses the strength of arising, it is 'power.' The division is the appearance of awareness as the two: cyclic existence <note>samsara</note> and liberation <note>nirvana</note>."

"King, even the wild beasts of my hermitage are respected. Will you kill this deer that has come for refuge?" Thus the sage spoke to the king. Then the army arrived and asked, "Your Majesty, to whom is this man speaking so rudely?" The King replied, "To me." They said, "O Wise One, what is the punishment for one who speaks so harshly to the King?" He replied, "Your Majesty, the punishment is death." If that was the case, the sage was completely abandoned. As they prepared to kill him, he made a perverse prayer: "By this king's quarrelsome act of seeking to kill me, though I am innocent and have done no harm, wherever he is born, may I be the one to deprive him of life!" Then he thought, "These kings are very well-hidden, very well-guarded, and very well-protected. If I take birth elsewhere, I will never find an opportunity. Therefore, by this prayer, may I be born in the womb of his noble queen." Because of that perverse prayer, he was born in the womb of Gochen. On the very day he entered the womb, a rain of blood fell. Gochen developed a craving: "Oh, if only I could cut and eat the flesh from the King's back!" When the King was told of this, he summoned the diviners and asked them.

<leaf-break/>

"It will happen." The King thought, "Since he will surely deprive me of life for the sake of the kingdom, if I give him the kingdom myself, why would he kill me?" At that time, in Vaishali, there lived a Licchavi named Mingchen. In his pleasure grove was a grove of mango trees. There, a banana tree <note>or plantain</note> suddenly grew, which was seen by the keeper of the grove. Immediately flowers appeared, and being amazed, he told Mingchen. Mingchen summoned the diviners and asked them. They said, "Lord, please protect it. On the seventh day it will burst open, and a girl will emerge from within." When the householder Mingchen heard this, he was even more amazed. He stationed guards all around the grove and began counting the days. When seven days had passed, he cleared the stones, pebbles, and shards from the grove, sprinkled it with sandalwood water, prepared fragrant incense burners, hung many silk tassels, and scattered loose flowers. Surrounded by songs, instrumental music of many kinds, and friends and kinsmen, he went with his wife in great splendor.

དམར་ནག་ཝ་ལ་རྒན་བྱེད་ཕག་། །དམར་ནག་སྐྱེད་ཀ་སྔོན་མོ་བྱ། །གསུས་འཛིན་སེར་ནག་སྦྱང་སྡོང་མ་། །སྲིན་མོ་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་བརྒྱད་དབྱིངས་

རིགས་བཞི་དབང་ཆེན་བཞི་རྣམས་དབྱིངས་ནས་བཞེངས་། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་ཕྱིའི་བར་ཁྱམས་ནས་། །ཡེ་ཤེས་ཁྲོ་བོ་ཟིལ་གནོན་ཡབ༑
ཡུམ་ཅིག་མི་ཕམ་ཟིལ་ལྡན་ཡུམ་། །ལས་ཀྱི་ཁྲོ་བོ་ཟིལ་གནོན་ཡབ་། །ཡུམ་ཅིག་ཁྲོ་གཉེར་ཟིལ་གནོན་མ་། །ཡེ་ཤེས་མ་མོ་ཟིལ་
གནོན་ཡབ་། །ཡུམ་ཅིག་རོ་ལངས་ཟིལ་གནོན་མ་། །ཡེ་ཤེས ་ཁྱུང་ཆེན་ཟིལ་གནོན་ཡབ་། །ཡུམ ་ཅིག་ཟིལ་གནོན་རལ་ཅིག་མ།
ཕོ་རྒྱུད་ཟིལ་གནོན་ཁྲོ་བོ་ཡབ་། །ཡུམ་ཅིག་རྡོ་རྗེ་ལས་བྱེད་མ་། །མོ་རྒྱུད་ཟིལ་གནོན་ཁྲོ་བོ་ཡང་། །ཡུམ་ཅིག་གཤིན་རྗེ་ལས་བྱེད་མ། །
ཀླུ་རྣམས་ཟིལ་གནོན་ཁྲོ་བོ་ཡབ་།།ཡུམ་ཅིག་ཀླུ་མོ་ལས་བྱེད་མ་། །གཟའ་རྣམས་ཟིལ་གནོན་ཁྲོ་བོ་ཡང། །ཡུམ་ཅིག་གནོད་
<leaf-break/>
ལྡན་འདུལ་བྱེད་དཔལ་གྱི་ཁྱི་དང་སྤྱང་། །ཡེ་ཤེས་དཔལ་གྱི་ཁྱི་བརྒྱད་སྤྱང་བརྒྱད་དབྱིངས་ནས་བཞེངས། །སྐུ་ལས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་ཁམས་རྒྱ་
མོ། །གསུང་ལས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་ཁམས་རྒྱམོ། །ཐུགས་ལས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་ཁམས་རྒྱ་མོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་སྤྲུལ་པའི་ཁམས་རྒྱ་མོ་། །འཕྲིན་
ལས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་ཁམས་རྒྱ་མོ་།།གཉིས་མེད་སྤྲུལ་པའི་ཁམས་རྒྱ་མོ་།སྤྲུལ་སྐུ་ཁམས་རྒྱ་དྲུག་རྣམས་དབྱིངས་ནས་བཞེངས་། །ཤར་
ཕྱོགས་སྨྲ་ལོང་འཁོར་བ་དང་། །ལྷོ་ཕྱོགས་སྨྲ་ལོང་འཁོར་བ་དང། །ནུབ་ཕྱོགས་སྨྲ་ལོང་འཁོར་བ་ དང་། །བྱང་ཕྱོགས་སྨྲ་ལོང་འཁོར་
བ་དང་། །ཡེ་ཤེས་སྨྲ་ལོང་འཁོར་བ་དང་།།ཡེ་ཤེས་སྨུན་ལོང་དྲུག་རྣམས་དབྱིངས་ནས་ བཞེངས་། །དཀར་མོ་ཟླ་འདབ་འཇིགས་པའི་གཟུགྶ་
<leaf-break/>
དེ་ནས་ཕུར་པ་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཀྱི་ལྷ་ཚོགས་བསྐུལ་བ་ནི་འདི་སྐད་དོ། །ཧཱུཾ་སྣང་སྲིད་གྲུ་གསུམ་འབར་བའི་དཀྱིར་འཁོར་ནས་། །ཕུར་པ་འཕྲིན་
ལས་ཀྱི་ལྷ་ཚོགས་དབྱིངས་བཞེངས་། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་དབུས་ཀྱི་ལྟེ་བ་ནས་། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་(དཔལ་ཆེན་)རྡོ་རྗེ་གཞོན་ནུ་ཡབ་། །གཉིས་མེད་
ཡུམ་ཆེན་འཁོར་ལོ་རྒྱས་འདེབས་མ་། །དབུས་ཀྱི་གཙོ་མཆོག་ཡབ་ཡུམ་དབྱིངས་ནས་བཞེངས་། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོརའཁོར་ལོའི་
རྩིབ་སྟེང་ནས་། །སྲས་མཆོག་བྷུད་དྷ་ཀི་ལ་ཡ་། །སྲས་མཆོག་རད་ན་ཀི་ལ་ཡ་། །སྲས་མཆོགཔད་མ་ཀི་ལ་ཡ་། །སྲས་མཆོགཀརྨ་
ཀི་ལ་ཡ་། །སྲས་མཆོགབཞི་རྣམས་དབྱིངས་ནས་བཞེང་། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་བར་ཁྱམ་ནས་། །ཡབ་ཅིག་ཁྲོ་བོ་ཧཱུཾཀ་ར་། །

'—may such a precious person be born, and may I please him! May I not displease him!' The other girl made this prayer: 'May I be your sibling wherever you are born. May I support such a precious person as this!' The girl who was the hairdresser for the two siblings was also there. Having heard the prayers they made, immediately after hearing them, she also made offerings to the perfectly and completely enlightened Buddha Vipashyin and made a prayer: 'Alas! By this root of virtue, wherever these two are born, may I become their hairdresser and attendant, and may I please their precious son! May I not displease him!' Thus she made such a prayer. 'Venerable One, what did she do to please the Blessed One and not displease him, and after being ordained in the teaching of the Blessed One, abandon all afflictions, manifest Arhatship, and be declared by the Blessed One as the foremost of those who have initiated perseverance?' The Blessed One replied: 'She was ordained in the word of the perfectly and completely enlightened Buddha Kashyapa, from which—'

<leaf-break/>

"—may I please the Buddha, the Blessed One, who was prophesied as the Brahmin youth Uttara. May I not displease him. Having been ordained in his teaching and abandoned all afflictions, may I manifest Arhatship. Just as my female preceptor was declared by the perfectly and completely enlightened Buddha Kashyapa as the foremost of those who have initiated perseverance, so may I also be declared by that Shakyamuni, the King of the Shakyas, as the foremost of those who have initiated perseverance.' Monks, I have attained the state of being exactly equal to the perfectly and completely enlightened Buddha Kashyapa, equal in power, equal in deeds, and equal in methods. Thus she has pleased me and not displeased me. By being ordained in my own teaching and abandoning all afflictions, she manifested Arhatship, and now I have declared her the foremost of those who have initiated perseverance."

The story of "Lotus-Colored" <note>original: Utpalavarna</note>: The setting was in Shravasti. At that time, the Venerable Upasanda was traveling through the countryside of Rakshasas and arrived at a mountain retreat. How can the grasping of the essence of reality's own nature be erroneous? If one says: "Even though it is the essence of reality, because of the obsessive attachment to it as being erroneous, it is called 'erroneous' by the power of the worldly," what is meant here by "the worldly"? What kind of knowledge is that? If one says: "Whenever these are analyzed, the conventional which is undeniably pleasant is what it is," then even if it is not desired, one must accept that the very part of it that is suitable for engagement as an appearance to direct perception is the valid cognition for this conventionality; one should know that "being like an illusion" itself is not established by direct perception. However, if one establishes that which is established by direct perception as grasping only the nature of things as being "like an illusion" based on the power of the "valid cognition that harms the contrary" through inference, it has already been established that such a thing established by direct perception is not "worldly knowledge." If one says "reality is established," then if it were not so, the conventions of "knowledge" and "object of knowledge" would not engage; however, it will be shown later that they engage in the conventional. Therefore, just as it is in accordance with obsessive attachment, it is an inference possessing the certainty pervaded by its own valid cognition. Things are currently established as "like an illusion"; in that way they remain. Therefore, in the *Noble Lankavatara Sutra* and others, the Blessed One taught that "whatever appears is the conventional truth" and "the lineage <note>nature</note> as it is, is the ultimate truth." Enough with this extreme proliferation.

<leaf-break/>

If one says: "Because they are included in the essence of mere <note>consciousness</note>, non-duality itself is established," let it be so, but nevertheless, by relying on the systems that are established as separate from that appearance and so forth, do you conceptually construct other phenomena like "reality" and so forth, or is it that you have no such conceptualization? If the first position is taken, then whatever is non-erroneous consciousness does not grasp other super-imposed phenomena, just as some non-deluded knowledge of a jewel's form does not. Because this knowledge is also non-erroneous—this is the "apprehension of the contradiction of the pervader." Because all minds and mental factors that are free from conceptualization and devoid of all super-impositions are experienced as merely existing in themselves, it is not unestablished. Because it exists in the concordant class, it is also not contradictory. Because of grasping super-imposed phenomena, it would not know its own essence. Thus, because there is a valid cognition that harms the contrary, the reason is also not uncertain. In the second position, because of grasping super-imposed phenomena, its own essence is for its own sake <note>is self-known</note>. Because there is a valid cognition that harms the contrary, the reason is also not uncertain. If the second position is accepted, then at that time, when one cannot find fault in the object of appearance, this very realization of just the meaning devoid of super-imposed phenomena is "knowing as illusion." That is a mere dispute over names and is trivial. Whether it is called "non-dual" or "dual," because that itself is like an illusion, it has no core, for there is no valid cognition that establishes that point. In that way, by merely generating the mind,

<leaf-break/>

here too there is error. By realizing without error, one "touches" the Unsurpassed, meaning one attains it. Therefore, enlightenment is the purpose of fulfilling one's own benefit. "Thinking of that is the mind"; by that, through the very name "Bodhisattva" which possesses meaning, he obtains the names "Authentically Entered Being," "Excellent One," and "Good One." By that, the object of focus was shown. If one desires the ever-pure expanse of phenomena <term>dharmadhātu</term> to be the object of focus for non-dual primordial wisdom, how can their "ever-pure" state be described as a "progression in purification"? If one says: "It is desired to be pure like the element of water or the sky," then if that is so, for one who meditates on the nature of things as determined by the knowledge of hearing and thinking, because they engage with the obsessive attachment "I must directly perceive the reality of things just as they are," the seeds of the latencies of that obsessive attachment do not stop even through the distinction of meditation. If one says: "By the nature of being extremely meditative, one's conceptual constructions gradually become few," then if that were so, even the systems that desire external objects would abandon the conceptual constructions of Hearers and so forth, but that is not accepted. Therefore, because it does not abandon the latencies of conceptual construction, it would follow that it is "partial." If you ask "What is your system?", there is no fault. Because whatever slight essence of things there is, it is all "labeled." Because all these are not established as things by reasoning, they are non-existent.

པ་སོ་མ་བཏང་བ་ཆུས་རེག་པ་དང་ཞིག་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེས་ནི་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་གྱི་ཡོངས་སུ་བཟུང་བར་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དྲོ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རྗེས་ལ་ད་ནི་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ལ་ཇི་སྐད་བསྟན་པའི་ངེས་པར་འབྱེད་པའི་ཆ་དང་མཐུན་པ་དང་།
མཐོང་བའི་ལམ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཞན་ཡང་འབྱུང་བས་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་གཞིར་གྱུར་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་བསྟན་པར་བཞེད་ནས། ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུགས་ཏེ། གང་གིས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ཉིད་འཕགས་པས་ཆོས་རྟོགས་
པའི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། དེའི་བདག་ཉིད་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སྟེ། རང་བཞིན་དུ་གནས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རིགས་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་དེ་ཉིད། ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཁྱབ་ན་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་

Focusing on the Buddha for the sake of omniscience itself, and familiarizing oneself with selflessness as the means for that, is "training after the Buddha's phenomena"; it is training in the knowledge of the Bodhisattva's path. Therefore, "non-training" <term>aśaikṣa</term> is the "non-training" in sequence, because of being completely grasped by the power of wisdom and skill in means. For that very reason, "realizing without error" is the meaning of "training." One who completely knows the levels of Definite Distinction in that way will completely know the path of the Solitary Buddhas as described. To show the Definite Distinction, 

it says "Increase of form" and so forth. Regarding that, by expressing the general nature, "form" here refers to the five appropriated aggregates. "Increase" is accumulation. "Decrease" is the absence of accumulation. "Complete grasping" continues until "relying upon." 

The one who completely knows the determination of the meditation on the aspects as described is a "trainee" <term>śaikṣa</term>; he is one who enters. That for which the mind of enlightenment is "non-training": regarding the appropriated aggregates that are to be discarded, he does not train for the sake of completely grasping the increase or decrease of the aggregates. Regarding the various phenomena to be adopted, such as the applications of mindfulness, he does not train for the sake of completely grasping their increase or decrease. For that very reason, the Buddha does not completely grasp omniscience; he does not even show it with the mind, because it would be a bond. By such means, he has definitely emerged, and in that regard, he trains here:

<leaf-break/>

rejoicing in Buddhahood itself as the essence of compassion without focus. By this, the meaning of the word "Being" <term>sattva</term> was shown. By that, it is shown as follows: having abandoned the showing of a mere reflection <note>a facsimile</note> connected to the Great Being <term>Mahāsattva</term> the Bodhisattva, the Perfection of Wisdom itself is to be heard. This does not mean "only those forms," because since the three types of enlightenment do not occur without it, it is shown for the sake of mastery. Although it is spoken of by the general term "Perfection of Wisdom," nevertheless, by the power of the convention and so forth, it is understood to be the specific meaning, because the Perfection of Wisdom is the meaning of the nature of the mind of enlightenment that includes all aspects of all phenomena. By that, it says: "By thoroughly awakening the seed of great compassion, having taken the Bodhisattva vows and so forth, and having generated the mind of enlightenment whose essence is emptiness and compassion, one thinks: 'Having attained the perfectly complete Buddhahood, I shall perform the benefit of others according to their lot.'" Having made such a prayer, one should fulfill the accomplishment. The "aspiration" is characterized by the desire to realize the perfectly complete enlightenment, which is the result together with its cause, focusing on the benefit of others. The generation of the mind with the nature of "entering" <term>prasthāna</term> proceeds through the sequence of the levels such as the Accumulation, until the Buddha's "Complete Radiance" <term>Samantaprabha</term> stage, which is in every aspect

<leaf-break/>

The word "also" <note>Tibetan: 'ang</note> has the meaning of emphasis. Whatever Bodhisattva, in that way, through the aspect of the reality of completely knowing all phenomena such as the "external self" as being signless, does not "touch" nirvana <note>does not enter literal cessation</note> because he possesses the power of skill in conventional means. "Not touching" means non-apprehension. By the power of the ultimate, he dwells in the Perfection of Wisdom, in the expanse of phenomena <term>dharmadhātu</term>. This is the focusing on form and so forth as distinguished by signlessness and so forth; it possesses the result. If one asks what its "aspect" is, 

it says "This wisdom" and so forth. Among these, form and so forth, which one is it? Is it a substance, a quality, an action, a universal, a particular, or an inherence? Regarding "who is it," is it the self, or is it connected to form and so forth? "From what": is it from the self, or from phenomena, or in what? Or is it from the self, or from phenomena? Because all these phenomena are not born in reality. The word "whatever" <note>Tibetan: ji'i</note> should be applied everywhere: "this is not anything," "it belongs to no one," "it is in nothing." Thus, through wisdom, one conceptually analyzes all phenomena as non-apprehended. "Close investigation" is the close investigation of those; "thorough engagement" <note>original: rnam par spyod pa</note> is either that, or following these aspects, the Bodhisattva enters.

Because of delighting in familiarization, the Blessed One is the Perfection of Omniscience itself. The phrase "in sequence" is an addition to the words. Regarding the abandonment of the remaining afflictions: because one focuses again and again on the essence of the path previously shown, it is established as the Path of Meditation. Therefore, since the Bodhisattvas completely know through the very complete knowledge of the Path of Seeing, one should understand that it is not described as a separate Path of Meditation associated with Hearers and so forth, as it was in the Path of Seeing. By the power of the seeing of the Sons of the Conqueror who have become thus, they obtain mastery over their own path. Because they then sustain sentient beings to be tamed by other vehicles, they are "Completely Victorious" over the two paths.

In that same way, there is no wisdom in form. This is for the sake of realizing the Path of Seeing, which is the great benefit possessed of consciousness and so forth. Form is not wisdom; it does not exist in suchness. Likewise, there is no wisdom apart from form; there is no wisdom in anything such as consciousness, and the same applies to wisdom itself. However, like the element of space, these things such as form are empty. Because they are not produced through reasoning, all phenomena lack the characteristic of being distinct as support and supported. This continues until: they do not exist as a nature of various distinctions. As it is said: parts

<leaf-break/>

The identity of those things to be realized: "One should produce and accomplish the knowledge of hearing and so forth in the illusion-like Perfection of Wisdom." This is shown by the meaning. If one asks, "How does the production of the mind, which is the identity of Omniscience itself, connect to those through the Bodhisattvas' accomplishment of the Knowledge of the Path and so forth?" it says: "Where the Brave ones practice." "Where" refers to the Perfection of Wisdom. To be victorious over all phenomena of the discordant side and to be invincible is the "Practice of the Brave" Bodhisattvas. Entering with familiarization in its entirety is the nature of producing such things; this is the meaning of "Perfection of Wisdom." Therefore, the mind shown in this way has no other phenomenon apart from the Dharma. Even the instructions and so forth are only distinctions of the production of the mind in order to show the distinguished meaning. Therefore, its nature, Omniscience itself, will be shown first by condensing all the phenomena to be obtained by a Bodhisattva. It will be shown that it is "shown first." If that is so, one might ask: "Why does the *One Hundred Thousand Verse Sūtra* show the Bodhisattva's Knowledge of the Path and so forth as distinct?" It is said: because Omniscience itself is the result together with its causes, in view of obtaining that, it will be shown as the aspect of the Buddha, the Blessed One.

<leaf-break/>

If one asks for what purpose it is the cause: it says, "having closely investigated." Having closely investigated all phenomena as emptiness through the various aspects just shown, their objects and aspects, one is without discouragement because of being without attachment. Because it is endowed with reasoning, there is no fear. Furthermore, entering into that very reality without error is the "Peak." Through realizing the distinctions of small, medium, and great, the hearing of any enlightenment such as that of the Hearers is shown to be the cause that brings all enlightenments and Bodhisattvas close. 

Following the Peak is now "Patience." Because of the great dharma of patience, symbolized by the absence of lower realms, and to show the object of becoming patient, it says "If..." and so forth. "If one practices without knowledge" means practicing without realizing selflessness. "Investigation" is conceptualization. "Practicing with signs" is practicing the opposite. This refers to practicing from the attachment to form based on its general characteristics up to consciousness, without knowing the reality of phenomena. This is because it is harmed by valid cognition, like the knowledge of a mirage. It connects to: "practicing with the signs of an object." Thus it will be shown. Likewise, if one investigates the five aggregates of form and so forth as "empty" and practices with attachment, even if one practices without realizing the nature of phenomena at that time, because that attachment to emptiness is also harmed by valid cognition,
stored.66:
it is "practicing with signs." Likewise, the Bodhichitta that practices by turning away from the practice of attachment to the nature of things and non-things is the very state of non-arising. Because it is the support for the Path of Seeing and so forth, it is a "state." Practicing without attachment or fixation upon that is the "practice." Therefore, in the complete abandonment of nature, focusing on form and so forth as distinguished by "lack of nature" and so forth is the "practice." It is shown to be the object. 

If one asks what its "aspect" is: it says "Whatever form" and so forth. "Whatever" refers to practicing without a state because of non-arising. From the absence of form up to consciousness, it means not practicing with attachment to what is apprehended and not experiencing it. The Bodhisattva who practices without observing an apprehender because there is nothing apprehended "does not observe" the practice, meaning he does not realize it. Because of being completely unshakable by any aspects of signs through focusing on the aspects such as the essence of form and so forth having no nature, it is called the "teaching of wisdom." By this, the transformation is shown. 

If one asks for what purpose it is a cause: it says "The wise one of non-birth" and so forth. Likewise, the wise one who realizes the objects and aspects as non-arising, after realizing the distinctions of small, medium, and great patience, possesses the nature of one-pointed mental focus.

<leaf-break/>

"Childish beings" are those in whom the Path of the Aryas has not arisen. Their "sign" is in accordance with reasoning. These phenomena, as they appear, are "existent." According to reality and reasoning, they are "non-existent." That which is further to be abandoned is the basis for total affliction. Ignorance is the very object of the first conceptualization of the apprehended. It acts in accordance with total affliction. It "acts" in the sense of depositing, just as one deposits seeds for cleaning. Likewise, according to the object of the second conceptualization of the apprehended, which is the basis for the remedy to be adopted, it is deposited in accordance with conceptualization. 

Having thus established the conceptualizations of the apprehended, and beginning from these two, the teaching on meditating on them together with the objects of attachment as false and illusion-like is given by saying "knowledge and ignorance" and so forth. These two, knowledge and ignorance, are phenomena in which form and so forth are non-existent because they are not born in reality. Childish beings conceptualize "knowledge" and "ignorance" by the power of manifest pride. Any Bodhisattva who thoroughly knows through the sequence of hearing and so forth will "definitely emerge." By entering correctly from the bonds of error, he definitely emerges. Following the two conceptualizations of the apprehended, in order to show the first conceptualization of the apprehender, it says "Who" and so forth. Any Bodhisattva who apprehends the five aggregates as having a nature of substantially existent persons, through the power of reasoning, sees the aggregates as an illusion or a delusion.

<leaf-break/>

This is because it is the cause of obtaining the stages. It continues until: "is the one who experiences the application." In order for these four conceptualizations to be understood by those to be tamed among the gathered circle, the Blessed One previously spoke of nine aspects for each, divided by the distinction of objects. However, here they are shown in summary, focusing on the principal points. There is no need for an extensive teaching. Thinking that the division by objects in the *One Hundred Thousand Verse Sūtra* is not the primary concern here, the division of the object-basis for the stages of definite distinction is one thing. The division of conceptualization shown in view of the seeing of the peak realization and the Path of Meditation is another. 

Since this is the essence, from that characteristic where they exist having mutually abandoned one another, because there are no other aggregates, one should understand the subsequent ones in the same way, following the two previously shown conceptualizations of the apprehended and the apprehender. This shows the being sustained by the Spiritual Friend and skill in means. Because the previously shown distinctions arise through their power, it says "virtuous" and so forth. Because the person who teaches the Dharma without departing from the two truths causes the result of a happy rebirth to be obtained, they are a "Spiritual Friend." To possess that is to be "endowed." Having produced the knowledge of hearing and so forth through that, "possessing discernment" refers to reasoning.

རིན་པོ་ཆེས་ཆོག་པར་གྱུར་ནས ། ཕྱིར་ཡང་བདེ་བར་ཡུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་ཏེ ། དེའི་ཚེ་དགེ་བསྙེན་དེ་དང་ཚོང་པ་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཙམ་སངས་རྒྱས་གང་ན་བར་འོངས་ནས ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཞབས་ལ་སྤྱི་བོས་ཕྱག་
འཚལ་ཏེ ། སོ་སོ་ནས་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་ཐོགས་པ་དང་ ། རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ལྷས་བསྐུར་བ་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་དགེ་འདུནལ་ཕུལ་ཏེ ། དེ་དག་པུས་མོ་ས་ལ་བཙུགས་ནས་ཐལ་མོ་སྦྱར་ཏེ ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་
འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །བདག་ཅག་ཀྱང་སྟོན་པའི་བསྟན་པ་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་འབྱུང་ངོ་ཞེས་སྨྲས་ནས ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདསཀྱིས་དགེ་སློང་ལེགས་པར་འོངས་སོ་ཞེས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ་དང་ ། སྐྲ་དང་ཁ
སྤུ་རང་བྱི་སྟེ་ཆོས་གོས་གྱོན་པའི་དགེ་སློང་དུ་གྱུར་ཏོ། །དེ་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཅི་རིགས་སུ་ཆོས་བསྟན་ཅིང་ཕྱེ་བས་འདོད་པ་ཀུན་ཟད་དེ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །འཁོར་མང་པོ་དེ་དག་བཅོམ
ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་པ་ལ་ཡི་རང་ནས་མངོན་པར་དགའ་འོ། །རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ལྷས་དྲིས་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་ལྔ་པའོ།། །།བམ་པོ་གཉིས་པ།། །།ལྷའི

ཕྱུག་པོ་ཞིག་ལ་བུ་མེད་དོ། །དེའི་ཚེ་ན་ཆུ་ཀླུང་གངྒཱའི་འགྲམ་ན་མ་ཎི་བྷ་དྲ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ལྷའི་རྟེན་ཞིག་ཡོད་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་དེ་ལ་ཕྱག་འཚལ་ཞིང་མཆོད་པ་བྱེད་དོ། །བློན་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ཡང་ལྷའི་རྟེན་
གྱི་དྲུང་དུ་སོང་ནས་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །བདག་ལ་བུ་ཚ་མེད་དེ། ལྷ་ཁྱོད་ཡོན་ཏན་ཚད་མེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞེས་ཐོས་ཀྱིས། འགྲོ་བ་ཀུན་ལ་སྐྱོབ་པ་ཁྱོད་གཞན་གྱི་སྨོན་ལམ་བསྐང་བར་ནུས་ན།
བདག་ཀྱང་བསྐབ་ཏུ་གསོལ་ལོ། །གལ་ཏེ་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་བདག་ལ་བུ་ཅིག་སྩལ་ན། གསེར་དང་དངུལ་གྱིས་ལྷ་ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡང་གཡོག་ཅིང་བཞུགས་པའི་རྟེན་ཡང་སྤོས་དང་བྱུག་པས་བྱུག་གི །ཇི་སྟེ་མངོན་
རྟགས་མེད་ན་ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་རྟེན་ཡང་བཤིག་ལ་ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་ལུས་ལ་མི་གཙང་བ་བཤང་གཅེས་ཀྱང་བསྐུའོ་ཞེས་སྨྲས་པ། ལྷ་དེས་ཐོས་ནས་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བསམས་སོ། །བློན་པོ་འདི་ནི་ཕྱུག་ཅིང་བཙན་ལ་མཐུ་ཆེ་
བས་སྨད་རིགས་ཙམ་གྱིས་འདིའི་བུར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། བདག་མཐུ་ཆུངས་པས་འདིའི་སྨོན་ལམ་བསྐང་མི་ནུས་སོ། །གལ་ཏེ་སྔོན་པ་བཞིན་དུ་མ་བྱས་ན་གདོན་མི་ཟ་བར་མི་སྡུག་པར་མཐོ་བཙམས་སོ་སྙམ་
བསམས་ནས། རྟེན་བསྲུང་བའི་ལྷ་དེས་མ་ཎི་བྷ་དྲ་ལ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །དེ་ལ་ཡང་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་མཐུ་མེད་པས། རྣམ་ཐོས་ཀྱི་བུ་གང་ན་བ་དེར་སོང་སྟེ། རྣམ་ཐོས་ཀྱི་བུ་ལ་གསོལ་བ་དང་། རྣམ་ཐོས་ཀྱི་
བུས་ཀྱང་བདག་གི་མཐུ་ཙམ་གྱིས་བུ་ཡོད་པར་མི་ནུས་སོ་སྙམ་བསམས་ནས། རྣམ་ཐོས་ཀྱི་བུ་དེ་བརྒྱ་བྱིན་གང་ན་བ་དེར་སོང་སྟེ་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །བདག་གི་བློན་པོ་མ་ཎི་བྷ་དྲ་ཞེས་བགྱི་བ་དེར་དག་
བསམས་ནས། རྟེན་བསྲུག་བའི་ལྷ་དེས་མ་ཎི་བྷ་ཏྲ་ལ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །དེ་ལ་ཡང། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་མཐུ་མེད་པས་རྣམ་ཐོས་ཀྱི་བུ་གང་ན་བ། རྣམ་ཐོས་ཀྱི་བུ་གང་ན། རྣམ་ཐོས་ཀྱི་བུ་གང་ལ་གསོལ་བ་དང་། བདག་ནི་རབ་ཏུ་འབྱུང་བར་གསོལ་ལོ་ཞེས་སྨྲས་སོ། །དེའི་ཕ་མས་སྨྲས་པ། ཁོ་བོ་ནི་འདི་ལྟར་ཕྱུག་ཅིང་བཙན་ཏེ་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཆེན་པོ་དང་ལྡན་ལ། བུ་ནི་ཁྱོད་གཅིག་པུར་ཟད་དེ་ངའི་རིགས་བསབ་ཅིང་
ཕ་མ་གསོ་དགོས་ཀྱིས་མི་གནང་ངོ་ཞེས་བསྒོ་བ་དང་། ཁྱེའུ་དེས་བསམས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་མ་གྱུར་པས་ཤིན་ཏུ་མི་དགའ་སྟེ། འདི་སྙམ་དུ་ལུས་འདི་མེད་པར་བྱས་ལ། རིགས་ཐ་མལ་པ་ཞིག་ཏུ་སྐྱེས་ཏེ་རབ་
ཏུ་འབྱུང་བར་གསོལ་ན། འདི་བས་སླ་ཡང་སྲིད་སྙམ་བསམས་ནས་གསང་སྟེ། ཕྱི་རོལ་ཏུ་བྱུང་ནས་བྲག་མཐོན་པོ་ཞིག་ལ་མཆོངས་སོ། །བྲག་ལས་མཆོངས་ནས་ས་ལ་ལྷུང་ན་ཡང་སྣང་པའམ་ཉེས་པ་
མེད་དོ། །དེ་ནས་ཆུ་ཆེན་པོའི་འགྲམ་དུ་སོང་སྟེ་ཆུར་མཆོངས་ན་ཡང་ཆུས་གཡེངས་ཏེ་མཉེས་པར་ཕྱིར་བྱུང་ངོ་། །བཙན་དུག་ཟོས་ན་ཡང་དུག་གི་མཐུས་གནོད་པར་མ་གྱུར་ནས། ཡང་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བསམས་
སོ། །བདག་གིས་རྒྱལ་པོའི་ཁྲིམས་དང་འགལ་བ་ཞིག་བྱས་ན། རྒྱལ་པོས་བསད་ཀྱང་སྲིད་སྙམ་བསམས་ནས། རྒྱལ་པོའི་བཙུན་མོ་དང་སླས་རྣམས་ཕོ་བྲང་གི་ཕྱི་རོལ་ཏུ་བྱུང་སྟེ། སྐྱེད་མོས་
ཚལ་གྱི་རྫིང་དུ་ཁྲུས་བྱེད་དུ་དོང་ནས། དེ་དག་གི་གོས་དང་རྒྱན་བཀྲོལ་ཏེ་ཤིང་ལ་བཞག་གོ །དེ་ལྟར་གོས་དང་རྒྱན་ཤིང་ལ་བཞག་པ་གངྒཱ་དར་དེས་མཐོང་ནས་སྐྱེད་མོས་ཚལ་དུ་ཞུགས་ཏེ། བཙུན་མོ་དེ་དག་
གི་གོས་དང་རྒྱན་ཕང་པས་བཏབ་ནས་སྒོར་བྱུང་བ་དང་། སྒོ་སྲུངས་ཀྱིས་བཟུང་སྟེ་རྒྱལ་པོ་མ་སྐྱེས་དགྲ་ལ་ཕུལ་ལོ། །རྒྱལ་པོས་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་ཐོས་ནས་རབ་ཏུ་ཁྲོས་ཏེ། མདའ་གཞུ་བླངས་ནས་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཉིད་
